T1A01.concept: Part 97 opens with the reasons amateur radio exists: public service and emergency communication, advancing the radio art, building operator and technical skill, a pool of trained people, and international goodwill.
T1A01.hint: Think about why a government would set aside valuable spectrum for hobbyists. What does the public get back from people who experiment and learn?
why: Personal radio for as many citizens as possible describes services like CB or FRS. Amateur radio requires a license and has a different purpose.
Contesting is a popular activity, but it is not one of the purposes listed in the Basis and Purpose.
Improving skills in both the technical side and the operating (communication) side of radio is one of the purposes listed in the rules.
Only the item about advancing technical and communication skills is in the rules. Citizen radio for all and contesting are not listed purposes.

T1A02.concept: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is the US government agency that writes the amateur rules (Part 97), issues the licenses and enforces the rules.
T1A02.hint: Ask yourself who issues your license. The same body that grants it is the one that can enforce the rules and take it away.
why: The ARRL is a private membership association for amateurs. It represents hams and helps with exams, but it has no power to make or enforce law.
Homeland Security is a federal department, but it does not regulate the Amateur Radio Service.
The FCC is the federal agency that makes, administers and enforces the Amateur Radio Service rules in the United States.
Only one of these has legal authority over amateur radio. The ARRL is a private group and Homeland Security does not regulate the service.

T1A03.concept: A phonetic alphabet replaces letters with words (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie) so a call sign is understood through noise. The FCC rules recommend it for voice identification but do not make it mandatory.
T1A03.hint: Notice the difference between a rule that says you must do something and one that only suggests a good practice. Which kind of wording fits here?
why: There is no rule requiring phonetics for emergency messages. They are helpful, but not mandatory.
The rule says using a phonetic alphabet as an aid to correct identification is encouraged when identifying by voice (phone). It is a recommendation.
No rule requires phonetics when talking to stations in other countries, though it is often good practice.
The two choices that say phonetics are required are false, so they cannot all be correct.

T1A04.concept: The FCC works electronically and does not routinely mail paper licenses. You give a valid email address on your application and the FCC sends you a message pointing to your official license record.
T1A04.hint: Think about who actually grants the license, and how a modern government agency that asks for your email address would get in touch.
why: The FCC sends an email with a link to its system, where you can view and download the official copy of your license grant.
The FCC does not notify new licensees by postal mail. Its licensing correspondence is electronic.
Volunteer examiners give the exam and send in the paperwork, but the official notification comes from the agency that grants the license.
Volunteer examiners do not issue licenses, and the official notice does not come by postal mail.

T1A05.concept: A license exists once the FCC records the grant in its Universal Licensing System (ULS), the public online database of licenses. That record, not any piece of paper, is the proof.
T1A05.hint: Paper and messages can come from anyone. Think about what the FCC itself does at the moment it grants a license.
why: The completion certificate (CSCE) only shows you passed the exam. It comes from the examiners, not the FCC, and is not a license.
The NCVEC is the group of volunteer examiner coordinators. It maintains the question pools but does not grant licenses.
The grant is official when it shows in the FCC ULS database. That listing is the proof that the license has been issued.
A passing certificate and an NCVEC email are not proof of an FCC grant, so they cannot all be correct.

T1A06.concept: A beacon is a station that transmits on its own so others can check whether a band is open. Unattended (automatically controlled) beacons are confined to small set slices of spectrum; on HF that slice is in 10 meters.
T1A06.hint: Unattended transmitters are kept in a small, well-known slot so everyone knows where to listen. Ask how many HF bands have such a slot.
why: Automatic beacons are not allowed across the whole Technician part of 10 meters, only in one narrow slice of it.
There is no rule letting beacons go anywhere after registering with the FCC. The rules name specific segments.
The other HF bands have no segment for automatically controlled beacons. On HF the only one is in 10 meters.
The rules allow automatically controlled beacons on HF only in the 10-meter band from 28.200 MHz to 28.300 MHz.

T1A07.concept: Part 97 defines a space station by height alone: an amateur station more than 50 km above the Earth's surface. Satellites and the ham station on the ISS both count.
T1A07.hint: The FCC definition does not care whether there are people aboard or what the station does. It draws a simple line. Think about what that line measures.
why: Part 97 defines only amateur stations. Most satellites orbiting Earth are not amateur stations at all.
Having a crew is not part of the definition. Unmanned amateur satellites are space stations too.
The Part 97 definition is exactly this: an amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface.
A station on the ground that works through satellites is an Earth station. The space station is the one up above.

T1A08.concept: Repeaters in an area need different channels so they do not interfere. Hams organize this themselves: a volunteer frequency coordinator recommends channel pairs. The FCC does not assign them.
T1A08.hint: Amateur radio is largely self-policing. Think about whether channel planning for local repeaters is done by government or by the hams themselves.
why: The FCC does not appoint a spectrum manager to hand out amateur repeater channels. This is not a real FCC role in the amateur rules.
A frequency coordinator is a volunteer person or group, recognized by the local amateurs, that recommends transmit and receive channels to limit interference.
FCC field offices handle enforcement matters. They do not recommend repeater channels.
The ITU divides spectrum among radio services worldwide. It does not pick channels for local repeaters.

T1A09.concept: A frequency coordinator gets its standing from the local ham community. The amateurs in an area whose stations could be repeaters or auxiliary stations are the ones who recognize a coordinator.
T1A09.hint: A coordinator's recommendations only work if the people affected accept them. Who would be affected by repeater channel planning in a region?
why: This is not a real office that selects coordinators. The FCC does not choose frequency coordinators.
This is not how the rules define it. Part 97 leaves the choice to the amateurs in the area, not to a national office.
Part 97 says a coordinator is recognized by the amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations.
FCC field offices do not pick frequency coordinators. The choice belongs to the local amateur community.

T1A10.concept: RACES is an amateur service for civil defense communication during emergencies. To operate in it you need your FCC license and you must be signed up with a civil defense organization.
T1A10.hint: The name of the service mentions civil emergencies. Think about which kind of organization would need to have you on its books.
why: A recommendation from an ARRL official is not required. The ARRL is a private association and RACES is defined in the FCC rules.
ARES is a separate volunteer program run by the ARRL. Membership in it is not a RACES requirement.
The rules require the control operator to be certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in that organization.
A license alone is not enough. RACES also requires enrollment with a civil defense organization.

T1A11.concept: Amateurs share frequencies and nobody owns one. The rules forbid deliberately disrupting other stations. Accidental interference happens, but doing it on purpose is never allowed.
T1A11.hint: Two of these are ordinary, legal activities. Ask which one would harm other people's use of the bands.
why: Talking to other countries on VHF and higher bands is legal. Hams do it by satellite and other means.
Deliberately or maliciously interfering with any radio communication is specifically prohibited by the rules.
Passing messages for other people (third-party traffic) by digital modes is allowed, within the normal third-party rules.
International VHF contacts and digital third-party traffic are both legal, so not everything listed is prohibited.

T1B01.concept: Technicians get a piece of the 10-meter HF band. The lower part, 28.000 to 28.300 MHz, is for CW and data. The part from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz is where they may use voice (phone).
T1B01.hint: In most ham bands the Morse and data area sits at the bottom and voice sits above it. The Technician slice of 10 meters is 500 kHz wide in total.
why: 28.050 to 28.150 MHz is in the lower part of the band, where Technicians may use CW and data but not voice.
28.100 to 28.300 MHz is still in the CW and data part of the Technician segment. Voice is not allowed there.
28.300 to 28.500 MHz is the Technician phone segment on 10 meters, where SSB voice is allowed.
28.500 to 28.600 MHz is above the top of the Technician segment. It needs a General class or higher license.

T1B02.concept: The International Space Station carries an amateur station that uses VHF frequencies. Technicians have full privileges on the VHF bands, so a Technician or higher license is enough, with no extra permission.
T1B02.hint: The contact happens on VHF. Ask which license classes are allowed to transmit on those bands, and whether hams need anyone else's approval to use them.
why: A General license is not needed. Technicians already have full privileges on the VHF bands used.
Any ham with a Technician or higher license may transmit on the VHF frequencies used, so any of them may contact the ISS.
Neither a General license nor NASA approval is required to make an amateur contact with the ISS.
The license class part is right, but no NASA approval is needed. The amateur license is all the permission required.

T1B03.concept: A band's name is roughly its wavelength. Wavelength in meters is about 300 divided by the frequency in MHz. The 6-meter band runs from 50 to 54 MHz.
T1B03.hint: Divide 300 by each frequency in MHz to get a rough wavelength in meters, then check that it truly falls inside the ham band.
why: 300 / 49 is about 6.1 meters, which is close, but 49.00 MHz lies just below the band's 50 MHz lower edge. It is not an amateur frequency.
300 / 52.525 is about 5.7 meters, and 52.525 MHz sits inside the 50 to 54 MHz range of the 6-meter band.
300 / 28.50 is about 10.5 meters. 28.50 MHz is in the 10-meter band.
300 / 222.15 is about 1.35 meters. 222.15 MHz is in the 1.25-meter band.

T1B04.concept: A band's name is roughly its wavelength. Wavelength in meters is about 300 divided by the frequency in MHz. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
T1B04.hint: Divide 300 by the frequency in MHz. The result is the approximate wavelength in meters.
why: 6 meters is around 50 to 54 MHz, much lower in frequency than 146.52 MHz.
20 meters is an HF band near 14 MHz, far below 146.52 MHz.
70 centimeters is a UHF band in the 420 to 450 MHz range, well above 146.52 MHz.
300 / 146.52 is about 2.05 meters. The 2-meter band is 144 to 148 MHz, and 146.52 MHz is inside it.

T1B05.concept: FT8 is a popular weak-signal digital mode. Technicians may send data in their 10-meter segment below 28.300 MHz and have full privileges, including digital modes, on the bands above 50 MHz.
T1B05.hint: Go through the bands one at a time and ask: does a Technician have any data privileges there at all?
why: On 10 meters, Technicians may use data modes from 28.000 to 28.300 MHz, so FT8 is allowed there.
Technicians have full privileges on 6 meters, and digital modes are permitted there.
Technicians have full privileges on 2 meters, and digital modes are permitted there.
Technicians may use digital modes in parts of 10 meters, 6 meters and 2 meters, so all three are true.

T1B06.concept: HF means 3 to 30 MHz. Technicians have small HF privileges: CW only on parts of 80, 40 and 15 meters, and CW, data and voice on part of 10 meters. Voice on HF is limited to that one band.
T1B06.hint: Technicians can touch four HF bands, but on most of them only with Morse code. On how many can they actually talk?
why: Technicians do have some HF voice privileges, in a segment of one band.
Technician phone privileges on HF exist only on 10 meters, from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz.
Technicians may transmit on all four of these bands, but on 80, 40 and 15 meters they are limited to CW. Only 10 meters allows voice.
Technicians have no privileges on 30 meters, and voice is not allowed on that band for anyone.

T1B07.concept: CW is Morse code sent by switching a carrier on and off. On two VHF bands the bottom 100 kHz is set aside for CW alone. No other mode, not even voice or data, may be used in those slices.
T1B07.hint: Think of the two most popular VHF bands, and where in a band Morse-only territory usually sits.
why: The lowest 100 kHz of 6 meters (50.0 to 50.1 MHz) and of 2 meters (144.0 to 144.1 MHz) are limited to CW only.
219 to 220 MHz is set aside for a special kind of digital message forwarding, and the bottom of the 420 MHz band is not CW only.
The 902 MHz band has no CW-only segment at its bottom edge.
Only the 6-meter and 2-meter segments are CW only. The 219, 420 and 902 MHz segments listed are not.

T1B08.concept: Some spectrum is shared between radio services. The primary service has priority. A secondary service may use the spectrum but must not interfere with primary users and must accept interference from them.
T1B08.hint: Secondary means someone else is first in line. Think about what a guest owes the main user of a shared space.
why: Where amateurs are secondary, other radio services may be operating there, and amateurs must not cause them harmful interference.
Secondary status is about other radio services having priority, not about foreign amateurs coming before US amateurs.
Secondary status does not ban international contacts. It only concerns priority between radio services.
Secondary status does not ban digital modes. It only concerns priority between radio services.

T1B09.concept: Your signal is not a single point on the dial. It has width, and your radio's frequency reading is never perfect. All of your signal must stay inside the band, so you leave a margin at the edge.
T1B09.hint: Picture your signal as a wide stripe rather than a thin line, drawn by a pen that is not perfectly steady or perfectly placed.
why: The frequency display can be slightly off, so the true frequency may be a little different from what the dial shows.
A modulated signal spreads to the sides of the dial frequency. Those sidebands must stay inside the band too.
A transmitter's frequency can slowly shift as it warms up, which could carry a signal on the edge out of the band.
Display error, sideband width and drift are all real reasons to keep away from the band edge, so all three are true.

T1B10.concept: SSB (single sideband) is a narrow voice mode, popular for long-distance work. Every amateur band above 50 MHz has some part where phone is allowed, so SSB voice can be used on each of them.
T1B10.hint: Technicians have full privileges on these bands. Ask whether any of them has no voice segment at all.
why: Above 50 MHz there are no sub-bands reserved for General class and higher. Technicians have full privileges there.
SSB is mostly used directly between stations. Repeaters normally use FM, and SSB is not limited to them.
Each amateur band above 50 MHz has at least one segment where phone, including SSB, is allowed.
There is no rule tying SSB to a 25 watt limit. Where SSB may be used is set by band segments, not by power.

T1B11.concept: Peak envelope power (PEP) is the transmitter's output power at the highest peaks of the signal. Technicians have a reduced power limit in their HF segments, well below the general amateur maximum.
T1B11.hint: Technicians are held well below the full amateur maximum on HF. Do not confuse the legal limit with what typical radios happen to put out.
why: Technicians are limited to 200 watts PEP output in their HF band segments.
100 watts is the output of many HF radios, but it is not the legal limit for Technicians on HF.
50 watts is a common power for VHF mobile radios. It is not the Technician HF limit.
10 watts is not the Technician HF limit. The rule allows much more.

T1B12.concept: Peak envelope power (PEP) is output power at the signal's highest peaks. Above 30 MHz, Technicians have the same power limit as every other license class: the full amateur maximum, with a few exceptions.
T1B12.hint: Above 30 MHz, Technicians have full privileges. Their power limit there matches what an Amateur Extra operator gets.
why: 50 watts is a typical VHF mobile radio power. The legal limit is far higher.
100 watts is a common radio output level, not the legal limit above 30 MHz.
500 watts is not the general limit above 30 MHz. The rule allows more.
The general amateur limit of 1500 watts PEP output applies to Technicians above 30 MHz, apart from some specific restrictions.

T1C01.concept: Today there are three license classes you can earn, each with its own exam and more privileges than the last. Older classes still exist for people who hold them, but no new ones are issued.
T1C01.hint: Count the exams you can take today. Each one leads to exactly one license class.
why: Novice licenses are no longer issued. People who hold one may keep renewing it, but nobody new can get one.
Technician Plus is an old class that is no longer issued.
Novice, Technician Plus and Advanced are all old classes that are no longer issued to new licensees.
New licenses are issued only for these three classes: Technician, General and Amateur Extra.

T1C02.concept: A vanity call sign is one you choose yourself instead of the one assigned in sequence. Anyone holding an amateur license may apply, though the formats you may pick from depend on your license class.
T1C02.hint: Think about whether the FCC limits who may apply at all, or only limits which call signs each applicant may choose.
why: A General or higher license is not required. Technicians may apply for a vanity call sign too.
Amateur Extra licensees can choose from more formats, but they are not the only ones who may apply.
There is no rule requiring ten years as a licensee before choosing a call sign.
Any licensed amateur may request a vanity call sign, choosing from the formats open to their license class.

T1C03.concept: Contacts with hams in other countries must stay within what amateur radio is for: technical talk, operating, and friendly personal conversation. Business and broadcast-style content are out.
T1C03.hint: Think about what two hams in different countries normally chat about, and what amateur radio is never meant to be used for.
why: International contacts are limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and remarks of a personal character.
Business communications are not allowed on amateur radio, so anything incidental to conducting business does not fit.
Contest exchanges are allowed, but so are ordinary conversations. International contacts are not limited to contests.
Amateurs may not broadcast, so the content of an international broadcast station is not the standard.

T1C04.concept: You must keep a working email address on file with the FCC, because that is how it contacts you. If its messages cannot reach you, your license itself can be put at risk.
T1C04.hint: The FCC treats a correct contact address as a condition of holding the license. Think about what an agency can do to a license, rather than to a person.
why: The rule does not describe a fine. It describes action against the license itself.
The rule says the station license may be revoked or the operator license suspended if FCC correspondence is undeliverable.
Losing access to your record in the FCC system is not the consequence the rule describes.
There is such a requirement. You must give the FCC a valid email address and keep it current.

T1C05.concept: Call signs are sorted into groups by shape. Group D is the longest: two letters, one digit, then three letters (a 2x3 call). Technicians can be given these. The shortest formats are in the Amateur Extra group.
T1C05.hint: Count the letters before and after the digit in each call sign. Shorter call signs are scarcer, so think about who would get those.
why: KF1XXX has two letters, a digit and three letters. That 2x3 shape is the Group D format.
KA1X has two letters, a digit and one letter. That short 2x1 shape is not Group D. It is set aside for Amateur Extra.
W1XX has one letter, a digit and two letters. That short 1x2 shape is not Group D. It is set aside for Amateur Extra.
Only the two-letter, digit, three-letter call sign fits Group D. The two shorter ones do not.

T1C06.concept: Your FCC license also covers US-documented or registered ships and aircraft when they are in international waters or airspace. The person in command has the final say on any radio used aboard.
T1C06.hint: A ship at sea carries the law of its flag with it. Think about whose rules apply, and whose consent you would need on board.
why: Amateur operation is not banned in international waters. Hams operate from ships at sea, known as maritime mobile.
Operation at sea is not limited to emergencies. Normal amateur contacts are allowed.
No special FCC authorization is needed. Your regular license already covers it.
On a vessel documented or registered in the US, your FCC license applies, and you need the permission of the ship's master.

T1C07.concept: You cannot renew a license years early. The FCC accepts a renewal application only within a set window shortly before the expiration date.
T1C07.hint: The FCC wants renewals filed close to the expiration date, but it leaves you a reasonable margin to get it done.
why: 30 days is not the figure. The renewal window opens earlier than that.
A renewal may be filed starting 90 days before the license expires.
6 months is too early. The FCC will not take a renewal that far ahead of expiration.
1 year is too early. The FCC will not take a renewal that far ahead of expiration.

T1C08.concept: An amateur license does not last forever, but it lasts a long time. It is granted for a fixed term and can be renewed again and again without retaking the exam.
T1C08.hint: The term is a round number of years. It is long enough that people often forget to renew.
why: Five years is not the amateur license term.
Eight years is not the amateur license term.
An FCC amateur license is normally granted for a term of ten years, and then it can be renewed.
Amateur licenses are not issued for life. They must be renewed at the end of each term.

T1C09.concept: If your license expires you do not lose it at once. There is a grace period during which you can still renew without taking the exam again. You may not transmit until the renewal is granted.
T1C09.hint: Do not confuse the grace period with the length of the license term. The grace period is much the shorter of the two.
why: The grace period is two years from the expiration date. Within it you can renew without retesting.
Three years is not the grace period.
Five years is not the grace period.
Ten years is the length of a license term, not the grace period after it expires.

T1C10.concept: Passing the exam does not put you on the air. You may transmit once the FCC has actually granted the license, and the sign of that is your call sign appearing in the FCC's online license database.
T1C10.hint: Ask which event is the FCC itself saying yes. Until then you have no call sign to identify with.
why: For a first license, the completion certificate only shows you passed. You have no call sign yet, so you cannot transmit.
The ARRL is a private association. A listing on its website is not the official record of an FCC grant.
Once the grant shows in the FCC license database, the license is in effect and you may transmit.
You do not need to wait for any document. The FCC works electronically, and the grant in its database is what counts.

T1C11.concept: An expired license gives no operating privileges. The grace period only protects your right to renew without retesting. It does not keep you on the air.
T1C11.hint: Separate two things: the right to get the license back easily, and the right to transmit. Which one does a grace period protect?
why: The grace period is two years, but it is for renewing, not for operating. Transmitting during it is not allowed.
Applying is not enough. You have no privileges until the FCC actually grants the renewal.
There is no one-year allowance to keep transmitting after a license expires.
With an expired license you may not transmit. You must wait until the renewal shows as granted.

T1D01.concept: The ITU is the United Nations agency that coordinates radio worldwide. A country's government can tell the ITU it objects to amateur contacts with its stations, and US hams must then respect that.
T1D01.hint: This is a matter between governments. Which international body deals with radio matters at the level of national administrations?
why: If a country's government has formally told the ITU that it objects, US amateurs may not exchange communications with that country's stations.
The ARRL is a private US association. Foreign governments do not register objections with it.
The IARU is an international federation of amateur radio societies. It has no power to ban countries.
The ARRL is a private US association and cannot ban any country from communicating.

T1D02.concept: Amateur radio is meant for two-way contacts between hams. A few one-way transmissions are allowed, such as beacons, code practice and bulletins for hams, but not programs aimed at the general public.
T1D02.hint: Three of these are aimed at other hams or at controlling equipment. One is aimed at a completely different audience.
why: Announcements about ham radio events are information bulletins of interest to amateurs, which are an allowed one-way transmission.
Broadcasting means transmitting for the general public to receive. Amateurs are prohibited from doing it.
One-way transmissions to help people learn Morse code are specifically allowed.
Telecommand (sending control signals) and telemetry (sending back measurements) are allowed one-way transmissions.

T1D03.concept: Amateur transmissions must be open: anyone listening should be able to work out what is said. The one exception is control signals, where secrecy keeps strangers from taking over a satellite or model craft.
T1D03.hint: Think about a case where letting anyone copy and resend your signal could cause real trouble for a piece of equipment.
why: Contests and remote stations get no exception. Their messages must not be hidden.
Publicly documented digital codes are allowed because they do not hide meaning. They are not an exception for obscured messages.
Commands sent to control a space station or a radio-controlled model craft may be encoded to hide their meaning.
Never goes too far. The rules make an exception for control commands to space stations and model craft.

T1D04.concept: Music is banned on amateur radio so the bands are not used for entertainment. The one exception is music that happens to be in space communications a ham is authorized to relay.
T1D04.hint: The exception is not about how long, how clean or how high in frequency. It is about music that just happens to be in something else being relayed.
why: Music is allowed only when it is incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications.
Signal cleanliness has nothing to do with it. Music is banned regardless of spurious emissions.
There is no time allowance for music. Short clips are just as prohibited.
There is no frequency above which music becomes legal on amateur radio.

T1D05.concept: Hams may not do business over the air, but there is a small allowance: you may occasionally mention ham gear you have for sale or trade, as long as it is not a regular business activity.
T1D05.hint: Picture the difference between a hobbyist mentioning a spare radio now and then and a dealer advertising every week.
why: Never is too strict. The rules allow occasional notices about amateur equipment.
This is not the condition in the rules. The allowance is for amateur radio gear offered occasionally, not on a regular basis.
Profit is not the test. The test is the kind of equipment and whether it is done regularly.
You may tell other hams about amateur radio equipment for sale or trade if you do not do so on a regular basis.

T1D06.concept: Amateur frequencies are open for anyone to hear, including children. The rules flatly forbid obscene or indecent words, without spelling out a list.
T1D06.hint: Ask whether the rule is written as a blanket statement or as a detailed list that someone must maintain.
why: The FCC does not keep a list of banned words for amateur radio. The rule is a general prohibition.
The rules prohibit transmitting obscene or indecent words or language, with no exceptions.
The ITU does not keep a list of banned words for amateur frequencies.
There is a prohibition. Obscene or indecent language is not allowed on amateur radio.

T1D07.concept: An auxiliary station sends point-to-point signals within a system of cooperating ham stations. The classic use is a radio link carrying audio or control signals between the parts of a repeater system.
T1D07.hint: In the rules, auxiliary does not mean spare. Think of a behind-the-scenes link that joins the pieces of a larger system.
why: A one-way link from a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter is a point-to-point link inside a system, which is what an auxiliary station is.
A backup radio is just a spare piece of equipment. Auxiliary has a specific meaning in the rules that is not about spares.
MARS is a separate military-sponsored program. This is not what Part 97 means by an auxiliary station.
A second station in a contest setup is simply another station. It is not what the rules call an auxiliary station.

T1D08.concept: Hams may not be paid to operate, which keeps amateur radio non-commercial. A narrow exception lets teachers be paid their normal salary while using a station as part of teaching a class.
T1D08.hint: Look for the situation where the pay is for a different job and the radio use is just part of doing that job for learners.
why: Communications that help an employer sell equipment are business use, which is prohibited.
A teacher at an educational institution may be paid while operating when the communication is incidental to classroom instruction.
Gathering information for a broadcast station is not an exception that allows paid operation.
Only the classroom instruction case is allowed. The employer sales and broadcast station cases are not.

T1D09.concept: Amateur radio is not a tool for broadcasters or news media. The only exception is a real emergency, where life or property is at immediate risk and nothing else is available.
T1D09.hint: Many amateur rules bend in one situation only. Think about what that situation usually is.
why: This is allowed only when the communications directly concern the immediate safety of human life or protection of property and no other means exists.
There is no exception for broadcasting to or from a spacecraft. This is not what the rule describes.
There is no exception for non-commercial programming or for any particular network.
Never is too strict. The rules allow it where life or property is in immediate danger.

T1D10.concept: The key to the definition is the intended audience. A ham transmission is aimed at other hams. Broadcasting is aimed at everyone, like an AM or FM radio station.
T1D10.hint: Think about who an FM music station is trying to reach, compared with who you are trying to reach when you call another ham.
why: Two-way contacts between amateur stations are normal amateur operation, the opposite of broadcasting.
Not every transmission is broadcasting. The definition depends on who the transmission is meant for.
Messages meant only for amateurs, such as bulletins for hams, are not broadcasting.
The FCC defines broadcasting as transmissions intended to be received by the general public.

T1D11.concept: Normally every station must identify with its call sign. The control signals for radio-controlled models are excused, because the transmitter itself carries a label showing whose station it is.
T1D11.hint: Imagine a signal made only of control pulses, with no practical way to add a call sign. What kind of amateur activity works like that?
why: Brief test transmissions still need identification. Short does not mean exempt.
An unmodulated carrier still needs to be identified. There is no exemption for it.
There is no low-power level below which identification can be skipped.
Signals sent to control a model craft do not need on-air identification under the telecommand rules for model craft.

T1D12.concept: A test transmission is still a transmission. The normal identification rule applies, so anyone hearing the signal can tell which station is sending it.
T1D12.hint: Ask which rule applies to nearly everything a ham transmits, no matter how short or simple.
why: You must identify your station with your call sign, even when you are only testing.
There is no rule limiting test transmissions to night hours.
You do not need to tell the FCC before making test transmissions.
Only identifying is required. The time-of-day limit and FCC notice are not real requirements.

T1E01.concept: Every amateur transmission has a control operator, the licensed person responsible for it. Under automatic control that person need not be at the controls, but the station still has one.
T1E01.hint: Separate two ideas: a control operator being present at the controls, and a control operator existing at all.
why: Under automatic control no one has to be at the control point, but the repeater still has a control operator who is responsible for it.
The licensed amateur using the station is then the control operator, so the station is not without one.
An auxiliary station still has a control operator, even when it runs automatically.
An amateur station may never transmit without a control operator. Someone is always responsible.

T1E02.concept: Working a satellite is ordinary operating on an ordinary ham frequency. The uplink is the frequency you transmit on toward the satellite. If your license covers that frequency, you may use it.
T1E02.hint: The satellite does not check your license. Your privileges are decided by the frequency your own transmitter is on.
why: An Amateur Extra license is not required. Many satellites use bands open to Technicians.
There is no such thing as a satellite operator certification, and a General license is not required.
AMSAT is a private organization for amateur satellites. Membership is not a legal requirement, and neither is an Extra license.
Anyone whose license lets them transmit on the satellite's uplink frequency may be the control operator.

T1E03.concept: The station licensee is the person whose license covers the station. That person decides who is allowed to act as control operator, which may be themselves or another licensed ham.
T1E03.hint: Think about whose equipment and whose call sign are on the line. That person gets to decide who runs it.
why: The station licensee designates the control operator. If nobody else is named, the licensee is presumed to be the control operator.
The FCC issues licenses but does not pick who operates a given station.
A frequency coordinator recommends repeater channels. It has no say over who operates a station.
Another licensed ham cannot simply appoint a control operator for someone else's station.

T1E04.concept: Privileges follow the person in charge of the transmission, not the equipment or its owner. Whoever is the control operator at that moment sets the limits by the class of license they hold.
T1E04.hint: Picture a higher-class ham and a lower-class ham sharing one radio. The allowed frequencies change depending on who is in charge.
why: A frequency coordinator only recommends repeater channels. It does not set anyone's privileges.
A license grant does not list frequencies. Privileges come from the license class as set out in the rules.
Someone merely being on the premises does not count. Only the person acting as control operator matters.
The station may transmit only where the control operator's license class allows.

T1E05.concept: The control point is defined by what happens there, not by where the hardware sits. It is wherever the responsible person does the job of controlling the station.
T1E05.hint: The radio could be on a hilltop while the person running it sits at home. Which spot matters for control?
why: The antenna can be far from where the station is controlled. Its location is not the control point.
The transmitter can be remote from the person running it. Its location is not the control point.
The control point is the location at which the control operator function is performed.
A mailing address is only for correspondence. It has nothing to do with controlling the station.

T1E06.concept: A control operator may only use the frequencies their own license class allows. Whose station it is, and who else is in the room, does not change that.
T1E06.hint: Privileges belong to the person acting as control operator. Can someone else's license raise yours?
why: A Technician can never be the control operator in an Amateur Extra segment, since that is outside Technician privileges.
Being designated by an Extra does not help. The control operator's own license class sets the limits.
Contest teams get no exception. Each control operator stays within their own privileges.
The trustee's license class does not extend the privileges of other people acting as control operator.

T1E07.concept: Responsibility is shared when you let someone else operate your station. The person running it must follow the rules, and the person whose station it is remains answerable too.
T1E07.hint: Lending your station to another ham does not hand off all your responsibility. But the person at the controls is not off the hook either.
why: Simply being present does not make a ham responsible for the station's operation.
The licensee is responsible, but not alone. The person actually controlling the station is responsible too.
The control operator is responsible, but not alone. The station licensee is responsible too.
Both the control operator and the station licensee are responsible for the proper operation of the station.

T1E08.concept: There are three kinds of control. Local: you are at the radio. Remote: you control it from elsewhere over a link. Automatic: devices and procedures run it with no control operator at the control point.
T1E08.hint: Look for a station that keeps working on its own at 3 a.m. with nobody watching it.
why: A repeater retransmits signals on its own with no control operator at the control point. That is automatic control.
Controlling a station over the internet is remote control, because a person is actively running it from a distance.
A computer sending CW for you is just a tool. You are still at the controls, so the station is under your direct control.
A device that sends your call sign is a convenience. It does not change who is controlling the station.

T1E09.concept: Remote control means running a station from somewhere else through a control link. The rules do not restrict it to particular kinds of station.
T1E09.hint: Ask whether the rules single out any kind of station for this, or leave it open.
why: Remote control is not limited to repeaters.
Automatic control and remote control are different things. A station does not have to be automatic to be remotely controlled.
Remote control is not limited to digital stations. Voice stations can be run remotely too.
The rules allow any amateur station to be remotely controlled.

T1E10.concept: Remote control means the control operator runs the station indirectly, from a distance, through a control link. The operator is still actively in charge, just not sitting at the radio.
T1E10.hint: The key is the operator's own station being somewhere other than where the operator is. What could link the two?
why: A software defined radio is a type of radio design. It says nothing about where the operator is.
Running your station through an internet link from another place is remote control: you control it indirectly through a control link.
Controlling a model craft is telecommand of a model. It is not the Part 97 meaning of remote control of an amateur station.
Earth-Moon-Earth is bouncing signals off the Moon. It is a way signals travel, not a way to control a station.

T1E11.concept: The control operator is the licensed ham in charge of a station's transmissions at a given moment. The station licensee names that person, and it can be the licensee or someone else.
T1E11.hint: Focus on two things in the definition: how the person gets the role, and what the person is answerable for.
why: The person talking may be an unlicensed guest. The control operator is the licensed ham supervising, not always the one speaking.
The licensee is often the control operator, but the role can be given to another licensed ham.
The FCC database does not list control operators. The role is assigned by the station licensee.
A control operator is an amateur operator designated by the station licensee to be responsible for the transmissions and for following FCC rules.

T1F01.concept: Holding a license means accepting FCC oversight. An FCC representative may ask to see your station and its records, and you must allow it when asked.
T1F01.hint: Ask whether the rule gives the licensee any waiting period or paperwork to rely on before an inspection.
why: There is no ten-day waiting period in the rule.
The station and its records must be made available at any time an FCC representative asks.
The rule does not require written notice first. A request from an FCC representative is enough.
A warrant is not required by the rule. A request from an FCC representative is enough.

T1F02.concept: A tactical call sign is a descriptive name like Race Headquarters, used so people know who does what at an event. It is handy, but it does not replace your legal identification.
T1F02.hint: A tactical name adds to your FCC call sign rather than replacing it. So how often do the normal rules say to identify?
why: A tactical call is not a legal identification. Your FCC call sign is still required.
Once an hour is not often enough. The normal identification timing applies.
The normal rule still applies: give your FCC call sign at least every 10 minutes during the communication and at its end.
Identifying after every single transmission is more than the rules require.

T1F03.concept: Station identification lets anyone listening know who is transmitting. The rule sets a maximum time between identifications during a contact, plus one more when the contact finishes.
T1F03.hint: The rule has two parts: a timer that runs during the conversation, and one fixed moment in the contact. It is not the moment most people guess.
why: Identifying at the start is common practice, but the rules do not require it. They require it at the end.
You do not need to identify in every transmission. That is more than the rules require.
The timing is close, but 15 minutes is too long. The interval is shorter.
You must send your call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it.

T1F04.concept: You may hold a conversation in any language, but when you identify by voice the call sign must be given in one specific language, so that the FCC and other stations can understand it.
T1F04.hint: Think about which language the US regulator would need the call sign spoken in so its own monitors can understand it.
why: The rule does not refer to United Nations languages. It names a single language.
The rule does not refer to ITU languages. It names a single language.
When identifying by phone, the call sign must be given in English.
French and Spanish are not accepted for identification. Only one language is.

T1F05.concept: A station using voice (phone) has a choice of how to identify: it may say its call sign, or send it in Morse code (CW). Many repeaters identify in Morse.
T1F05.hint: Think about how a repeater that carries voice usually announces its own call sign.
why: RPT is not an indicator the rules require a phone station to add.
A station transmitting phone may identify by voice or by CW. Either method satisfies the rule.
The letter R is not an indicator the rules require a phone station to add.
Voice is not the only allowed method. Identifying in CW is also acceptable.

T1F06.concept: A self-assigned indicator is something you add to your call sign, such as the call district you are visiting. On voice, the separator between call sign and indicator can be said in several ways.
T1F06.hint: The written symbol is a single mark, /. Think about how many different spoken words mean that same mark.
why: Stroke is an accepted word for the separator between the call sign and the indicator.
Slant is an accepted word for the separator between the call sign and the indicator.
Slash is an accepted word for the separator between the call sign and the indicator.
Stroke, slant and slash all name the same separator and all are acceptable, so all three are true.

T1F07.concept: A third party is someone other than the two control operators, such as an unlicensed friend talking over your radio. For contacts abroad, the two governments must have agreed to allow it.
T1F07.hint: This is an international matter. Think about what would need to exist between the two governments involved.
why: Citizenship is not the test. The rule is about the country at the other end of the contact.
Third-party communications with a foreign station are allowed only if that country has a third-party agreement with the United States.
This is not the special restriction the rule places on a non-licensed person speaking to a foreign station.
Only the third-party agreement requirement applies. The citizenship item is false, so they are not all correct.

T1F08.concept: In a normal contact there are two parties: the two control operators. A third party is anyone else whose message is being passed, such as a friend sending birthday greetings by ham radio.
T1F08.hint: Count the people, not the radios. Who is the extra person in the conversation?
why: A message sent from one control operator to another on behalf of another person is the Part 97 definition of third-party communications.
Three stations talking together is just a three-way contact. Every operator there is a party to it.
Using a station licensed to someone else is ordinary operation by a designated control operator.
There is no such temporary authorization for unlicensed people to transmit on their own.

T1F09.concept: Some stations listen on one frequency and send out what they hear on another at the same moment. Placed up high, they let small handheld radios reach across a wide area.
T1F09.hint: Think about a station that hears you on one frequency and passes your signal along on another, without any delay.
why: A beacon sends its own signal so people can study propagation. It does not retransmit anyone else.
Remote control describes how a station is controlled from a distance. It is not a type of station that relays signals.
A repeater simultaneously retransmits another amateur station's signal on a different channel or channels.
Message forwarding systems store and pass along messages. They do not retransmit signals at the same instant.

T1F10.concept: A repeater sends out whatever it hears, straight away, with no one able to screen it first. So responsibility for what is said rests with the person who said it.
T1F10.hint: Ask who actually decided what was transmitted. A machine that simply passes signals along made no choice.
why: The control operator of the station that originated the communication is accountable for the violation.
The repeater's control operator is not held accountable for content retransmitted inadvertently.
The repeater's owner did not originate the communication and is not held accountable for an inadvertent retransmission.
Accountability is not shared with the repeater owner. It rests with the originating station.

T1F11.concept: A club can hold its own station license and call sign. To qualify it has to be a real group with a minimum number of people, and it names a licensed trustee who holds the license for it.
T1F11.hint: Ask what makes a group a real club in the FCC's eyes, as opposed to extras that a private organization or a license class might add.
why: The trustee must be a licensed amateur, but an Amateur Extra license is not required.
A club must have at least four members to be granted a club station license.
A club does not need to be registered with the ARRL. The ARRL is a private association.
Only the four-member requirement is real. The Extra trustee and ARRL registration items are false.

T2A01.concept: A repeater listens on one frequency and retransmits on another. The gap between the two is the offset, and each band has a customary size. On 2 meters the usual gap is 600 kHz, up or down.
T2A01.hint: The 2-meter band is only 4 MHz wide, so the gap between a repeater's two frequencies has to be fairly small. Think in kilohertz.
why: A 5 MHz gap is the usual offset on the 70-centimeter band. It would not even fit inside the 4 MHz wide 2-meter band.
On 2 meters, repeaters normally listen 600 kHz above or below the frequency they transmit on.
500 kHz is close, but it is not the customary 2-meter offset. The standard figure on this band is 600 kHz.
1 MHz is not the customary 2-meter offset. The standard gap on this band is smaller, at 600 kHz.

T2A02.concept: A calling frequency is an agreed meeting spot where stations listen for and make first contact. For FM simplex (direct, no repeater) on 2 meters, that spot is 146.520 MHz.
T2A02.hint: First rule out anything outside the 2-meter band, which runs from 144 to 148 MHz. Then pick the one hams treat as the FM meeting spot.
why: 146.520 MHz is the nationally agreed spot on 2 meters where FM stations call each other directly, without a repeater.
145.000 MHz is inside the 2-meter band, but it is not the national FM simplex calling frequency.
432.100 MHz is in the 70-centimeter band, not 2 meters. It is used there as a calling frequency for weak-signal work.
446.000 MHz is the FM simplex calling frequency for the 70-centimeter band, not for 2 meters.

T2A03.concept: A repeater's offset is the gap between the frequency it listens on and the one it transmits on. The 70-centimeter band is much wider than 2 meters, so its customary offset is much bigger: 5 MHz.
T2A03.hint: The 70-centimeter band runs from 420 to 450 MHz, far wider than 2 meters. Ask how that extra room might change the customary gap.
why: On 70 centimeters, repeaters normally listen 5 MHz above or below the frequency they transmit on.
600 kHz is the usual offset on the 2-meter band, not on 70 centimeters.
500 kHz is not the customary offset on 70 centimeters. The standard gap on this band is 5 MHz.
1 MHz is not the customary offset on 70 centimeters. The standard gap on this band is 5 MHz.

T2A04.concept: Calling a known station on a repeater works like calling a friend across a room: say their name first so they notice, then say who is calling. No special words are needed.
T2A04.hint: Think about how you would get one particular friend's attention in a busy room, and what you would say right after.
why: Saying break is for cutting into a conversation already under way, often for urgent traffic. It is not how you start a normal call.
Their call sign first gets their attention, and your call sign tells them who is calling and identifies your station.
CQ means calling any station. It makes no sense when you want one particular station, and CQ is not normally used on repeaters.
You do not have to wait for them to call CQ. If you know the call sign you can simply call that station directly.

T2A05.concept: The usual order in any call is the other station's call sign first, then your own. Theirs shows who you are talking to; yours shows who is answering.
T2A05.hint: Think about what the calling station needs to hear first to know the reply is meant for it, and what it needs to learn next.
why: Repeating CQ would mean you are also calling any station. To answer, you address the station that called.
This has the two call signs in the reverse of the customary order. The station being called is named first.
Their call sign first shows you are answering them, and your call sign after it tells them who you are.
A signal report comes later, once contact is made. And without their call sign, nobody knows who you are answering.

T2A06.concept: CQ is the general invitation: any station that hears it may answer. On simplex you say CQ a few times, give your call sign, then stop and listen so someone has a chance to reply.
T2A06.hint: You want anyone at all to answer. Think about what people tuning across the band need to hear to notice you, and what you must do to hear a reply.
why: Giving your call sign and saying you are listening is repeater style. Said once on simplex it is too short to be noticed by people tuning by.
QTC is a Q signal about having messages to pass. It is not an invitation for any station to call you.
An unmodulated carrier is a signal with no voice on it. Ten seconds of it tells listeners nothing and just occupies the frequency.
A few CQs give listeners time to tune you in, your call sign says who is calling, and the pause lets them answer.

T2A07.concept: A repeater cannot listen and transmit on one frequency at once, so it uses two. The offset is the gap between them. Your radio shifts its transmit frequency by that gap when you key up.
T2A07.hint: Offset means being shifted away from something by a set amount. Ask what a repeater has two of.
why: The repeater listens on one frequency and transmits on another. The offset is the size of the gap between the two.
Offset is about frequency, not time. A time delay is not what the term means.
The squelch tail is the short burst of noise heard when a signal drops. Delays for handling it are not called the offset.
Offset has nothing to do with money. There is no fee by that name.

T2A08.concept: CQ is a general call. It tells everyone listening that you would like a contact with whoever wants to answer.
T2A08.hint: Picture someone walking into a room and asking if anybody would like to chat. Who is that question aimed at?
why: CQ is not short for Contest QSO. It is used in contests, but also in everyday operating.
CQ does not stand for Communication Quality and has nothing to do with how clear the audio is.
This is the opposite idea. CQ invites anyone to reply, not one named station only.
CQ is the general call inviting any station that hears it to answer.

T2A09.concept: Repeaters are shared, channelised and often monitored, so long calls are not needed. A station simply announces that it is there and available, and anyone who wants to talk answers.
T2A09.hint: On a repeater people are already tuned to the channel. A short announcement of who is there and available is enough.
why: CQ is not customary on repeaters, and you identify with your own call sign, not the repeater's.
Giving your call sign and saying you are listening tells everyone on the repeater who is there and that you welcome a call.
Saying the repeater's call sign and then yours looks like calling the repeater itself. It does not invite a contact.
QSY means changing frequency. It does not say you are looking for a contact.

T2A10.concept: FCC rules set which frequencies and modes are legal. A band plan goes further: it is a voluntary agreement among hams about where each kind of activity goes, so they stay out of each other's way.
T2A10.hint: FCC rules are law. Ask what hams themselves might agree on, on top of the law, so that different activities stay out of each other's way.
why: A band plan is a voluntary guide to which parts of a band are used for which modes and activities, such as repeaters, simplex or weak-signal work.
A band plan divides up frequencies by use. It is not a timetable of when people operate.
A list of net frequencies is just a directory. A band plan covers how the whole band is shared among all activities.
A band plan is a widely shared guideline for all amateurs, not something one club draws up for itself.

T2A11.concept: Simplex means both stations transmit and receive on one single frequency, taking turns. It is direct radio-to-radio contact, with no repeater shifting the signal to another frequency.
T2A11.hint: Each of these terms describes how frequencies or signals are arranged. Count how many frequencies the station in the question uses.
why: Full duplex means transmitting and receiving at the same moment, which needs two different frequencies, like a telephone call.
Diplex refers to sharing one antenna or feed line between two bands. It is not about using a single frequency.
Simplex is the term for sending and receiving on the same frequency, with stations taking turns.
Multiplex means combining several signals onto one channel. It is not the term for same-frequency operation.

T2B01.concept: Normally you hear a repeater on its output and transmit on its input. The reverse function swaps the two, so you hear what the repeater hears. It shows if you can hear the other station directly.
T2B01.hint: Reverse swaps your two repeater frequencies. Work out which one you normally transmit on, because that is where you will now be listening.
why: Lowering power is done with the radio's power setting. The reverse function swaps frequencies and leaves power alone.
Reverse does not raise power. It only swaps the frequencies you transmit and listen on.
Reverse lets you hear the frequency stations transmit on to reach the repeater, so you can tell if you hear them directly.
You already listen on the repeater's output in normal operation. No special function is needed for that.

T2B02.concept: CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System) adds a steady, very low tone under your voice. A receiver set for that tone stays quiet until it hears it, so only intended signals get through.
T2B02.hint: The tone is too low to hear and it runs the whole time you talk. Look for the name built from those ideas.
why: Carrier squelch opens the receiver for any signal that is strong enough. It does not use a tone at all.
A tone burst is a short audible tone sent at the start of a transmission, not a continuous one hidden under the voice.
DTMF tones are the audible keypad tones, as on a telephone. They are not sub-audible and not sent along with speech.
CTCSS is the continuous low tone, below normal voice audio, that tells a receiver to open its squelch.

T2B03.concept: Linked repeaters are joined together, by radio or the internet, so they act as one big system. A signal that reaches any one of them comes out of all of them, covering a much larger area.
T2B03.hint: Linked means joined together. Think about what should happen at the far end of the chain when you talk into the near end.
why: In a linked network, what one repeater receives is retransmitted by every repeater in the network, extending coverage.
One repeater with several receivers is still a single repeater. It improves how well it hears, but it is not a network.
Sharing a control operator is about who is responsible. It does not connect the repeaters' signals together.
APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) sends position and short data. It is not what defines a linked repeater network.

T2B04.concept: Hearing a repeater only proves your receiver is right. To get in, your transmitter must hit its input frequency (the right offset) and carry whatever tone or code the repeater demands.
T2B04.hint: Hearing is one thing and being heard is another. List every setting that affects only your transmitted signal.
why: With the wrong offset you transmit on a frequency the repeater is not listening to, so it never hears you.
CTCSS is a low tone sent under your voice. If the repeater requires one and yours is wrong, it ignores your signal.
DCS (Digital Coded Squelch) is a digital code used like a tone. A wrong code keeps the repeater from opening for you.
A wrong offset, a wrong CTCSS tone or a wrong DCS code would each keep you out, so all three are possible reasons.

T2B05.concept: In FM, a louder voice swings the signal's frequency further. That swing is called deviation. Too much of it pushes the signal outside what the receiver accepts, and the audio cuts out.
T2B05.hint: In FM, the loudness of your voice controls how far the signal swings. Ask what happens when it swings too far, and what would cause that.
why: An inverted offset would put you on the wrong frequency altogether. You would not be heard at all, not just lose the peaks.
Deviation is how far FM audio swings the frequency. Too little of it makes you sound quiet, it does not make peaks drop out.
A loud voice causes too much deviation. On peaks the signal swings beyond what the receiver passes, and the audio drops out.
High power makes the signal stronger. It does not change how far your voice swings the frequency.

T2B06.concept: DTMF stands for Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency. Each key on the keypad sends two audio tones at once, the same system as a touch-tone telephone. Repeaters use it for control commands.
T2B06.hint: Picture a keypad laid out in rows and columns. Each key press sends one tone for its row and one for its column, both at once.
why: DTMF sends a pair of audio tones together for each key pressed. The 'dual-tone' in its name says exactly that.
CTCSS uses a single continuous low tone under the voice, not two tones at once.
GMRS is the General Mobile Radio Service, a separate radio service. It is not a type of signaling.
D-STAR is a digital voice and data system for amateur radio. It is not a two-tone signaling method.

T2B07.concept: A talkgroup is a labelled group on a digital voice system. Each has a number. Your radio only passes traffic for the groups it is programmed with, so joining is a matter of radio setup.
T2B07.hint: Joining is something you do at your own radio, not by asking permission. Think about what identifies one group among many.
why: A frequency coordinator recommends repeater frequencies to avoid interference. They do not handle talkgroup membership.
Signing up with the control operator is not how a talkgroup is joined. It is selected in your own radio.
Programming the talkgroup's ID or code into your radio makes it send and receive that group's traffic.
DTMF tones are analog keypad tones. Digital talkgroups are picked by an ID number, not by a DTMF tone.

T2B08.concept: No amateur station owns a frequency. All amateurs share the bands equally, so when two stations clash the answer is courtesy: talk it over and work out who goes where.
T2B08.hint: Nobody owns a frequency in amateur radio. Ask what two equal parties do when they both want the same thing.
why: Since neither station has a superior claim, the fair fix is to work out between them how the frequency will be used.
Nothing requires both to leave. One moving, or the two taking turns, solves it, and that is worked out by talking.
Being first gives no special right. No amateur station has a prior claim to any frequency.
Tones only hide the other signal from your speaker. Both stations still transmit on top of each other.

T2B09.concept: Repeaters are a shared resource for reaching distant stations. Band plans set aside simplex channels (direct, same-frequency contact) so nearby stations can talk without occupying one.
T2B09.hint: If the person you want to talk to is just down the road, ask if you really need the big shared machine on the hill.
why: Stations close enough to hear each other directly can use a simplex channel and leave the repeater free for others.
Simplex channels are for everyday direct contacts. They are not set aside for contests.
DX means distant stations. Simplex channels are meant for stations within direct range, not only for long-distance work.
Simplex means not using a repeater at all. It has nothing to do with a simple transmitter reaching one.

T2B10.concept: Q signals are three-letter shorthand. QRM means interference from other stations. A memory aid: M for man-made, N (in QRN) for natural noise.
T2B10.hint: Two of these are about unwanted noise. One comes from people and one from nature, and the last letter can remind you which.
why: QRM means interference from other stations. Think of the M as man-made.
QRN means static noise from natural sources such as lightning. Think of the N as natural.
QTH means your location. It has nothing to do with interference.
QSB means the signal is fading in and out. That is a change in strength, not interference from another station.

T2B11.concept: Q signals are three-letter shorthand. QSY means changing to another frequency. Hams say it when moving a contact off a busy channel.
T2B11.hint: Each of these has its own meaning: nothing to send, moving, received, and who is calling. Match the one about moving.
why: QRU means 'I have nothing for you', or as a question, 'do you have anything for me'. It is not about moving.
QSY is the Q signal for changing frequency.
QSL means 'I acknowledge receipt'. It confirms that a message or a contact was received.
QRZ means 'who is calling me'. It is used when you heard a call but missed the call sign.

T2B12.concept: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) repeaters use a color code, a number programmed into your radio. If it does not match the repeater's, the repeater ignores you. It does the job CTCSS does on FM.
T2B12.hint: Think about the low tone an analog FM repeater may require before it lets you in. DMR needs something that plays the same role.
why: The color code is a number your DMR radio must send to match a particular repeater. Without the right one, the repeater will not respond.
The color code does not set the offset. The offset is programmed separately as part of the channel's frequencies.
The color code does not name a CODEC, which is the method used to turn voice into digital data.
The color code is not a status report from the repeater. It is a setting your transmitter must match.

T2B13.concept: With no signal, an FM receiver produces loud hiss. Squelch is a gate that keeps the speaker silent until a signal arrives, so you are not listening to noise between transmissions.
T2B13.hint: Imagine an FM radio left on an empty channel all day. Think about what you would hear, and what you would want done about it.
why: Key clicks come from a Morse (CW) transmitter switching on and off too sharply. Squelch is a receiver feature and does not affect them.
Squelch silences the receiver's audio when there is no signal, and opens when one appears.
Parasitic oscillations are unwanted signals made inside an amplifier. They are fixed in the amplifier circuit, not by squelch.
Reducing impulse noise, such as ignition pops, is the job of a noise blanker, not of squelch.

T2B14.concept: A DMR talkgroup is like a labelled channel inside a shared digital system. Traffic is tagged with the group's ID, and your radio plays only the groups you have chosen.
T2B14.hint: Many conversations share one digital repeater. Think about what lets your radio play only the ones you care about.
why: People sharing email on a topic are a mailing list. A talkgroup is a feature of a digital radio system.
A talkgroup is a DMR identifier that sorts traffic, so users hear the group they selected and not everything else.
Operators meeting on the air around a shared interest are a net. A talkgroup is an identifier, not a set of people.
A talkgroup does not alert members to a frequency. It labels traffic so radios can filter it.

T2C01.concept: An amateur station is always an amateur station. Emergency groups such as RACES and ARES work inside FCC Part 97 rules, not in place of them. No organization can switch those rules off.
T2C01.hint: Ask who issued your license, and whether joining a volunteer group or working with another agency could change that.
why: RACES is itself part of FCC Part 97. Operating under it means following FCC rules, not escaping them.
FEMA is an emergency management agency. It does not write rules that replace the FCC's rules for amateur stations.
ARES is a volunteer program for amateurs. It has no power to set aside FCC rules.
Whenever an amateur station is operating, FCC Part 97 rules apply. There is no situation in this list that removes them.

T2C02.concept: A net is an organized on-air meeting. The Net Control Station (NCS) is its chairperson: it opens the net, takes check-ins and decides who talks to whom and when, so traffic moves in order.
T2C02.hint: Think of the person chairing a meeting. Separate what they do during the meeting from what was arranged beforehand or is each member's own job.
why: The net's schedule and frequency are set by its organizers ahead of time. Running the session is the control station's job.
Each operator is responsible for staying within their own license privileges. Net control does not check licenses.
Opening the net and directing who talks to whom, in order, is exactly what a Net Control Station does.
Not all three are duties. Picking the meeting time and checking licenses are not typical jobs of the Net Control Station.

T2C03.concept: Many letters sound alike on the air, such as B, D, P and T. A standard phonetic alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) gives each letter a distinct word, so spelled words arrive correctly.
T2C03.hint: Think about how you would give an unusual surname over a noisy phone line so that each letter could not be mistaken.
why: Sending a voice message again in Morse code is not the standard practice, and many operators could not copy it.
Asking for a read-back with the Q signal QSR is not the standard technique for this. Spelling the words phonetically is.
Spelling with a standard phonetic alphabet replaces each letter with a distinct word, so unusual words are copied correctly.
Not all three are right. Sending in Morse as well and asking for a read-back with QSR are not the standard technique.

T2C04.concept: RACES is the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service. It is defined in FCC Part 97 and lets amateurs registered with a civil defense organization provide its communications in emergencies.
T2C04.hint: Spell out the letters. The middle words of the name point to the kind of organization it serves.
why: RACES involves amateur radio only. It does not combine with citizens band operators or frequencies.
RACES is not an experimenters' society. It is an emergency communications service.
Despite the name, RACES has nothing to do with contests. It is not a competition.
RACES is the service set out in FCC Part 97 for amateurs providing civil defense communications in national emergencies.

T2C05.concept: In net language, traffic means messages. It usually refers to formal written messages passed from station to station in a set format so they arrive exactly as written.
T2C05.hint: When net control asks if anyone has traffic, they are asking if you have something to pass along. Think about what that something is.
why: Traffic is the term for the formal messages that net stations pass to one another.
The stations joining and leaving are check-ins and check-outs. They are not called traffic.
Mobile and portable operation describes where a station is, not the messages it handles.
A count of how often the net meets is a statistic. It is not what traffic means.

T2C06.concept: ARES is a volunteer program. Licensed amateurs sign up ahead of time, listing their skills and gear, so they can be called on to provide public service communications when needed.
T2C06.hint: Focus on two things: who is able to join, and how they come to be on the list.
why: ARES is made up of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their skills and equipment for public service communications.
ARES members do not have to be in the military. It is open to licensed amateurs who volunteer.
ARES is a group of volunteer operators, not a licensing course. Its members are already licensed.
ARES is not a certification program for RACES. The two are separate organizations.

T2C07.concept: A net runs smoothly because one station, net control, decides who talks next. Everyone else waits to be called. The one exception is an emergency, which can be reported at any time.
T2C07.hint: In a chaired meeting, think about when you speak and what would justify interrupting.
why: You check in as net control asks, usually with your call sign. Giving your address from the FCC database is not standard.
Logging the time of every transmission is not a standard net practice.
Waiting until net control directs you keeps the net orderly. An emergency is the one reason to break in.
Not all three are standard. Giving your address and timing each transmission are not normal net practice.

T2C08.concept: Winlink is a system that carries email over amateur radio. Each user's address is built from their call sign, so messages can travel by radio where the internet is down.
T2C08.hint: Three of these are ways of sending signals on the air. One is a complete message delivery system. Look for that one.
why: Winlink is a radio email system in which each user's address is based on their amateur call sign.
FT8 is a digital mode for short, structured contacts with very weak signals. It does not carry email.
PSK31 is a digital mode for live keyboard-to-keyboard chat. It is not an email system.
AMTOR is an older error-correcting teletype mode. It is not the callsign-based email system described.

T2C09.concept: Saving a life comes before the normal limits of a license. When human life or property is in immediate danger, a station may use any means of radio communication available to get help.
T2C09.hint: Ask what could be important enough to outweigh the normal limits of a license, regardless of any organization or plan.
why: There is an exception. A true emergency involving life or property allows it.
Being part of a FEMA plan does not grant extra frequencies. The exception depends on the emergency itself, not on any plan.
RACES membership does not grant extra frequency privileges. The exception depends on the emergency, not on a plan.
When human life is in immediate danger or property needs immediate protection, operating outside your privileges is permitted.

T2C10.concept: A formal message (a radiogram) starts with a preamble. It works like the tracking label on a parcel: message number, origin, date and similar details that let the message be followed.
T2C10.hint: Think of the label on a parcel that lets it be followed through the system, as opposed to the name and address of the person receiving it.
why: An email address of the originating station is not part of the preamble.
The recipient's address goes in the address section, which comes after the preamble.
The addressee's telephone number belongs with the address, not in the preamble.
The preamble holds the details used to track the message as it is relayed.

T2C11.concept: The check is a word count for the text of a radiogram. The receiving operator counts the words copied and compares. If the numbers differ, something was missed or added.
T2C11.hint: Here 'check' is used as in 'double-check'. Think of a simple number that would reveal a missing word.
why: The check is the count of words, or word equivalents, in the message text. It lets the receiver confirm nothing was lost.
The originating station's call sign is a separate part of the header, called the station of origin.
A list of relaying stations is not what the check is. The check is a number.
The check is not a tick box on the form. It is a number that the receiver compares with their own count.

T2C12.concept: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) serves civil defense organizations. To take part, an amateur must be enrolled and certified by the civil defense agency being served.
T2C12.hint: Three of these are volunteer or military-sponsored programs. One is a service written into the FCC rules to work for government emergency agencies.
why: ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service) is a volunteer program. It does not need civil defense certification.
RACES operators must be certified by, and registered with, the civil defense organization they serve.
MARS (Military Auxiliary Radio System) is a military-sponsored program. It is not certified by a civil defense agency.
SKYWARN is a volunteer weather spotter program. It does not involve civil defense certification.

T3A01.concept: Multipath: a VHF signal reaches your antenna directly and also by bouncing off buildings, hills and cars. The copies add up in some spots and cancel in others, so strength changes over a very short distance.
T3A01.hint: A 2-meter wave is only about 6 feet long. Think about what happens when two copies of the same wave arrive by routes of slightly different length.
why: Water vapor does not change enough over a few feet to matter, and it has little effect at VHF anyway.
VHF signals normally do not travel by the ionosphere at all, so this is not the cause of local strength changes.
Copies of the signal arriving by different paths add together in some spots and cancel in others, and those spots can be just a few feet apart.
The Doppler effect is a frequency shift caused by motion. It does not explain a strength change between two fixed antenna positions.

T3A02.concept: Leaves and branches hold water and soak up radio energy at UHF and microwave frequencies. The shorter the wavelength, the more trees in the path weaken the signal.
T3A02.hint: Imagine a weak UHF signal passing through a thick stand of wet, leafy trees. Does it come out stronger, weaker or unchanged?
why: Knife-edge diffraction is the bending of waves over a sharp edge such as a ridge. It is not what foliage does, and it does not distort voice peaks.
Vegetation absorbs UHF and microwave energy, so weak signals that pass through trees can drop too low to receive well.
Plants are passive. They cannot add energy to a signal, so they cannot amplify it.
Trees do have an effect at these frequencies: they take energy out of the signal.

T3A03.concept: Polarization is the direction of the wave's electric field, set by how the antenna is oriented. By convention, weak-signal CW and SSB work on VHF and UHF uses antennas with elements parallel to the ground.
T3A03.hint: Polarization here is a convention, so that both stations match. Think about how the long beam antennas used for weak-signal work are usually mounted.
why: Circular polarization of the right-hand kind is used mostly for satellite work, not for ordinary long-distance CW and SSB contacts on these bands.
Circular polarization of the left-hand kind is also mainly a satellite technique, not the normal choice for these contacts.
