Horizontal polarization is the accepted standard for long-distance (weak-signal) CW and SSB on VHF and UHF, so both stations match.
Vertical polarization is the standard for FM and repeater work on VHF and UHF, not for weak-signal CW and SSB.

T3A04.concept: On a direct line-of-sight path the wave keeps its polarization. If the receiving antenna is turned at right angles to the wave (one vertical, one horizontal), it picks up much less of the signal.
T3A04.hint: Picture a handheld antenna tipped on its side while the repeater antenna stands upright. What happens to how well they couple?
why: Sidebands are part of the modulation and are set in the transmitter. Antenna orientation cannot invert them.
An antenna at right angles to the wave's polarization captures far less energy, so the received signal is much weaker.
An echo comes from hearing the same signal by two paths of different length, not from mismatched polarization.
The effect is significant: cross-polarized antennas on a line-of-sight path can lose most of the signal.

T3A05.concept: VHF and UHF signals bounce off large objects such as buildings and hills. If the straight path is blocked, a beam antenna can be aimed at a reflecting surface to reach the other station by a bounce.
T3A05.hint: Think of a billiards player whose direct shot is blocked by another ball.
why: Changing polarization does not get the signal around a building, and it would mismatch the repeater's vertical antenna.
Aiming the directional antenna at a building or hill that reflects the signal toward the repeater can give a usable path around the blockage.
Long path means going the long way around the Earth on HF. It does not apply to reaching a nearby repeater on VHF or UHF.
SWR (standing wave ratio) measures how well the antenna matches the feed line. A higher SWR only wastes power.

T3A06.concept: A moving station passes quickly through spots where reflected signals add and spots where they cancel. The signal chops in and out rapidly, like seeing light flicker through the slats of a fence as you drive by.
T3A06.hint: Imagine driving past a slatted fence with the sun behind it, then think about what a mobile radio signal sounds like in a city.
why: Taking turns transmitting in a net is normal net procedure, not what this term means.
Picket fencing is the rapid flutter heard on a mobile signal as the vehicle moves through points where multipath signals cancel and reinforce.
Ground systems for vertical antennas use radial wires. That is not what this term describes.
Cable TV leakage is a real interference source, but it is not what this term describes.

T3A07.concept: Microwave wavelengths are very short, at the highest frequencies approaching the size of raindrops. Water falling through the path absorbs and scatters the signal, which is often called rain fade.
T3A07.hint: Microwave wavelengths are very short. Ask which kind of weather actually puts something in the signal's path that could soak up or scatter it.
why: Wind is moving air and does not absorb radio waves, though it can shake an antenna out of aim.
Low pressure by itself does not absorb or scatter microwave signals.
Rain, snow and other precipitation absorb and scatter microwave energy, so range drops.
Cold air by itself does not weaken microwave signals.

T3A08.concept: A signal bent back by the ionosphere usually arrives by several paths at once, and the ionosphere keeps shifting. The copies drift in and out of step, so the combined signal fades up and down irregularly.
T3A08.hint: The ionosphere is not a single smooth mirror. Think about a signal that reaches you several ways at once, with each way slowly changing.
why: Faraday rotation twists a wave's polarization as it passes through the ionosphere. It does not shift the frequency.
Thunderstorms cause static crashes (noise), not fading of the signal itself.
Intermodulation distortion is unwanted mixing of signals inside equipment. It has nothing to do with the path through the ionosphere.
Signals arriving by different, constantly changing paths combine at random, sometimes adding and sometimes cancelling, which is heard as irregular fading.

T3A09.concept: The ionosphere twists a wave's polarization, so a skip signal arrives elliptically polarized: a changing mix of vertical and horizontal. Matching antenna polarization therefore matters little on HF skip paths.
T3A09.hint: Elliptical polarization means the wave's electric field keeps turning instead of holding one direction. Think about what that means for a fixed antenna.
why: Digital modes work well over ionospheric paths and are used on HF every day.
Because the wave arrives as a mix of polarizations, a vertical or a horizontal antenna will each pick up part of it, so either can be used.
Elliptical polarization does not make FM voice unusable. This is not a result of how the wave is polarized.
Matching polarization matters on line-of-sight paths. After the ionosphere scrambles the polarization, the antennas do not need to match.

T3A10.concept: With multipath, delayed copies of a signal arrive on top of the direct one. For data, the late copies smear or cancel the symbols being sent, so the receiver misreads more of them.
T3A10.hint: Imagine listening to someone read numbers aloud in a room with a strong echo. What happens to your accuracy?
why: No rule ties data rate to the number of paths, and sending faster would make the overlap between delayed copies worse.
Slowing down can help, but there is no fixed rule to divide the rate by the number of paths.
FM does not protect against multipath. Reflected copies still cancel and distort the signal.
Delayed and cancelling copies corrupt the data symbols, so more errors are likely.

T3A11.concept: The ionosphere is the upper part of the atmosphere where sunlight strips electrons from gas atoms. This electrically charged layer can bend HF radio waves back to Earth, which lets them travel far beyond the horizon.
T3A11.hint: HF waves return to Earth from a high, thin region where sunlight knocks electrons off gas atoms. What are atoms called once they carry a charge?
why: The stratosphere is a lower layer, home of the ozone layer. It is not charged enough to return HF waves to Earth.
The troposphere is the lowest layer, where weather happens. It can bend VHF and UHF slightly but does not reflect HF.
The ionosphere contains charged particles (ions and free electrons) that bend HF radio waves back toward the ground.
The electrosphere is not one of the atmospheric regions used to describe radio propagation, and it is not what reflects HF.

T3A12.concept: Rain and fog droplets are tiny compared with a wave several meters long, so the wave passes them almost untouched. Weather in the path matters at microwave frequencies, not on long-wavelength bands.
T3A12.hint: Compare the size of a raindrop with a wave that is 6 or 10 meters long.
why: Absorption by rain and fog is a problem at microwave frequencies, where wavelengths are close to droplet size, not at 10 or 6 meters.
Droplets are far smaller than these wavelengths, so fog and rain have little effect on 10-meter and 6-meter signals.
Droplets are too small compared with these long waves to deflect them noticeably.
Fog and rain do not extend range on these bands. They simply make almost no difference.

T3B01.concept: A radio wave is an electric field and a magnetic field travelling together. The two fields are perpendicular to each other and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
T3B01.hint: Hold out your thumb, first finger and middle finger so each points along a different axis. Two of them are the fields; the third is the direction of travel.
why: The two fields are parts of the same wave and travel together at the same speed.
The fields are not parallel. Each is turned 90 degrees from the other.
The fields do not revolve in opposite directions. They rise and fall together while staying perpendicular.
The electric and magnetic fields are at right angles (90 degrees) to each other and to the direction the wave travels.

T3B02.concept: Polarization names the direction in which a wave's electric field points. A vertical antenna produces a vertical electric field, so its wave is vertically polarized.
T3B02.hint: A radio wave has two fields at 90 degrees to each other. By convention only one of them is used to name the wave's polarization.
why: Polarization is defined by the direction of the electric field: vertical field, vertical polarization.
The magnetic field is at right angles to the electric field. It is not the one used to name the polarization.
Polarization is about direction, not about a ratio of energy between the two fields.
Velocity divided by wavelength gives frequency, which has nothing to do with polarization.

T3B03.concept: A radio wave is electromagnetic: it is made of an electric field and a magnetic field that travel through space together, each sustaining the other.
T3B03.hint: Once the energy leaves the antenna there are no wires or components. Ask what can exist and travel in empty space.
why: Impedance and reactance describe opposition to current in a circuit. They are not parts of a wave.
Voltage and current exist in wires and components. Once the energy leaves the antenna it travels as fields.
A radio wave consists of an electric field and a magnetic field travelling together.
Ionizing and non-ionizing are categories of radiation by energy. Radio waves are non-ionizing; these are not components of a wave.

T3B04.concept: Radio waves and light are the same kind of thing, electromagnetic waves, at different frequencies. In free space (empty space with nothing in the way) they travel at the same speed.
T3B04.hint: Radio waves belong to a family of waves that all share one speed in empty space. Think about which other members of that family you know.
why: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, just like light, so in free space they travel at the speed of light.
Sound is a pressure wave in air and is roughly a million times slower. Radio waves do not need air at all.
Waves slow to a fraction of light speed inside cables, but in free space there is nothing to slow them.
This figure is tied to the speed of sound, which has nothing to do with radio waves.

T3B05.concept: All radio waves travel at the same speed, so wavelength and frequency trade off. More cycles each second means each cycle has less room: higher frequency, shorter wavelength.
T3B05.hint: Shake a rope faster while the ripples move along at a fixed speed. What happens to the spacing between ripples?
why: This is backwards. Packing more cycles into each second leaves less distance for each one.
Because the speed is fixed, raising the frequency makes each wave shorter.
Wavelength changes with frequency. That is why the 2-meter and 70-centimeter bands have different names.
The length of the path does not change either the frequency or the wavelength of a signal.

T3B06.concept: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency. The speed is about 300 million meters per second, so with frequency in megahertz (millions of hertz) the millions cancel and 300 is left on top.
T3B06.hint: Test each formula with a band you know: about 146 MHz should come out near 2 meters.
why: Multiplying makes wavelength grow with frequency, which is backwards, and hertz is the wrong unit to pair with 300.
Frequency is on top here, so wavelength would grow as frequency rises, which is backwards.
The unit is right but the fraction is upside down: 146 divided by 300 gives about 0.49, not 2 meters.
300 divided by the frequency in megahertz gives meters: 300 / 146 is about 2, matching the 2-meter band.

T3B07.concept: Amateur bands are named by their approximate wavelength, such as 2 meters or 70 centimeters, as well as by frequency. You can convert between the two with 300 divided by megahertz.
T3B07.hint: Think about how hams say which band they are on, for example the band around 146 MHz.
why: Hams name bands by approximate wavelength: the band near 146 MHz is called 2 meters, and the band near 440 MHz is 70 centimeters.
Letter/number designators are not the customary way amateur bands are named. Hams name a band by its frequency or its approximate wavelength.
Channel numbers identify single frequencies in services such as CB. Amateur bands are not identified that way.
Only the wavelength item is the customary one. Letter/number designators and channel numbers are not how amateur bands are normally named.

T3B08.concept: The radio spectrum is divided into ranges that each cover a factor of ten. The ladder runs MF, HF, VHF (very high frequency), UHF, with the megahertz ranges built from the numbers 3, 30, 300 and 3000.
T3B08.hint: Each named range covers a factor of ten. Think of an amateur band you know is VHF and check which range its frequency falls in.
why: 30 kHz to 300 kHz is LF (low frequency), far below VHF.
VHF runs from 30 MHz to 300 MHz. It includes the 6-meter, 2-meter and 1.25-meter bands.
300 kHz to 3000 kHz is MF (medium frequency), where AM broadcast stations are.
300 MHz to 3000 MHz is UHF (ultra high frequency), the next range above VHF.

T3B09.concept: UHF means ultra high frequency. It is the range just above VHF on the spectrum ladder, and each range covers a factor of ten.
T3B09.hint: Each named range covers a factor of ten. Think of an amateur band you know is UHF and check which range its frequency falls in.
why: 30 to 300 kHz is LF (low frequency), far below UHF.
30 to 300 MHz is VHF (very high frequency), the range just below UHF.
300 to 3000 kHz is MF (medium frequency). The numbers match but the unit is kilohertz, not megahertz.
UHF runs from 300 to 3000 MHz. It includes the 70-centimeter band.

T3B10.concept: HF means high frequency. It sits just below VHF on the spectrum ladder and is the range best known for long-distance contacts by way of the ionosphere.
T3B10.hint: Each named range covers a factor of ten. Think of an amateur band you know is HF and check which range its frequency falls in.
why: 300 to 3000 MHz is UHF (ultra high frequency), two steps above HF.
30 to 300 MHz is VHF (very high frequency), the range just above HF.
HF runs from 3 to 30 MHz. It includes amateur bands from 80 meters through 10 meters.
300 to 3000 kHz is MF (medium frequency), the range just below HF.

T3B11.concept: Radio waves travel at the speed of light: about 300 million meters every second. This is where the 300 in the wavelength formula comes from.
T3B11.hint: The wavelength shortcut uses the number 300 with megahertz. Think about where that 300 comes from, and check the units.
why: 150,000,000 meters per second is only half the real figure.
The speed of light is about 300,000,000 meters per second, and radio waves in free space travel at that speed.
The number is familiar but the unit is wrong. The figure is in meters per second, not miles per hour.
Both the number and the unit are wrong here.

T3B12.concept: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the speed of light in free space, whatever its frequency. Frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
T3B12.hint: When frequency goes up, wavelength goes down. Ask yourself what must stay fixed for that trade-off to work.
why: Microwaves have a very high frequency, but that shortens their wavelength. It does not make them faster.
UHF waves travel at the same speed as every other radio wave in free space.
VHF waves travel at the same speed as every other radio wave in free space.
In free space all radio waves move at the speed of light. Only wavelength changes with frequency.

T3C01.concept: HF waves can be bent back to Earth by the ionosphere, but UHF waves normally pass straight through it into space. With no bounce from above, UHF is limited to about line of sight.
T3C01.hint: Think about what carries HF signals around the curve of the Earth, and whether that works at much higher frequencies.
why: UHF signals are not especially weak. They reach satellites and spacecraft. The limit is the curve of the Earth, not strength.
There is no FCC rule limiting how far a signal may travel. This is not a real regulation.
The ionosphere usually does not bend UHF signals back to Earth, so they carry on in a straight line and are not heard beyond the radio horizon.
D region absorption affects the lower HF bands in daytime. UHF signals pass through the ionosphere with little loss.

T3C02.concept: HF (3 to 30 MHz) is regularly bent back to Earth by the ionosphere, so signals skip across continents and oceans. VHF and higher frequencies usually pass through the ionosphere and stay near line of sight.
T3C02.hint: Think about why hams choose HF when they want to talk to other countries without a satellite or the internet.
why: HF wavelengths are longer, so HF antennas are generally larger, not smaller.
HF bands are narrow, so they suit narrow signals. Wide signals fit better on VHF and higher bands, where there is more room.
The ionosphere routinely returns HF signals to Earth, so long-distance contacts are far more common on HF than on VHF and above.
Atmospheric static is stronger on HF than on VHF and above, not weaker.

T3C03.concept: An aurora is a moving curtain of charged particles that can reflect VHF signals. Because the curtain is constantly shifting, the reflected signal is smeared and sounds rough.
T3C03.hint: Picture a signal bouncing off a shimmering, fast-moving curtain instead of a smooth mirror. How clean would it sound?
why: Auroral contacts are regional, not worldwide. They do not reach anything like 10,000 miles.
The rapidly moving aurora smears the signal, giving it a distorted, raspy or buzzing sound.
Aurora follows solar activity and is not limited to winter nights.
Stations aim toward the aurora, which lies toward the pole, not toward the west.

T3C04.concept: Now and then, dense patches of ionization form in the E region of the ionosphere. They come and go unpredictably and can reflect 10-, 6- and sometimes 2-meter signals for strong contacts far beyond the horizon.
T3C04.hint: The key word in the question is occasional. Think about what could appear in the ionosphere for a short time and then vanish again.
why: Backscatter returns weak signals scattered back toward the transmitter. It is not known for strong signals on these bands.
Sporadic E is reflection from occasional dense patches in the ionosphere's E region, giving strong signals on 10, 6 and sometimes 2 meters.
D region absorption weakens signals on the lower HF bands in daytime. It does not carry signals anywhere.
Gray-line propagation is an HF effect along the line between day and night, not the usual cause of these VHF openings.

T3C05.concept: Diffraction is the bending of a wave as it passes a sharp edge. A radio wave passing over a ridge or rooftop bends partly downward behind it, so some signal reaches the far side.
T3C05.hint: Think about how sound can still be heard on the far side of a wall. Which of these effects is about a wave changing direction at an obstacle?
why: Knife-edge diffraction bends radio waves over a sharp obstacle such as a ridge or building edge, so signal reaches the area behind it.
Faraday rotation is the twisting of a wave's polarization in the ionosphere. It does not carry signals past obstructions.
Quantum tunneling is a real effect in physics and electronics, but it is not a way radio signals get past hills or buildings.
Doppler shift is a change in frequency caused by motion. It does not bend signals around anything.

T3C06.concept: Layers of air at different temperatures in the lower atmosphere (the troposphere) can trap VHF and UHF waves and guide them along the Earth's surface, like a pipe, for hundreds of miles.
T3C06.hint: VHF and UHF usually pass through the ionosphere, so look lower down, to the part of the atmosphere where weather happens.
why: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals between layers of air and carries them over the horizon, regularly to about 300 miles.
The D region is the lowest part of the ionosphere and mainly absorbs lower HF signals. It does not return VHF or UHF to Earth.
The F2 region returns HF signals to Earth over very long distances. It is not the regular carrier of VHF and UHF.
Faraday rotation is the twisting of a wave's polarization in the ionosphere. It is not a way of extending range.

T3C07.concept: Meteors burning up leave short-lived trails of ionized gas high in the atmosphere. These trails reflect lower VHF frequencies best and for the longest time, so a lower-frequency VHF band works best.
T3C07.hint: A meteor's ionized trail is thin and lasts only moments. Ask whether higher or lower frequencies are easier to reflect from weak ionization.
why: 33 centimeters is a UHF band. Its frequency is too high for meteor trails to reflect well.
6 meters is the lowest-frequency band listed, and meteor trails reflect it best and for the longest time.
Meteor scatter is possible on 2 meters, but reflections are shorter and weaker there than on 6 meters.
70 centimeters is a UHF band. Meteor trails reflect it poorly.

T3C08.concept: Air normally gets cooler with height. In an inversion, a layer of warm air sits above cooler air. The boundary bends VHF and UHF waves back down, forming a duct that guides them a long way.
T3C08.hint: Ducting happens low down, in the air where weather is. Think about what could arrange that air into layers that bend radio waves back down.
why: Lightning produces static noise. It does not create ducts.
Sunspots and solar flares affect the ionosphere, which is far above the troposphere where ducting happens.
Violent storm updrafts mix the air. Ducts need calm, stable layers.
A temperature inversion, warm air over cool air, forms a boundary that bends VHF and UHF waves back down and traps them in a duct.

T3C09.concept: The Sun's radiation charges the F region of the ionosphere. A band as high in frequency as 10 meters needs strong charging to be returned to Earth: full sunlight and an active Sun.
T3C09.hint: The ionosphere gets its charge from the Sun. Ask when, in the day and in the solar cycle, it would be charged most strongly.
why: Daylight keeps the F region strongly charged, and high sunspot activity strengthens it further, so 10 meters opens for long distances.
After dark the F region weakens and usually can no longer return 10-meter signals, even with high sunspot activity.
Daytime is right, but with few sunspots the F region is often too weak to return 10-meter signals.
Darkness and low sunspot activity together give the weakest ionosphere: the worst case for 10 meters.

T3C10.concept: The more sunspots, the more strongly the F region is charged and the higher the frequency it can return to Earth. At the cycle's peak this can extend up to the lowest VHF band, but not to UHF.
T3C10.hint: Even a very active Sun only lifts the ionosphere's upper frequency limit so far. Which bands sit closest to HF?
why: 10 meters (top of HF) and 6 meters (bottom of VHF) are low enough in frequency for a strongly charged F region to return them to Earth.
23 centimeters is a microwave band. Its signals pass straight through the ionosphere.
70 centimeters and 1.25 meters are too high in frequency for the F region to return, even at the sunspot peak.
Not all are true: the 23-centimeter, 70-centimeter and 1.25-meter bands pass through the F region instead of being returned.

T3C11.concept: Air gets thinner with height, and this bends (refracts) radio waves gently downward so they follow the Earth's curve a little. VHF and UHF signals therefore reach somewhat past the horizon you can see.
T3C11.hint: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. Think about what the atmosphere, denser near the ground, might do to a radio wave's path.
why: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, never faster.
Dust has almost no effect on VHF and UHF radio waves, but that does not explain reaching past the visual horizon.
The atmosphere bends radio waves slightly downward, so they curve a little way around the Earth and reach beyond the visual horizon.
Dust does not block VHF and UHF radio waves, and blocking would shorten the range, not extend it.

T4A01.concept: Mobile radios are built for a car's electrical system, about 13.8 volts. A transmitter is not perfectly efficient, so it draws considerably more power from the supply than it sends out as RF.
T4A01.hint: Two things to settle: what voltage does a car's electrical system run at, and is volts times amps comfortably more than 50 watts?
why: 24 volts is the wrong voltage for a typical mobile radio, which is designed for a 12-volt vehicle system, and it could damage the radio.
The voltage is right, but 13.8 V x 4 A is only about 55 watts in. A real transmitter loses far too much as heat to get 50 watts out of that.
12 amperes is a suitable current, but 24 volts is the wrong voltage for a radio designed for a 12-volt vehicle system.
13.8 volts matches a vehicle system, and 13.8 V x 12 A is about 166 watts, enough for 50 watts out plus the power lost as heat.

T4A02.concept: An SWR meter shows how well the antenna system is matched to the feed line. Each meter is built for a certain frequency range and a certain range of power, and reads properly only inside them.
T4A02.hint: A test instrument has to suit the signal it measures. What two things describe the signal your transmitter sends down the feed line?
why: A meter only reads accurately within the frequency range and power range it was designed for, so those must match your station.
How far the meter sits from the antenna is an installation detail, not a rating you pick a meter by.
An SWR meter can display high or low SWR alike, so the highest SWR you expect is not what you choose a meter by.
An SWR meter only measures the match. It cannot correct or compensate for a poor match.

T4A03.concept: Every wire has some resistance, and current flowing through it loses voltage along the way. A thin or long wire has more resistance. A radio draws its highest current when transmitting.
T4A03.hint: Think Ohm's law in the power cable itself: lots of current through a little resistance. What does the radio see at its end of the wire?
why: Short, thick wire has very little resistance, so little voltage is lost in the cable when the radio draws heavy current to transmit.
Power supplies and DC cables are not impedance matched the way antennas and feed lines are, so this is not the reason.
Wire length and thickness are chosen here for DC resistance. RF interference is dealt with by filtering, shielding and bonding.
A DC power cable is not meant to radiate, so there are no radiative losses to minimize. The loss that matters is resistance.

T4A04.concept: FT8 is a weak-signal digital mode where software on a computer turns messages into audio tones and decodes received tones. The radio and the computer simply trade audio in both directions.
T4A04.hint: The FT8 program makes and listens to sounds. Which part of the station is able to hand sound to the radio and take sound back?
why: A terminal program with a terminal node controller (a packet modem box) is the classic packet radio setup, not how FT8 is done.
Radio receive audio goes into the computer's audio input, and the computer's audio output feeds the radio, with FT8 software doing the rest.
There is no separate FT8 conversion unit with a keyboard and monitor. The work is done by software on an ordinary computer.
FT8 is not decoded by a website. The software runs on your own computer and exchanges audio directly with your radio.

T4A05.concept: An RF power meter measures the radio-frequency power flowing from the transmitter toward the antenna. To measure that power, the meter has to sit in the path the RF takes.
T4A05.hint: Follow the path the transmitted signal takes after it leaves the radio. The meter must sit somewhere along that path.
why: RF power travels down the feed line from transmitter to antenna, so the meter goes in line there to measure it.
The power supply output carries DC, not RF. A meter there would show supply voltage or current, not transmitted power.
The push-to-talk line only tells the radio to transmit. It carries no RF power, so this arrangement measures nothing useful.
The power supply cable carries DC to the radio. RF output power can only be measured on the antenna side.

T4A06.concept: For digital modes the computer needs to hear the radio, send its own tones to the radio, and switch the radio between receive and transmit. Those three jobs are the whole interface.
T4A06.hint: Imagine the computer taking the place of a human operator. What does an operator do with ears, voice and the push-to-talk button?
why: Mode, status and location are not the signals a digital mode interface carries. It carries sound and a transmit command.
Antenna and RF power connections belong between the radio and the antenna, not between the computer and the radio.
The computer takes in receive audio, sends out transmit audio, and keys the transmitter (switches it to transmit).
NMEA is a GPS data format, useful for position reporting, and DC power runs the radio. Neither is the digital mode interface.

T4A07.concept: Audio flows from an output to an input. The computer must listen to what the radio receives, so the radio's audio output connects to the computer's audio input.
T4A07.hint: Match outputs to inputs. Decide which connectors on each device send sound out and which take sound in.
why: Line out carries audio, and push-to-talk is an on-off switch line, not an audio input. Transmit audio belongs at the microphone input.
Line in is an input and push-to-talk is a control line that carries no audio, so nothing useful would pass between them.
The speaker connector is the radio's audio output and line in is the computer's audio input, so the computer can hear received signals.
Line out and the speaker connector are both outputs. Connecting two outputs together passes no useful signal.

T4A08.concept: Bonding means connecting equipment together so it all sits at the same voltage. RF current flows on the surface of a conductor, so a wide, flat conductor gives it an easy, low-impedance path.
T4A08.hint: RF current travels on the surface of a conductor. Which shape gives the most surface for the amount of metal?
why: Braid pulled off coax is a loose weave of fine strands that corrodes and loosens over time, so it is not the preferred choice.
Copper-clad steel wire is strong and is used for wire antennas, but a round wire has more inductance than a wide strap.
Twisted-pair cable is for carrying signals or data on two wires, not for bonding equipment together.
A flat, wide strap has a large surface and low inductance, giving RF current a low-impedance path.

T4A09.concept: A battery's ampere-hour rating says how much current it can deliver for how long. Ampere-hours divided by amperes leaves hours, like dividing a tank's litres by litres used per hour.
T4A09.hint: Look at the units. Which combination of a battery rating and an equipment figure leaves you with just hours?
why: Using peak power assumes the equipment draws its maximum all the time, which it does not, so the run time comes out wrong.
Ampere-hours divided by the average amperes drawn gives hours of run time, since the amperes cancel.
Watts per hour is not a meaningful measure of consumption, and multiplying ratings together does not produce a time.
Current squared times resistance is the formula for power in watts. It does not give a length of time.

T4A10.concept: A hotspot is a small, very low power personal device. It talks by radio to a digital handheld a few metres away and passes the traffic on through the internet.
T4A10.hint: Think of a home Wi-Fi router: a short radio hop to a small box, which then links you to something much bigger.
why: A hotspot links nearby digital radios to a digital voice or data network, usually through an internet connection.
FT8 is run with software on a computer exchanging audio with a transceiver. That is not what a hotspot does.
RTTY is a keyboard text mode. Encoding and decoding it is not the job of a hotspot.
Meteor scatter bounces signals off meteor trails using a normal station and suitable software, not a hotspot.

T4A11.concept: The radio's return current needs a solid, low-resistance path back to the battery. The point where the battery's negative lead bolts to the vehicle body is the vehicle's main ground.
T4A11.hint: Current leaves the battery and must get all the way back to it. Where is the most direct and dependable place to complete that loop?
why: The battery's chassis ground point is the vehicle's main ground, giving the return current a solid, low-resistance path.
The shell of a power connector is not a ground point and is not made to carry the radio's return current.
Some metal parts are poorly connected to the rest of the vehicle, which can cause voltage drop and noise.
A mounting bracket is a mechanical support. Paint, plastic and loose bolts make it an unreliable electrical path.

T4A12.concept: Morse code is made of short and long elements called dits and dahs. A keyer is a circuit that forms them with correct timing while the operator works a pair of paddles.
T4A12.hint: The name comes from the Morse key. Think about what part of sending code by hand could be automated.
why: Switching an antenna between transmitting and receiving is the job of a transmit-receive switch, not a keyer.
Voice activated switching from receive to transmit is called VOX. It has nothing to do with Morse code.
A keyer generates evenly timed dits and dahs as the operator presses paddles, making hand-sent Morse easier and cleaner.
A keyer is not a lock or security device. The word refers to keying, which means sending Morse code.

T4B01.concept: Microphone gain sets how hard your voice drives the transmitter. Driven too hard, the transmitter cannot follow the voice peaks and flattens them, like an overloaded loudspeaker.
T4B01.hint: Think of someone shouting into a cheap loudspeaker with the volume all the way up. What happens to the sound?
why: The transmitter's frequency is set by its oscillator, not by how loud the microphone audio is.
Too much gain overdrives the transmitter, clipping the voice peaks so the audio sounds harsh and hard to understand.
SWR depends on how well the antenna system matches the feed line, not on microphone settings.
Which sideband is transmitted is chosen by the mode setting. Microphone gain cannot swap it.

T4B02.concept: A transceiver gives you two direct ways to choose a frequency: turn the tuning control, called the VFO (variable frequency oscillator), or type the numbers in.
T4B02.hint: Separate the controls that pick where you are on the band from the features that send tones or make automatic corrections.
why: You can type the frequency on the keypad or turn the VFO knob to tune to it.
CTCSS and DTMF encoders produce tones sent along with your signal. They do not set the operating frequency.
Automatic Frequency Control keeps a receiver centred on a signal. It is not a way to enter a frequency.
Tone encoders and Automatic Frequency Control do not enter a frequency, so not all the choices are correct.

T4B03.concept: Squelch is a gate that mutes the speaker until a signal is stronger than a set threshold. That hides the hiss between transmissions, but it also hides signals weaker than the threshold.
T4B03.hint: Picture the gate and a signal too weak to push it open. What would have to happen to the gate for that signal to reach the speaker?
why: With the threshold set so the audio is always on, the squelch is open and nothing is muted, so even a very weak signal is heard.
The volume control only works on audio that gets past the squelch. A muted receiver stays silent however far it is turned up.
Anti-squelch is not a standard receiver control, and it is not how a weak signal is brought through the squelch.
Squelch enhancement is not a real control for hearing weak signals.

T4B04.concept: An FM receiver expects the signal to be centred in its filter and detector. If the signal sits off to one side, part of it is cut off or detected unevenly, and the recovered audio is garbled.
T4B04.hint: FM audio is recovered from frequency swings around a centre point. Picture what happens when the receiver's centre is in the wrong place.
why: A rise in voice pitch is what mistuning does to a single-sideband signal, not to FM.
A drop in voice pitch is also a single-sideband mistuning effect, not an FM one.
Being off frequency does more than make an FM signal quieter. The sound quality itself suffers.
The signal no longer sits centred in the receiver's filter and detector, so the audio comes out distorted.

T4B05.concept: Scanning steps the receiver automatically through a set of channels or frequencies and pauses when it finds a signal, so you do not have to tune around by hand.
T4B05.hint: Think of the seek button on a car radio and what it is looking for.
why: Deviation is how far an FM signal swings in frequency. Checking it needs test equipment, not the scan function.
Scanning is a receive feature. It does nothing to prevent interference to repeaters.
The radio steps through frequencies or memory channels and stops when it hears a signal.
Finding an antenna's resonant frequency is done with an antenna analyzer or SWR meter, not by scanning.

T4B06.concept: On single sideband, the pitch of a voice depends on exactly where your receiver is tuned. A small receive-only tuning adjustment fixes the pitch without moving your transmit frequency.
T4B06.hint: You want to shift only your receive tuning a little while your transmit frequency stays where the other station found you.
why: AGC (automatic gain control) and limiters deal with signal strength and loudness. They do not change voice pitch.
Bandwidth selection changes how wide a slice of spectrum you hear, which helps with interference but not with pitch.
Tone squelch keeps an FM receiver quiet until it hears a certain sub-audible tone. It has no effect on single-sideband pitch.
RIT (receiver incremental tuning), also called a clarifier, shifts only the receive frequency slightly to correct the voice pitch.

T4B07.concept: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) is a digital voice system. A DMR radio needs a large set of settings before it works: frequencies, your ID, repeaters and groups. That set is saved as one file.
T4B07.hint: Despite the hardware-sounding name, this is not something you can hold in your hand. Think about what a DMR radio needs loaded before it will work.
why: A cable that connects a radio to a computer is a programming cable. The code plug is not a physical item.
A code plug is the file of settings loaded into the radio: channels, repeaters, talkgroups and your ID.
An update to the programming software is just a software update, not the settings loaded into your own radio.
A codec does convert voice to digital data and back, but it is a part of the radio, not the code plug.

T4B08.concept: Each mode takes up a different width of spectrum. A filter only as wide as the signal lets the signal through and shuts out the noise and other stations on either side.
T4B08.hint: Picture a window. If it is much wider than what you want to see, what else comes in through it?
why: Selecting a filter does not let the receiver monitor several modes at once. One filter is in use at a time.
Matching the filter width to the mode passes the wanted signal while rejecting noise and interference beside it.
Filter bandwidth has nothing to do with how many frequencies the memory can hold.
The offset between receive and transmit frequencies is a separate setting, used for repeaters, and filters do not change it.

T4B09.concept: On DMR, a digital voice system, many groups of users share the same repeaters. Each group, called a talkgroup, has its own number, and the radio only unmutes for the numbers it is set to.
T4B09.hint: Many groups share one repeater on this system. What tells one group's traffic apart from another's?
why: Recalling a frequency gets you onto a repeater, but many groups share that frequency, so it does not pick out one group.
CTCSS is a sub-audible tone used on analog FM repeaters. DMR does not select groups with it.
Each talkgroup has an identification number, and entering or selecting it directs your radio to that group.
A code plug is a file of settings, not a physical five-pin plug that you insert.

T4B10.concept: The best filter is just wide enough to pass the whole signal. Narrower cuts off part of the signal; wider lets in extra noise. A single-sideband voice signal is roughly 2 to 3 kHz wide.
T4B10.hint: Recall roughly how wide a single-sideband voice signal is, then look for the filter that fits it most closely.
why: 500 Hz suits narrow signals such as Morse code. It would cut away most of a voice signal.
1000 Hz is still much narrower than a voice signal, so speech would be muffled and hard to understand.
2400 Hz is about the width of a single-sideband voice signal, so it passes the voice and little else.
5000 Hz is wider than the signal, so it lets in extra noise and nearby stations along with the voice.

T4B11.concept: D-STAR is a digital voice system that sends your identity as data along with your voice. The network uses it to recognize and route stations, so the radio must be given it first.
T4B11.hint: Think about what a digital network needs to know about each transmission before it can recognize and route it.
why: D-STAR sends your call sign as data in every transmission, so it has to be programmed into the radio first.
Output power is an ordinary control you can change at any time. It is not something D-STAR needs programmed.
The codec, which turns voice into digital data, is built into a D-STAR radio. You do not program its type.
Output power and codec type do not have to be programmed, so not all the choices are correct.

T5A01.concept: Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second, like litres per minute in a hose. Its unit is the ampere, often shortened to amp.
T5A01.hint: Think of water in a hose: one unit is for the pressure, one for the flow, one for the narrowness of the hose, one for the work done.
why: Volts measure voltage, the electrical push or pressure, not the amount of flow.
Watts measure power, the rate at which energy is used.
Ohms measure resistance, the opposition to flow.
The ampere is the unit of current, the amount of charge flowing each second.

T5A02.concept: Power is how fast electrical energy is being used or delivered. Its unit is the watt. A 100 watt lamp uses energy ten times faster than a 10 watt lamp.
T5A02.hint: Think of the number printed on a light bulb or a transmitter that tells you how strong it is.
why: Volts measure voltage, the electrical push, not the rate of using energy.
The watt is the unit of power, the rate at which energy is used.
Watt-hours measure a total amount of energy (power multiplied by time), not the rate.
Amperes measure current, the flow of charge.

T5A03.concept: Current is the flow of electrons through a circuit, like water moving through a pipe. Voltage is the push that makes them move; current is the movement itself.
T5A03.hint: Separate the push from the movement. The question asks for the name of the movement itself.
why: Voltage is the push that causes electrons to move, not the flow itself.
The ampere is the unit used to measure the flow; amperes per second is not the name of the flow.
The volt is the unit of electrical push; volts per second is not what the question describes.
Current is the name for the flow of electrons in a circuit.

T5A04.concept: Alternating current swings one way, then the other, then repeats. Frequency counts how many of these complete cycles happen each second.
T5A04.hint: The words 'times per second' describe how often something repeats. What do we call how often a wave repeats?
why: Pulse rate is not the term used for the cycles per second of an alternating current.
Wave number counts waves per unit of distance, not cycles per second.
Frequency is the number of complete cycles an alternating current makes each second.
Wavelength is the distance a wave travels during one cycle, a length rather than a count per second.

T5A05.concept: Electrons move when there is a difference in electrical pressure between two points, just as water flows when pressure is higher at one end of a pipe. That pressure difference is voltage.
T5A05.hint: Water flows through a pipe when the pressure differs between its ends. What is the electrical version of pressure?
why: A difference in voltage, the electrical push, between two points is what makes electrons flow.
Ampere-hours measure how much charge a battery can supply over time, not the push that starts flow.
Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field; it is not the push that moves electrons.
Inductance is the ability to store energy in a magnetic field; it is not the push that moves electrons.

T5A06.concept: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). One hertz means one complete cycle per second.
T5A06.hint: Frequency counts cycles each second. Three of these units are named after scientists; work out which quantity each one measures.
why: The hertz is the unit of frequency: one hertz is one cycle per second.
The henry is the unit of inductance, the property of a coil.
The farad is the unit of capacitance, the property of a capacitor.
Epicycles per second is not a unit of frequency; an epicycle is a term from old astronomy.

T5A07.concept: A material conducts electricity when it has electrons that are free to move from atom to atom. Metals have many of these loosely held electrons.
T5A07.hint: Current is a flow of tiny charged particles. What must a material have plenty of for that flow to happen easily?
why: Density is how heavy a material is for its size; it does not decide how well it conducts.
Metals have many electrons that are free to move, so current flows through them easily.
Protons are locked in the centre of each atom and do not move through a wire.
Young's modulus measures how stiff a material is, a mechanical property, not an electrical one.

T5A08.concept: An insulator is a material whose electrons are tightly held, so almost no current can flow through it. Glass, ceramic, plastic and dry air are common insulators.
T5A08.hint: Think about what the supports that hold bare wires on old power and telegraph poles were made of.
why: Sea water conducts electricity because of the salt dissolved in it.
Glass holds its electrons tightly, so it passes almost no current and is a good insulator.
Stainless steel is a metal and conducts electricity.
Graphite is a form of carbon that conducts electricity.

T5A09.concept: Alternating current (AC) regularly reverses direction: it flows one way, then the other. Direct current (DC) only ever flows one way, even if it pulses on and off.
T5A09.hint: Ask what the current must do to count as alternating: is switching on and off enough, or must something else change?
why: Current that goes between positive and zero never reverses; that is pulsing direct current.
Current that goes between negative and zero never reverses either; that is also pulsing direct current.
Alternating current reverses, flowing in the positive direction and then the negative direction.
Only one description is true: the two that alternate with zero never reverse direction, so they are not AC.

T5A10.concept: Power is the rate at which electrical energy is used, measured in watts. Energy is the total amount; power is how fast it is being spent.
T5A10.hint: The key word is 'rate'. Which electrical quantity tells you how fast energy is being spent?
why: Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms.
Current is the flow of electrons, measured in amperes.
Power is the rate at which electrical energy is used, measured in watts.
Voltage is the electrical push that causes current to flow, measured in volts.

T5A11.concept: Resistance opposes any flow of current. It does not matter whether the current is steady, reversing slowly, or reversing millions of times a second.
T5A11.hint: Does a resistor care which way the electrons are moving, or how often they change direction?
why: Resistance opposes direct current, which flows steadily in one direction.
Resistance opposes alternating current, which keeps reversing direction.
Resistance opposes RF (radio frequency) current, which is alternating current at a very high frequency.
Resistance opposes every kind of current flow, so direct, alternating and RF current are all true.

T5B01.concept: Milli means one thousandth. One ampere contains 1000 milliamperes, so going from amperes to the smaller unit multiplies the number by 1000.
T5B01.hint: Moving to a smaller unit makes the number bigger. How many thousandths fit in one whole?
why: 0.0000015 comes from dividing 1.5 by 1,000,000; the number should grow, and by 1000.
0.0015 comes from dividing 1.5 by 1000 instead of multiplying.
1.5 amperes x 1000 = 1500 milliamperes, because there are 1000 milliamperes in one ampere.
1,500,000 comes from multiplying 1.5 by 1,000,000, which is the micro step, not milli.

T5B02.concept: Kilo (k) means one thousand and mega (M) means one million. To turn hertz into kilohertz, divide by 1000; to turn hertz into megahertz, divide by 1,000,000.
T5B02.hint: Try dividing 1,500,000 by 1000, and by 1,000,000, and see which result appears with the matching unit.
why: 1,500,000 Hz / 1000 = 1500 kHz. It is also 1.5 MHz.
1500 MHz is 1,500,000,000 Hz, a thousand times too large.
15 GHz is 15,000,000,000 Hz, far too large.
150 kHz is only 150,000 Hz, ten times too small.

T5B03.concept: The prefix kilo means one thousand. A kilovolt is 1000 volts, just as a kilometre is 1000 metres.
T5B03.hint: Think of other everyday words that start with kilo, such as a distance or a weight, and what the prefix does to them.
why: One one-thousandth of a volt is a millivolt.
One hundred volts is ten times too small; kilo means one thousand, not one hundred.
Kilo means one thousand, so one kilovolt is one thousand volts.
One million volts is a megavolt.

T5B04.concept: The prefix micro means one millionth. A microvolt is a very small voltage, the kind of signal level a receiver picks up from its antenna.
T5B04.hint: Micro makes things small. The question is how small: compare it with milli, which is one thousandth.
why: Micro means one millionth, so one microvolt is one one-millionth of a volt.
One million volts is a megavolt, the opposite direction.
One thousand kilovolts is 1,000,000 volts, a megavolt.
One one-thousandth of a volt is a millivolt.

T5B05.concept: Milli means one thousandth, so 1000 milliwatts make one watt. To go from milliwatts to watts, divide by 1000.
T5B05.hint: How many milliwatts make one whole watt? Is 500 more or less than that?
why: 5 watts would be 5000 milliwatts; this comes from dividing by 100 instead of 1000.
500 milliwatts / 1000 = 0.5 watts, half a watt.
500,000 comes from multiplying by 1000 instead of dividing.
500,000,000 comes from multiplying by 1,000,000; the number should get smaller, not larger.

T5B06.concept: There are 1000 milliamperes in one ampere. To go from milliamperes to amperes, divide by 1000.
T5B06.hint: Going from a small unit to a bigger one makes the number smaller. Move the decimal point three places.
why: 0.003 comes from dividing by 1,000,000, three places too far.
0.3 comes from dividing by 10,000, one place too far.
3,000,000 comes from multiplying by 1000 instead of dividing.
3000 milliamperes / 1000 = 3 amperes.

T5B07.concept: One megahertz is 1000 kilohertz. To go from MHz to kHz, multiply by 1000, which moves the decimal point three places to the right.
T5B07.hint: Kilohertz is the smaller unit, so the number must get bigger. By how many decimal places?
why: 0.003525 comes from dividing by 1000; the number should grow when moving to the smaller unit.
35.25 comes from multiplying by only 10.
3,525,000 comes from multiplying by 1,000,000; that is the value in hertz, not kilohertz.

T5B08.concept: Pico means one millionth of a millionth and micro means one millionth, so one microfarad holds 1,000,000 picofarads. To go from pF to microfarads, divide by 1,000,000.
T5B08.hint: Pico is a much smaller prefix than micro. Work out how many picofarads fit into one microfarad.
why: 0.001 microfarads is only 1000 picofarads; this divides by 1,000,000,000 instead of 1,000,000.
1,000,000 picofarads / 1,000,000 = 1 microfarad.
1000 microfarads is 1,000,000,000 picofarads; this divides by only 1000.
1,000,000,000 comes from multiplying by 1000; going to the larger unit, the number should get smaller, not larger.

T5B09.concept: Decibels (dB) compare two power levels. Doubling the power is about +3 dB, and halving it is about -3 dB. Ten times the power is +10 dB.
T5B09.hint: First work out the ratio between the two powers. Then recall the decibel value that goes with that ratio.
why: 2 is the power ratio (10 / 5 = 2), not the decibel value.
10 watts / 5 watts = 2, a doubling of power, and doubling is about 3 dB.
5 is the difference in watts (10 - 5); decibels come from the ratio, not the difference.
10 dB means ten times the power, which would be 50 watts.

T5B10.concept: Each halving of power is about -3 dB. Decibels add up, so halving twice (one quarter of the power) is about -6 dB.
T5B10.hint: Find the ratio, then count how many times you must halve the starting power to reach the final power.
why: -1 dB is a small loss that leaves about four fifths of the power, not one quarter of it.
-3 dB is one halving, which would leave 6 watts.
12 watts halved is 6, halved again is 3. Two halvings is -3 dB + -3 dB = -6 dB.
-9 is the difference in watts (3 - 12); -9 dB would be three halvings, leaving 1.5 watts.

T5B11.concept: A power change of ten times is exactly 10 dB. Decibels depend on the ratio of the two powers, not on how many watts were added.
T5B11.hint: Divide the larger power by the smaller one. That ratio is a round number with a well known decibel value.
why: 200 watts / 20 watts = 10, and ten times the power is 10 dB.
12 dB is about sixteen times the power, which would be about 320 watts.
18 dB is about sixty-four times the power, far more than 200 watts.
28 dB is more than six hundred times the power, far more than 200 watts.

T5B12.concept: One megahertz is 1000 kilohertz. To go from kHz to MHz, divide by 1000, which moves the decimal point three places to the left.
T5B12.hint: Megahertz is the bigger unit, so the number gets smaller. Move the decimal point three places.
why: 28.400 kHz keeps the kilohertz unit but shrinks the number, so it is 1000 times too small.
2.800 MHz is 2800 kHz; the decimal is moved one place too far and a digit is lost.
284.00 MHz is 284,000 kHz; the decimal is moved only two places.

T5B13.concept: Giga (G) means one billion, so one gigahertz is 1000 megahertz. To go from MHz to GHz, divide by 1000.
T5B13.hint: Gigahertz is the bigger unit, so the number gets smaller. How many megahertz make one gigahertz?
why: 0.002425 GHz is only 2.425 MHz; this divides by 1,000,000 instead of 1000.
24.25 GHz is 24,250 MHz; this divides by only 100.
242.5 GHz is 242,500 MHz; this divides by only 10.

T5C01.concept: A capacitor is two metal plates separated by an insulator. Charge builds up on the plates and energy is stored in the electric field between them. That ability is capacitance.
T5C01.hint: An electric field forms between two charged plates held apart. Which component is built that way?
why: Inductance is the ability to store energy in a magnetic field, as a coil does.
Resistance opposes current and turns energy into heat; it does not store it.
Frequency is the number of cycles per second of an alternating current.
Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, as a capacitor does.

T5C02.concept: Capacitance is measured in farads. One farad is very large, so real parts are usually marked in microfarads or picofarads.
T5C02.hint: Each of these units goes with one electrical property. Match the one that belongs to the capacitor.
why: The farad is the unit of capacitance.
The ohm is the unit of resistance and impedance.
The volt is the unit of voltage, the electrical push.
The henry is the unit of inductance.

T5C03.concept: Current flowing through a coil of wire creates a magnetic field around it, and energy is stored in that field. That ability is inductance, and the component is an inductor.
T5C03.hint: A magnetic field appears around a coil of wire carrying current. Which property belongs to a coil?
why: Admittance is a measure of how easily alternating current flows, the inverse of impedance.
Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, not a magnetic one.
Resistance opposes current and turns energy into heat; it does not store it.
Inductance is the ability to store energy in a magnetic field, as a coil does.

T5C04.concept: Inductance is measured in henrys. Coils in radio circuits are often marked in millihenrys or microhenrys.
T5C04.hint: Each of these units goes with one electrical property. Match the one that belongs to the coil.
why: The coulomb is the unit of electric charge.
The farad is the unit of capacitance.
The henry is the unit of inductance.
The ohm is the unit of resistance and impedance.

T5C05.concept: Impedance is the total opposition a circuit gives to alternating current. Because it is a kind of opposition, like resistance, it is measured in the same unit.
T5C05.hint: Impedance is a kind of opposition to current. Which unit do we already use for opposition to current?
why: The volt is the unit of voltage, the electrical push.
The ampere is the unit of current.
The coulomb is the unit of electric charge.
The ohm is the unit of impedance, the same unit used for resistance.

T5C06.concept: Unit abbreviations are case sensitive. The prefix kilo is a lower case k, and hertz is written Hz with a capital H because it is named after a person.
T5C06.hint: Look only at the capital letters. Which prefix letters are small, and how is a unit named after a person written?
why: kHz has the lower case k for kilo and the capital H, small z for hertz.
khz has a small h, but the hertz symbol starts with a capital H.
KHz has a capital K, but the prefix kilo is written with a lower case k.
KHZ is all capitals; kilo needs a lower case k and hertz ends with a small z.

T5C07.concept: The prefix mega is a capital M. A lower case m means milli, one thousandth, so the case of that letter changes the value by a factor of a billion.
T5C07.hint: One letter here has two meanings depending on whether it is a capital. Which meaning is the large one?
why: mHz would be millihertz, one thousandth of a hertz, because lower case m means milli.
mHZ has the lower case m for milli, and hertz is not written with a capital Z.
Mhz has the right M for mega but a small h; the hertz symbol starts with a capital H.
MHz has the capital M for mega and Hz, capital H and small z, for hertz.

T5C08.concept: Power in watts equals current in amperes multiplied by voltage in volts: P = I x E. More push or more flow both mean more power.
T5C08.hint: Power grows if you raise the push and also if you raise the flow. Which way of combining them does that?
why: Power is current (I) multiplied by voltage (E).
Voltage divided by current gives resistance in ohms, not power.
Current squared belongs with resistance in another power formula (P = I² x R), not with voltage.
Current divided by voltage does not give power; power rises when either one rises.

T5C09.concept: Power in watts is voltage multiplied by current: P = E x I. 13.8 volts is the usual supply voltage for mobile radios.
T5C09.hint: Decide which operation joins volts and amperes to give watts, then do it with these two numbers.
why: P = E x I = 13.8 volts x 10 amperes = 138 watts.
About 0.7 comes from dividing 10 by 13.8 instead of multiplying.
23.8 comes from adding 13.8 and 10 instead of multiplying.
3.8 comes from subtracting 10 from 13.8 instead of multiplying.

T5C10.concept: Power in watts is voltage multiplied by current: P = E x I.
T5C10.hint: Decide which operation joins volts and amperes to give watts, then do it with these two numbers.
why: 4.8 comes from dividing 12 by 2.5, which would give resistance in ohms, not power.
P = E x I = 12 volts x 2.5 amperes = 30 watts.
14.5 comes from adding 12 and 2.5 instead of multiplying.
0.208 comes from dividing 2.5 by 12 instead of multiplying.

T5C11.concept: Rearranging P = I x E gives current: I = P / E. Divide the power in watts by the voltage in volts to get amperes.
T5C11.hint: Start from the power formula and rearrange it so the quantity you want is alone on one side.
why: 0.1 comes from dividing upside down: 12 / 120.
I = P / E = 120 watts / 12 volts = 10 amperes.
12 is just the voltage repeated, not a calculated current.
132 comes from adding 120 and 12 instead of dividing.

T5C12.concept: Impedance is the total opposition a circuit gives to alternating current (AC). It combines resistance with reactance, the extra opposition from coils and capacitors. Unit: ohms.
T5C12.hint: The everyday word 'impede' means to get in the way of something. What is being held back in a circuit?
why: Impedance is the opposition to the flow of alternating current, measured in ohms.
The inverse of resistance is called conductance, a measure of how easily current flows.
The inverse of reactance is called susceptance, not impedance.
Power handling capability is a rating in watts; it is not what impedance means.

T5D01.concept: Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance. More push means more flow; more resistance means less.
T5D01.hint: Picture the Ohm's law triangle: cover the letter you want and look at how the other two are arranged.
why: Multiplying voltage by resistance gives a meaningless number here; current gets smaller as resistance grows, not larger.
Current is the voltage (E) divided by the resistance (R): the push divided by what opposes it.
Squaring the voltage belongs to a power formula (P = E² / R), not to finding current.
E² / R is the formula for power in watts, not current in amperes.

T5D02.concept: Ohm's law: voltage equals current multiplied by resistance. Pushing more current through more resistance takes more voltage.
T5D02.hint: Picture the Ohm's law triangle: cover the letter you want and look at how the other two are arranged.
why: Voltage is the current (I) multiplied by the resistance (R).
Dividing current by resistance does not give voltage; voltage rises when resistance rises.
I² x R is the formula for power in watts, not voltage.
Squaring the current belongs to a power formula (P = I² x R), not to finding voltage.

T5D03.concept: Ohm's law: resistance equals voltage divided by current. If a large push produces only a small flow, the resistance must be high.
T5D03.hint: Picture the Ohm's law triangle: cover the letter you want and look at how the other two are arranged.
why: Voltage multiplied by current gives power in watts, not resistance.
Resistance is the voltage (E) divided by the current (I).
Adding voltage and current mixes two different units and has no meaning.
Subtracting current from voltage mixes two different units and has no meaning.

T5D04.concept: Ohm's law for resistance: R = E / I. Divide the voltage in volts by the current in amperes to get ohms.
T5D04.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with resistance alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: 3 is just the current repeated, not a calculated resistance.
R = E / I = 90 volts / 3 amperes = 30 ohms.
1/30 comes from dividing upside down: 3 / 90.
270 comes from multiplying 90 by 3, which gives power in watts, not resistance.

T5D05.concept: Ohm's law for resistance: R = E / I. Divide the voltage in volts by the current in amperes to get ohms.
T5D05.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with resistance alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: 18 comes from multiplying 12 by 1.5, which gives power in watts, not resistance.
0.125 comes from dividing upside down: 1.5 / 12.
R = E / I = 12 volts / 1.5 amperes = 8 ohms.
13.5 comes from adding 12 and 1.5 instead of dividing.

T5D06.concept: Ohm's law for resistance: R = E / I. Divide the voltage in volts by the current in amperes to get ohms.
T5D06.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with resistance alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: R = E / I = 12 volts / 4 amperes = 3 ohms.
16 comes from adding 12 and 4 instead of dividing.
48 comes from multiplying 12 by 4, which gives power in watts, not resistance.
8 comes from subtracting 4 from 12 instead of dividing.

T5D07.concept: Ohm's law for current: I = E / R. Divide the voltage in volts by the resistance in ohms to get amperes.
T5D07.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with current alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: 9600 comes from multiplying 120 by 80 instead of dividing.
200 comes from adding 120 and 80 instead of dividing.
0.667 comes from dividing upside down: 80 / 120.
I = E / R = 120 volts / 80 ohms = 1.5 amperes.

T5D08.concept: Ohm's law for current: I = E / R. Divide the voltage in volts by the resistance in ohms to get amperes.
T5D08.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with current alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: 20,000 comes from multiplying 200 by 100 instead of dividing.
0.5 comes from dividing upside down: 100 / 200.
I = E / R = 200 volts / 100 ohms = 2 amperes.
100 comes from subtracting 100 from 200 instead of dividing.

T5D09.concept: Ohm's law for current: I = E / R. Divide the voltage in volts by the resistance in ohms to get amperes.
T5D09.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with current alone on one side. Which number is divided by which?
why: 2400 does not come from Ohm's law; dividing 240 by 24 gives a much smaller number.
0.1 comes from dividing upside down: 24 / 240.
I = E / R = 240 volts / 24 ohms = 10 amperes.
5760 comes from multiplying 240 by 24 instead of dividing.

T5D10.concept: Ohm's law for voltage: E = I x R. Multiply the current in amperes by the resistance in ohms to get volts.
T5D10.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with voltage alone on one side, then combine the two numbers that way.
why: E = I x R = 0.5 amperes x 2 ohms = 1 volt.
0.25 comes from dividing 0.5 by 2 instead of multiplying.
2.5 comes from adding 2 and 0.5 instead of multiplying.
1.5 comes from subtracting 0.5 from 2 instead of multiplying.

T5D11.concept: Ohm's law for voltage: E = I x R. Multiply the current in amperes by the resistance in ohms to get volts.
T5D11.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with voltage alone on one side, then combine the two numbers that way.
why: 1 is just the current repeated, not a calculated voltage.
E = I x R = 1 ampere x 10 ohms = 10 volts.
11 comes from adding 10 and 1 instead of multiplying.
9 comes from subtracting 1 from 10 instead of multiplying.

T5D12.concept: Ohm's law for voltage: E = I x R. Multiply the current in amperes by the resistance in ohms to get volts.
T5D12.hint: Pick the form of Ohm's law with voltage alone on one side, then combine the two numbers that way.
why: 8 comes from subtracting 2 from 10 instead of multiplying.
0.2 comes from dividing 2 by 10 instead of multiplying.
12 comes from adding 10 and 2 instead of multiplying.
E = I x R = 2 amperes x 10 ohms = 20 volts.

T5D13.concept: In a series circuit the parts are joined end to end in a single loop. There is only one path, so all the current must pass through every part and the current is the same everywhere.
T5D13.hint: Picture water in one pipe with no side branches. Whatever flows through the first section must flow through the rest.
why: A series circuit has only one path, so the same current flows through every component.
A parallel circuit splits the current among its branches; it is the voltage that is the same there.
Resonant describes a circuit tuned to one frequency, not how the current is shared among parts.
Branch is a name for one path of a parallel circuit, not a circuit type with equal current everywhere.

T5D14.concept: In a parallel circuit every part is connected across the same two points, side by side. Each one therefore has the same voltage across it, while the current divides among them.
T5D14.hint: Picture several lamps each wired directly across the same two battery terminals. What do they all share?
why: A series circuit divides the voltage among its components; it is the current that is the same there.
Parallel components all connect across the same two points, so each has the same voltage across it.
Resonant describes a circuit tuned to one frequency, not how the voltage is shared among parts.
Branch is a name for one path of a parallel circuit, not a circuit type in itself.

T6A01.concept: A resistor opposes current and turns some electrical energy into heat. It does this the same way for steady direct current (DC) as for changing current.
T6A01.hint: Think of a narrow section in a water pipe. Which part acts like that for steady current, turning some energy into heat?
why: An inductor is a coil that opposes changes in current. To steady DC it looks almost like a plain wire.
A resistor opposes current flow, even steady DC, and turns the lost energy into heat.
An inverter is a circuit that changes DC into AC. It is not a part that opposes current.
A transformer changes AC voltage up or down using two coils. It does not work on steady DC.

T6A02.concept: A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact, usually turned by a knob. Moving the contact changes how much of the signal is passed on, which is how a volume knob works.
T6A02.hint: A volume knob has to change something smoothly as you turn it. Which part has a moving contact inside?
why: A fixed resistor has one value that cannot be changed, so it cannot be turned up or down.
A power resistor is built to handle a lot of heat. That says nothing about being adjustable.
A potentiometer is an adjustable resistor with a knob or slider, the classic volume control.
A transformer changes AC voltage with two coils. It is not a knob-adjusted volume control.

T6A03.concept: A potentiometer is a variable resistor. Turning its shaft slides a contact along a strip of resistive material, changing the resistance between its terminals.
T6A03.hint: A potentiometer is a strip of material with a sliding contact. What property of that strip changes with the length used?
why: Inductance is the property of a coil. A variable inductor changes it, not a potentiometer.
A potentiometer is a variable resistor, so turning it changes resistance.
Capacitance is the property of a capacitor. A variable capacitor changes it, not a potentiometer.
Field strength describes how strong a radio signal or field is. It is not set by a potentiometer.

T6A04.concept: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between two conductive plates held apart by an insulator. An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field instead.
T6A04.hint: An electric field forms between two surfaces holding opposite charges. Which part is built from two such surfaces?
why: A resistor does not store energy. It turns electrical energy into heat.
A capacitor holds charge on two plates, and the energy is stored in the electric field between them.
An inductor stores energy too, but in the magnetic field around its coil.
A diode lets current flow in one direction only. It is not an energy storage part.

T6A05.concept: A capacitor is two conductive plates with an insulator, called the dielectric, between them. Charge builds up on the plates but cannot cross the gap.
T6A05.hint: Picture a sandwich: metal, something that does not conduct, then metal again. Which part stores charge on facing surfaces?
why: A resistor is a single piece of material that conducts poorly. It has no insulated gap.
A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact, not plates separated by an insulator.
An oscillator is a circuit that produces a signal at some frequency. It is not a single part built this way.
A capacitor is exactly this: conductive surfaces separated by an insulator.

T6A06.concept: An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field that forms around a wire when current flows. Winding the wire into a coil makes that field stronger.
T6A06.hint: Current flowing in a wire creates magnetism around it. Which part is built to make the most of that?
why: A resistor does not store energy. It turns electrical energy into heat.
A capacitor stores energy too, but in an electric field between its plates.
An inductor is a coil, and current through it builds a magnetic field that holds energy.
A diode lets current flow in one direction only. It is not an energy storage part.

T6A07.concept: An inductor is usually a coil of wire. Coiling concentrates the magnetic field made by the current, which is where the inductor stores its energy.
T6A07.hint: Winding wire into loops strengthens the magnetic field around it. Which part depends on a magnetic field?
why: A transistor is made of semiconductor material, not wound wire.
A capacitor is made of conductive plates separated by an insulator, not a coil.
A diode is a semiconductor part that passes current one way. It is not a coil.
An inductor is typically a coil of wire, sometimes wound around a core.

T6A08.concept: Switch names count poles and throws. A pole is a circuit being switched; a throw is a position it can connect to. SPDT means single-pole double-throw.
T6A08.hint: Spell out the four letters. One pair tells how many circuits are switched, the other how many places each can connect to.
why: Opening or closing a single circuit is a single-pole single-throw (SPST) switch, a simple on-off switch.
Opening or closing two circuits at once is a double-pole single-throw (DPST) switch.
Single-pole double-throw: one circuit (the pole) is connected to either of two others (the throws).
Switching two circuits each between two others is a double-pole double-throw (DPDT) switch.

T6A09.concept: In figure T-2, component 3 is two small circles with one slanted line hinged at one circle and lifted away from the other. One moving arm and one contact make a simple on-off switch.
T6A09.hint: Count the moving arms in the symbol, then count how many contacts that arm can land on.
why: The symbol has one arm (single pole) and one contact for it to touch (single throw): a plain on-off switch.
A single-pole double-throw symbol would show one arm with two contacts to choose between. This has only one.
A double-pole single-throw symbol would show two arms moving together. This has only one arm.
A double-pole double-throw symbol would show two arms, each with two contacts. This has one arm and one contact.

T6A10.concept: Rechargeable batteries use chemistry that can be reversed by pushing current back in. Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion and lead-acid are all rechargeable types.
T6A10.hint: Think about where you meet each chemistry in daily life, and whether you plug that thing in or throw the battery away.
why: Nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) cells are rechargeable, common as AA cells and in handheld radio packs.
Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable, used in phones, laptops and many handheld radios.
Lead-acid batteries are rechargeable, like the battery in a car.
Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion and lead-acid can all be recharged, so all three choices are true.

T6A11.concept: Some battery chemistries can be reversed by charging and some cannot. Carbon-zinc cells are single-use; trying to recharge a non-rechargeable cell can make it leak or burst.
T6A11.hint: Three of these are found in devices you plug in to charge. One is a cheap throwaway cell.
why: Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) cells are rechargeable.
Carbon-zinc cells are inexpensive single-use batteries and are not made to be recharged.
Lead-acid batteries are rechargeable, like the battery in a car.
Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable, like the ones in phones.

T6B01.concept: A diode needs a small voltage across it before it conducts, called the forward voltage drop. Its size depends on the diode type, and it is subtracted from what reaches the load.
T6B01.hint: Diodes are made from different materials and in different ways. Would you expect every kind to lose the same small voltage?
why: Forward drop depends on the diode type. A Schottky diode, for example, drops less than an ordinary silicon diode.
Peak inverse voltage is the reverse voltage a diode can withstand. It is a separate rating, not tied to forward drop.
Every working diode has a forward voltage drop. It is normal, not a sign of a fault.
The forward drop is lost across the diode, so the load receives that much less voltage.

T6B02.concept: A diode is a one-way valve for current. It conducts when voltage is applied in the forward direction and blocks when the voltage is reversed.
T6B02.hint: Think of a one-way valve in a pipe. Which part does that job for electricity?
why: A resistor opposes current equally in both directions.
A fuse passes current both ways and melts open if the current gets too high.
A diode conducts in one direction and blocks in the other.
A driven element is the part of an antenna connected to the feed line. It is not a one-way component.

T6B03.concept: A transistor uses a small signal on one lead to control a larger current through the other two. Driven fully on or fully off, it acts as a switch with no moving parts.
T6B03.hint: A switch needs a control input that turns a current path on or off. Which part has a separate lead for control?
why: A varistor is a resistor whose resistance drops at high voltage, used to absorb voltage spikes.
A potentiometer is a resistor adjusted by hand, not switched by an electrical signal.
A transistor can be turned fully on or off by a small control signal, making it an electronic switch.
A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes with temperature, used for sensing heat.

T6B04.concept: A bipolar junction transistor is built from three layers of semiconductor material, arranged NPN or PNP. Each layer has its own lead.
T6B04.hint: Three layers means three leads. Which solid-state part is known for having three leads?
why: An alternator is a rotating machine that generates alternating current. It is not a semiconductor device.
A transistor can be made of three semiconductor regions, such as N-type, P-type and N-type.
A triode is a vacuum tube with three elements. It is not made of semiconductor regions.
A pentode is a vacuum tube with five elements. It is not made of semiconductor regions.

T6B05.concept: Transistors come in two main families with different lead names. A field-effect transistor has a gate, drain and source; a bipolar junction transistor has an emitter, base and collector.
T6B05.hint: The gate does its controlling with a voltage, not a current. What does a voltage across a gap create?
why: A varistor is a voltage-dependent resistor with two leads, not a transistor.
A field-effect transistor (FET) has a gate that controls current flowing between source and drain.
Hall effect describes sensing a magnetic field. It is not the transistor type with these three lead names.
A bipolar junction transistor has an emitter, base and collector instead.

T6B06.concept: A diode must be installed the right way round, so the package shows which end is the cathode, the end that current flows out of when it conducts. A band at that end is the usual mark.
T6B06.hint: Small diode bodies have little room for printing. What simple mark could show which end is which?
why: The word cathode is not normally printed on a diode package. The usual marking is much simpler.
A stripe or band printed around one end of the body marks the cathode lead.
A letter C is not the common package marking for the cathode.
K can stand for cathode on diagrams, but the usual mark on the package itself is a stripe.
