T6B07.concept: A light-emitting diode (LED) is a diode that gives off light when current flows through it in the forward direction. Reversed, it blocks current and stays dark.
T6B07.hint: An LED is still a diode. In which condition does any diode actually conduct?
why: Current flowing through the LED in its forward (conducting) direction makes it emit light.
An LED blocks reverse current, like any diode, so it stays dark.
A capacitively-coupled RF signal is not what lights an LED. It needs forward current through it.
An inductively-coupled RF signal is not what lights an LED. It needs forward current through it.

T6B08.concept: FET is short for field-effect transistor. An electric field made by the voltage on its gate controls the current flowing between its source and drain.
T6B08.hint: This part is a kind of transistor controlled by a voltage rather than a current. What does a voltage on a gate create?
why: Frequency Emission Transmitter is not a real term.
Fast Electron Transistor is not a real term.
Free Electron Transmitter is not a real term.
FET stands for Field Effect Transistor: an electric field at the gate controls the current.

T6B09.concept: A diode has two electrodes, the anode and the cathode. When the diode conducts, conventional current flows in at the anode and out at the cathode.
T6B09.hint: A diode has only two leads. The same two names are also used for the electrodes of vacuum tubes and batteries.
why: Plus and minus label battery terminals or voltage polarity. They are not the names of diode electrodes.
Source and drain are two of the three electrodes of a field-effect transistor.
A diode's two electrodes are the anode and the cathode. Forward current flows from anode to cathode.
Gate belongs to a field-effect transistor and base to a bipolar junction transistor, not to a diode.

T6B10.concept: Power gain means more signal power comes out than went in, with the extra drawn from a power supply. Only active devices such as transistors can do this.
T6B10.hint: Passive parts can only pass on or lose the power they receive. Which part can draw on a power supply to boost a signal?
why: A transformer can raise voltage, but current falls by the same factor, so power does not increase.
A transistor uses a small signal to control larger power from a supply, so it can provide power gain.
A reactor is another name for an inductor, a passive part that cannot add power.
A resistor only turns power into heat. It always loses power and never adds it.

T6B11.concept: Gain is how much bigger a signal is at an amplifier's output than at its input. It is a ratio, and it can be stated for voltage, current or power.
T6B11.hint: Gain compares what comes out with what went in. Ask yourself how many ways a signal's size can be measured.
why: Voltage gain is the output signal voltage compared with the input signal voltage. This is true.
Current gain is the output signal current compared with the input signal current. This is true.
Power gain is the output signal power compared with the input signal power. This is true.
Gain can be expressed as a voltage, current or power ratio, so all three choices are true.

T6B12.concept: A bipolar junction transistor has three layers and three leads: emitter, base and collector. A small current into the base controls a much larger current between the other two.
T6B12.hint: Each transistor family has its own three lead names. For this family, the outer two send out and gather up the charge.
why: Signal, bias and power are general circuit words, not the names of transistor electrodes.
A bipolar junction transistor's electrodes are the emitter, base and collector.
Input, output and supply describe connections to a circuit, not the electrodes of this transistor.
Pole one, pole two and output are not the names of transistor electrodes. Poles belong to switches.

T6C01.concept: A schematic is a drawing of a circuit that uses standard symbols for the parts and lines for the connections. It shows how a circuit is wired, not how it looks.
T6C01.hint: Think of the kind of drawing found in a radio's service manual, full of zigzags, coils and lines.
why: Connection chart is not the standard name for a diagram drawn with component symbols.
Instrumentation system is not the name of a circuit diagram.
A schematic is the diagram that shows a circuit using standard component symbols.
A flow chart shows the steps of a process or program, not electrical parts and connections.

T6C02.concept: In figure T-1, component 1 is a zigzag line drawn in the middle of a wire. The zigzag is the schematic symbol for a resistor.
T6C02.hint: Look at the shape: a wire that zigzags back and forth. A bent, longer path suggests the current has a harder time getting through.
why: The zigzag line is the standard symbol for a resistor.
A transistor is drawn as a circle with three leads and an arrow, like component 2.
A battery is drawn as alternating long and short parallel lines, like component 4.
A connector is not drawn as a zigzag. The input terminals at the left of the figure are the connection points.

T6C03.concept: In figure T-1, component 2 is a circle holding a thick bar, with one lead to the bar and two slanted leads leaving it, one with an arrowhead. Three leads and an arrow mean a transistor.
T6C03.hint: Count the leads on this symbol and notice the small arrowhead on one of them.
why: A resistor is a zigzag line with two leads, like component 1.
A circle with a bar, three leads and an arrow on one lead is the symbol for a transistor.
An indicator lamp has only two leads. In this figure the lamp is the small dome shape, component 3.
A connector is not drawn as a circle with three leads and an arrow.

T6C04.concept: In figure T-1, component 3 is a small dome, like a bulb, with a loop inside for the filament. That is the symbol for a lamp.
T6C04.hint: Compare the outline with everyday objects. This symbol looks a bit like the real thing it stands for.
why: A resistor is a zigzag line, like component 1.
A transistor is the circle with three leads and an arrow, component 2.
A dome with a filament loop inside is the symbol for a lamp.
The ground symbol is a line ending in three short slanted strokes, as at component 5.

T6C05.concept: In figure T-1, component 4 is a stack of parallel lines, alternating long and short. Each long and short pair stands for one cell, so a stack of them is a battery.
T6C05.hint: Look for parallel lines of two different lengths, stacked up. Each pair represents one cell.
why: A resistor is a zigzag line, like component 1.
A transistor is the circle with three leads and an arrow, component 2.
The ground symbol is three short slanted strokes on the end of a line, drawn just below component 4.
Alternating long and short parallel lines are the symbol for a battery.

T6C06.concept: In figure T-2, component 6 is one straight line and one curved line facing each other with a gap between. Two plates that do not touch are the symbol for a capacitor.
T6C06.hint: The symbol shows two lines facing each other across a gap. Which part is built from two surfaces that never touch?
why: A resistor is a zigzag line, like component 7.
Two facing lines with a gap, one straight and one curved, picture the two plates of a capacitor.
A regulator IC would be drawn as a box with labeled leads, not two facing lines.
A transistor symbol has three leads, usually inside a circle. This symbol has two.

T6C07.concept: In figure T-2, component 8 is a triangle pointing at a bar, the diode symbol, with two small arrows pointing away from it. The arrows show light leaving, so it is an LED.
T6C07.hint: Start with the triangle-and-bar shape, then ask what the two little arrows pointing away from it might be showing.
why: A resistor is a zigzag line, like component 7 just above it.
An inductor is drawn as a row of loops, like the coils in component 4.
A regulator IC would be drawn as a box with labeled leads, not a triangle and bar.
A diode symbol with small arrows pointing away, showing light coming out, is a light emitting diode.

T6C08.concept: In figure T-2, component 9 is a zigzag line with an arrow touching it from below. The zigzag is a resistor, and the arrow is a movable contact that makes it adjustable.
T6C08.hint: Find the basic symbol first, then ask what an added arrow usually means on a schematic.
why: A variable capacitor is two facing plates with an arrow, not a zigzag.
A variable inductor is a row of loops with an arrow, not a zigzag.
A zigzag (resistor) with an arrow touching it is a variable resistor. The arrow is the sliding contact.
A variable transformer would show coils with a sliding tap. This symbol has no coils.

T6C09.concept: In figure T-2, component 4 is two separate columns of loops side by side with two straight lines between them. Two coils sharing a core make a transformer.
T6C09.hint: Count the coils in the symbol and notice they are not wired to each other, only placed side by side.
why: A variable inductor is a single coil with an arrow. This symbol has two coils and no arrow.
A double-pole switch would show two moving arms and contacts, not coils.
A potentiometer is a zigzag resistor with an arrow contact, not coils.
Two coils side by side, with lines between them for the core, are the symbol for a transformer.

T6C10.concept: In figure T-3, component 3 is a column of loops, the coil symbol, with an arrow pointing into its side. A coil is an inductor, and the arrow means its value can be adjusted.
T6C10.hint: Find the basic symbol first, a row of loops, then ask what the added arrow tells you.
why: A connector is not drawn as a column of loops.
A meter is normally drawn as a circle with a letter or pointer inside, not as loops.
A variable capacitor is two facing plates crossed by an arrow, like component 2.
Loops are the symbol for an inductor, and the arrow touching the coil shows it is variable.

T6C11.concept: In figure T-3, component 4 is a triangle pointing down with a vertical line through its center, sitting at the top of a wire. That is the symbol for an antenna.
T6C11.hint: The symbol sits at the very top of the circuit, at the end of the signal path. What does a radio circuit usually end in?
why: A triangle pointing down with a vertical line through it, at the top of a wire, is the antenna symbol.
A transmitter would be drawn as a labeled box, not this triangle shape.
A dummy load is a resistor that absorbs transmitter power without radiating. It is not drawn like this.
Ground is the line ending in three short slanted strokes at the bottom of the figure.

T6C12.concept: A schematic shows which parts are in a circuit and how they are connected. It is not a picture: where things sit, how long wires are and how parts look are left out.
T6C12.hint: A schematic is like a subway map. Ask what such a map gets right and what it ignores.
why: Lines on a schematic are drawn for clarity. Their lengths say nothing about real wire lengths.
Parts are shown as standard symbols, which do not look like the real components.
A schematic accurately shows which component leads connect to which. That is its purpose.
Wire lengths and physical appearance are not shown accurately, so not all of the choices are true.

T6D01.concept: Alternating current (AC) reverses direction many times a second. A rectifier, built from diodes, passes current one way only, so its output flows in one direction but still varies.
T6D01.hint: Which kind of part passes current one way only? A circuit built from those parts takes its name from setting current right.
why: A transformer changes AC to a higher or lower AC voltage. Its output is still AC.
A rectifier uses diodes to pass current in one direction only, turning AC into varying DC.
An amplifier makes a signal larger. It does not change AC into DC.
A reflector is an element of a directional antenna. It is not a circuit that changes AC to DC.

T6D02.concept: A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet. A small current through its coil pulls the contacts open or closed, so one circuit can switch another.
T6D02.hint: Picture an electromagnet pulling a metal arm that makes or breaks a contact. What everyday job is that doing?
why: A relay is a switch whose contacts are moved by current through a coil instead of by a finger.
A relay only opens and closes contacts. It does not amplify a signal.
An inverting amplifier is a circuit whose output is the opposite polarity of its input. It is not a relay.
A pass transistor carries load current in a voltage regulator. It is not a relay.

T6D03.concept: Shielded wire has a conductive layer, such as a braid or foil, wrapped around the inner conductor. The shield blocks stray signals from getting onto the wire or leaking off it.
T6D03.hint: The shield is a metal layer wrapped around the inner wire. Think about what a barrier like that keeps in or out.
why: Resistance depends on wire thickness, length and material. A shield does not lower it.
Current capacity comes from using thicker wire, not from adding a shield.
The shield stops unwanted signals from coupling onto the wire or radiating from it.
Receiver overload comes from very strong signals reaching the receiver. It is not the reason for shielded wire.

T6D04.concept: A meter measures an electrical quantity such as voltage, current or resistance and shows the result as a number you can read.
T6D04.hint: Which of these would you look at to find out how many volts or amperes are present?
why: A potentiometer is an adjustable resistor. It sets a value but does not display one.
A transistor amplifies or switches signals. It displays nothing.
A meter measures a quantity such as voltage or current and shows it as a numeric value.
A relay is an electrically-controlled switch. It displays nothing.

T6D05.concept: A voltage regulator holds a power supply's output at a set voltage even when the input voltage or the load changes.
T6D05.hint: The supply must keep its output steady while the load and input change. What do we call something that keeps a value under control?
why: A regulator controls the output voltage of a power supply and keeps it steady.
An oscillator generates a signal at a set frequency. It does not control supply voltage.
A filter passes some frequencies and blocks others. In a supply it smooths ripple but does not set the voltage.
A phase inverter produces a signal opposite in phase to its input. It does not control supply voltage.

T6D06.concept: A transformer has two coils sharing a magnetic field. AC in one coil induces AC in the other, and the ratio of turns sets whether the voltage goes up or down.
T6D06.hint: The input is AC and the output is still AC, only lower. Which part passes energy between two coils by a changing magnetic field?
why: A variable capacitor is an adjustable capacitor used for tuning circuits, not for changing power voltage.
A transformer steps AC voltage up or down. With fewer turns on the output coil, 120 V AC becomes a lower AC voltage.
A transistor amplifies or switches signals. It is not the part that steps down AC power voltage.
A diode passes current one way, which turns AC into varying DC. It does not give a lower AC voltage.

T6D07.concept: A visual indicator is a part that shows you something by lighting up, such as a power-on light. A light-emitting diode does this with very little current and lasts a long time.
T6D07.hint: A visual indicator has to be seen. Go through each part and ask whether it produces anything visible.
why: An LED (light-emitting diode) glows when forward current flows, so it is widely used as an indicator light.
An FET is a field-effect transistor used to amplify or switch. It gives off no light.
A Zener diode is used to hold a steady voltage. It gives off no light.
FETs and Zener diodes are not visual indicators, so not all of the choices are true.

T6D08.concept: A resonant circuit swaps energy back and forth between a magnetic field and an electric field at one natural frequency. That takes one part of each kind.
T6D08.hint: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field. Resonance needs a partner that stores energy in the other kind of field.
why: A resistor only turns energy into heat. It cannot trade energy back and forth with an inductor.
A Zener diode is used to hold a steady voltage. It does not form a resonant circuit with an inductor.
A potentiometer is a variable resistor. Like any resistor, it only loses energy as heat.
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. Paired with an inductor, energy swings between them at one frequency.

T6D09.concept: An integrated circuit (IC) packs many transistors, diodes, resistors and other parts onto one small chip in a single package, doing the job of a whole circuit.
T6D09.hint: Think of the small black chips with many pins on a circuit board. Their name describes many parts merged into one.
why: A transducer changes one form of energy into another, as a microphone or speaker does.
A multi-pole relay is an electrically-controlled switch with several sets of contacts, not a package of semiconductors.
An integrated circuit combines many semiconductors and other components in one package.
A transformer is coils of wire sharing a magnetic core. It contains no semiconductors.

T6D10.concept: In figure T-1, component 2 is a circle with a thick bar, three leads and an arrow on one lead: a transistor. A small signal at its control lead sets how much current flows through the lamp.
T6D10.hint: First name the part: a circle with three leads and an arrow. Then recall what that part does with a small signal on its middle lead.
why: Giving off light is the job of the lamp, the small dome shape marked as component 3.
Supplying electrical energy is the job of the battery, the stacked long and short lines at component 4.
Component 2 is a transistor. The small input signal lets it control the current flowing through the lamp.
Turning electrical energy into radio waves is what an antenna does. There is no antenna in this figure.

T6D11.concept: A resonant or tuned circuit pairs an inductor (coil) with a capacitor. Energy swings between them at one natural frequency, so the circuit favors that frequency.
T6D11.hint: Tuning to one frequency takes two parts that store energy in different ways and pass it back and forth.
why: An inductor and a capacitor connected in series or in parallel form a resonant circuit, tuned to one frequency.
A linear voltage regulator holds a steady DC voltage. It is not tuned to a frequency.
Resistors behave the same at all frequencies, so a resistor circuit is not resonant or tuned.
High-fidelity audio circuits are meant to treat a wide range of frequencies equally, the opposite of tuned.

T7A01.concept: Two key receiver qualities: one is how weak a signal it can still hear, the other is how well it separates signals that are close together in frequency. This question is about hearing the faintest signals.
T7A01.hint: Think of your own hearing: what word describes ears that can pick up a very faint whisper?
why: RF gain is a control that sets how much the receiver amplifies incoming radio signals. It is a knob setting, not the name of the receiver's ability to detect weak signals.
Sensitivity is how weak a signal a receiver can detect. A more sensitive receiver hears fainter signals.
Selectivity is the ability to separate one signal from others nearby in frequency, not the ability to detect that a signal is there.
Total harmonic distortion measures how much an amplifier adds unwanted multiples of a signal's frequency. It is not about detecting signals.

T7A02.concept: Most ham radios put the part that sends and the part that listens in one box, sharing a tuning dial and an antenna. The name of the box is built from the names of its two halves.
T7A02.hint: Break the word into two pieces. Which two radio words were blended to make it?
why: A transceiver is a transmitter and a receiver combined in one unit: trans(mitter) plus (re)ceiver.
Matching a feed line's impedance to 50 ohms is the job of an antenna tuner or matching network, not a transceiver.
A device that sends and decodes Morse code automatically is a keyer or code reader, not what a transceiver is.
A device that converts a radio's receive and transmit frequencies to another band is a transverter, a similar-sounding but different thing.

T7A03.concept: A mixer combines two signals and produces new signals at the sum and the difference of their frequencies. Radios use this to shift a signal from one frequency to another.
T7A03.hint: Which circuit takes in two signals and gives out their sum and difference frequencies?
why: A phase splitter produces two copies of a signal with different phase (timing). The frequency stays the same.
A mixer combines the signal with a second one and produces sum and difference frequencies, moving the signal to a new frequency.
An inverter flips a signal's polarity or, in power equipment, turns DC into AC. It is not the circuit radios use to shift a signal's frequency.
An amplifier makes a signal stronger without changing its frequency.

T7A04.concept: Two key receiver qualities: one is how weak a signal it can hear, the other is how well it picks one signal out from others close by in frequency. This question is about picking one out.
T7A04.hint: Imagine a crowded party. What do you call the ability to choose one voice and ignore the ones around it?
why: Discrimination ratio is not the standard term for this receiver ability, even though the question uses the word discriminate.
Sensitivity is the ability to detect weak signals, not to separate signals from each other.
Selectivity is the ability to select the wanted signal and reject others close to it in frequency. Filters in the receiver provide it.
Harmonic distortion is unwanted energy at multiples of a signal's frequency. It is a flaw in an amplifier, not a receiver's ability to separate signals.

T7A05.concept: An oscillator is a circuit that creates its own steady, repeating signal at a set frequency. Nearly every transmitter and modern receiver relies on one.
T7A05.hint: Most circuits change a signal they are given. Which kind makes a steady repeating signal all by itself?
why: A reactance modulator changes the frequency or phase of an existing signal to produce FM. It does not create the signal.
A phase modulator shifts the phase (timing) of an existing signal to carry information. It does not generate the signal.
A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones. It removes signals, it does not generate them.
An oscillator generates a signal at a specific frequency, set by parts such as a crystal or a tuned circuit.

T7A06.concept: A transverter sits between a transceiver and the antenna and shifts both the transmitted and the received signals to a different band, letting one radio work on a band it does not cover.
T7A06.hint: The name blends the word transceiver with the word for something that changes one thing into another.
why: A high-pass filter passes frequencies above a cutoff and blocks those below. It does not move signals to another band.
A low-pass filter passes frequencies below a cutoff and blocks those above. It does not move signals to another band.
A transverter converts a transceiver's RF output and input to another band, so a radio can be used on a band it does not cover itself.
A phase converter is power equipment that changes single-phase AC into three-phase AC. It has nothing to do with radio bands.

T7A07.concept: PTT stands for push-to-talk. Pressing the button connects the PTT line to ground, and that tells the radio to stop listening and start transmitting.
T7A07.hint: Spell out what the three letters stand for, then think about what happens when you press that button on a microphone.
why: A Morse key plugs into a separate key input. The PTT line is the push-to-talk control.
Grounding the PTT (push-to-talk) input switches the transceiver from receive to transmit. Releasing it returns the radio to receive.
Sending a tuning tone is not what the PTT input does. It only switches the radio between receive and transmit.
A preamplifier tuning tone input is not what PTT is. PTT means push-to-talk.

T7A08.concept: A plain radio wave (the carrier) carries no information. Modulation is the process of changing the carrier in step with your voice or data so the wave carries the message.
T7A08.hint: A bare carrier says nothing. What is the general word for the process of impressing information onto it?
why: Impedance matching makes a load look like the impedance a source expects so power transfers well. It does not add speech to a signal.
Oscillation is generating a steady repeating signal. That makes the carrier but does not put speech on it.
Modulation is combining speech (or other information) with an RF carrier, by varying the carrier's amplitude, frequency or phase.
Low-pass filtering removes frequencies above a cutoff. It does not combine speech with a carrier.

T7A09.concept: SSB signals vary in strength with your voice, so an amplifier must be set to follow them faithfully (linear operation). CW and FM have constant strength and can be amplified in a more efficient but non-linear way.
T7A09.hint: The amplifier only boosts what the radio sends it. Ask what the amplifier itself needs to know to handle each kind of signal well.
why: The mode is chosen at the transceiver. The amplifier only boosts the signal it is given and cannot change its mode.
The switch sets up the amplifier, such as its bias, to work properly with the chosen mode. SSB needs linear amplification; CW and FM do not.
The switch does not shift the amplifier's frequency range. The band segment used is set by the transceiver's tuning.
A transmit amplifier's mode switch has nothing to do with reducing noise on received signals.

T7A10.concept: To get more transmit power than the radio itself produces, you add a separate stage after it that takes the radio's signal and makes it stronger.
T7A10.hint: You want the same signal, only stronger. Which kind of circuit makes signals stronger?
why: A potentiometer is a variable resistor. It can only reduce a signal, not increase power.
An RF power amplifier takes the transceiver's output and boosts it to a higher power level before it goes to the antenna.
An impedance multiplier is not a real device for increasing transmitter power.
Only the RF power amplifier increases output power. A potentiometer cannot, and an impedance multiplier is not a real device for this.

T7A11.concept: A VFO is an oscillator whose frequency you can change with the tuning knob. Turning the knob moves the frequency the radio listens and transmits on.
T7A11.hint: Which control do you turn to move around the band? Think about what that knob is adjusting inside the radio.
why: The VFO is the tunable oscillator that sets the frequency the transceiver receives and transmits on. Turning the tuning knob adjusts it.
Automatic frequency control is a different circuit that keeps a receiver locked onto a signal. The VFO is tuned by the operator.
The oscillator injected to make CW audible is the beat frequency oscillator (BFO), not the VFO.
Generating and demodulating single sideband is done by modulator and detector circuits, not by the VFO.

T7B01.concept: On FM, louder audio makes the signal swing farther in frequency. That swing is called deviation. Too much audio makes the signal too wide and distorted.
T7B01.hint: On FM, the loudness reaching the microphone sets how far the signal swings in frequency. How would you reduce it?
why: Talking louder increases deviation (the frequency swing of an FM signal), making the problem worse.
Temperature is not the cause. Over-deviation comes from too much audio reaching the transmitter.
Transmitter power does not set deviation. More power gives a stronger signal that is still over-deviating.
Moving back from the microphone lowers the audio level reaching it, which reduces deviation (the frequency swing of an FM signal).

T7B02.concept: A strong nearby transmitter can overwhelm a receiver even when the transmitter is clean and on its own frequency. This is called fundamental overload, and the weakness is in the receiver.
T7B02.hint: The ham signal is not on a broadcast frequency, yet the broadcast radio hears it. Which piece of equipment is failing to do its job?
why: A broadcast receiver with poor filtering cannot reject a strong signal from outside its band, so the amateur signal gets in. This is called fundamental overload.
Too much microphone gain distorts the transmitted audio. It does not make a broadcast radio pick up an out-of-band signal.
An overloaded transmitter audio amplifier distorts your voice. It is not why a broadcast receiver picks up the transmission.
Low deviation only makes an FM signal sound quiet. It does not cause a broadcast radio to receive the transmission.

T7B03.concept: Interference can come from the receiver being overwhelmed by a strong clean signal, or from the transmitter putting out unwanted signals on frequencies other than the intended one.
T7B03.hint: Consider each item separately: could it, by itself, put unwanted signal into someone's receiver?
why: Fundamental overload is a receiver being overwhelmed by a strong signal on the transmitter's intended frequency. It does cause interference.
Harmonics are unwanted signals at whole-number multiples of the transmit frequency. They can land on other services and interfere.
Spurious emissions are any unwanted signals outside the intended transmission. They can interfere with other receivers.
Fundamental overload, harmonics and spurious emissions are all real causes of radio frequency interference.

T7B04.concept: SWR (standing wave ratio) shows how well the antenna system is matched to the transmitter. With a poor match, power reflects back, and solid-state radios cut their output to protect themselves.
T7B04.hint: Modern radios protect their final transistors. Which antenna system condition would make a radio deliberately hold back its power?
why: Noise figure describes how much noise an amplifier adds to weak received signals. It does not explain low transmit power.
Poor linearity causes distortion of the signal, not what the question describes as low power output.
A low SWR means a good match, which lets the transceiver deliver full power.
A high SWR means a poor match with power reflected back. The transceiver's protection circuit reduces output to protect the final transistors.

T7B05.concept: When a clean amateur signal overloads another receiver, the cure belongs at that receiver: a filter at its antenna input that keeps the amateur signal out while letting the wanted signals through.
T7B05.hint: The amateur signal is legitimate and on its proper frequency. Where must the unwanted energy be stopped?
why: A filter at the affected receiver's antenna input blocks the amateur signal before it can overload the receiver, while passing the signals the receiver wants.
A filter on the transmitter that blocked the interfering signal would block the amateur's own intended transmission, since that signal is the one being received.
Changing from FM to SSB still puts a strong signal at the receiver's input. It is not the fix the question describes.
A narrow-band mode is still a strong signal on the same frequency, so the affected receiver is still exposed to it.

T7B06.concept: When a neighbor reports interference, first check your own house: confirm your station works properly and see whether it disturbs your own radio or TV on the same channel.
T7B06.hint: Before anything else, how could you find out whether your own equipment is at fault? Think about what is in your own home.
why: Checking that your station works properly and does not interfere with your own radio or TV on the same channel is the sensible first step.
Shutting down and calling the FCC is not the expected response. Operators are expected to investigate and resolve interference themselves first.
A harmonic doubler is not a real interference cure. Doubling harmonics would be the opposite of what you want.
Not all are right. Contacting an FCC office is not the proper step, and a harmonic doubler is not a real fix.

T7B07.concept: A strong signal on a nearby frequency can overload a receiver. A band-reject (notch) filter blocks one range of frequencies and lets the rest pass, so it can remove the offender and keep the wanted signals.
T7B07.hint: You want to knock down one known range of frequencies and leave everything else alone. What kind of device does that?
why: A preamplifier boosts everything, including the strong unwanted FM broadcast signal, so it makes overload worse.
Better shielded coax does not help, because the broadcast signal arrives through the antenna along with the wanted signals.
Bypass capacitors on the microphone cable deal with RF getting into transmit audio, not with a strong signal overloading the receiver.
A band-reject filter blocks the FM broadcast band while passing 2-meter signals, keeping the strong station out of the receiver.

T7B08.concept: When a neighbor's device interferes with your station, handle it cooperatively: confirm your own station is in order, help find the source, and courteously explain the rules.
T7B08.hint: Think about a good-neighbor approach. Would any of these steps be unreasonable or untrue?
why: Working with your neighbor to find the offending device is a proper step. You cannot fix it until the source is identified.
Politely telling the neighbor that FCC rules prohibit devices from causing harmful interference is a proper and true step.
Checking that your own station meets good amateur practice is a proper step, so you know the problem is not at your end.
All three are appropriate: work with the neighbor, politely explain the FCC rules, and make sure your own station is in good order.

T7B09.concept: Coaxial cable TV systems are shielded, so signals should stay inside and outside signals should stay out. Loose or badly fitted connectors break that shield and let your signal leak in.
T7B09.hint: A cable system is meant to be a sealed pipe for signals. Where is such a pipe most likely to leak?
why: A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones. Adding one to the TV input is not the first step and could block wanted TV signals.
A high-pass filter may help in some cases, but it is not the first step. Check the basic integrity of the cable system first.
A preamplifier would boost the interfering signal along with everything else. It is not a fix.
Poorly installed coaxial connectors let outside signals leak into the cable system, so checking them is the first step.

T7B10.concept: Bad audio through an FM repeater has several common causes: being off frequency, too much audio into the microphone, or a weak or reflected path from where you stand.
T7B10.hint: Consider each item separately: could it, by itself, make your voice hard to understand through a repeater?
why: Being slightly off frequency makes the repeater's receiver recover your audio poorly, so it sounds distorted.
Speaking too loudly or too close to the microphone causes over-deviation (too wide an FM signal), which distorts the audio.
A bad location gives a weak signal or reflections into the repeater, making audio noisy or broken up.
Being off frequency, overdriving the microphone and being in a bad location can each cause distorted or unintelligible audio.

T7B11.concept: Your own transmitted signal can be picked up by the microphone cable and get into the audio circuits, distorting your voice. A ferrite choke clipped on the cable blocks that stray RF.
T7B11.hint: Think about your own radio signal sneaking back into the radio along a wire it should not be on. How do you stop RF on a cable?
why: Adding feed line does not fix an antenna mismatch, and SWR is not what distorts voice audio in this way.
Switching the radio off and on is not a cure for distorted transmit audio. It does not remove the cause.
A clip-on ferrite choke on the microphone cable stops transmitted RF from travelling along the cable back into the transmitter's audio.
Squelch only mutes the receiver's speaker when no signal is present. It has no effect on your transmitted audio.

T7C01.concept: A dummy load is a resistor that stands in for the antenna. The transmitter sees a proper load, but the power turns to heat, so you can test without putting a signal on the air.
T7C01.hint: The word dummy means a stand-in for the real thing. What is it standing in for, and what does that let you avoid?
why: A dummy load absorbs the transmitter's power as heat in place of an antenna, so tests do not put signals over the air.
Over-modulation is controlled by audio level settings such as microphone gain, not by a dummy load.
A dummy load replaces the antenna during tests. It does nothing to make an antenna more efficient.
A dummy load is used for transmitter testing. It does not improve a receiver's signal-to-noise ratio.

T7C02.concept: An antenna is resonant at the frequency where its feed point looks like a pure resistance. An antenna analyzer sends a tiny test signal across a range of frequencies and shows SWR and impedance at each one.
T7C02.hint: Which instrument is made to connect to the feed line and show how the antenna behaves across a range of frequencies?
why: A VTVM is a vacuum tube voltmeter. It measures voltage and cannot show where an antenna is resonant.
An antenna analyzer measures an antenna's SWR and impedance across frequency, showing where it is resonant.
A Q meter measures the quality factor (Q) of coils and tuned circuits. It is not the tool used to check antenna resonance.
A frequency counter measures the frequency of a signal. It does not tell you how an antenna responds at that frequency.

T7C03.concept: A dummy load must look like a perfect 50-ohm antenna to the transmitter and safely get rid of the power as heat. So it is a pure resistance with a way to shed heat.
T7C03.hint: The load must present what most ham transmitters expect to see, and all the power has to go somewhere. Where does it go?
why: A power supply and an AC relay are not a dummy load. A dummy load is a passive part that absorbs power.
A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor matches the transmitter and turns its power into heat, which the heat sink carries away.
A power supply and a DC relay are not a dummy load. A dummy load needs no power supply.
Inductive reactance stores and returns energy and does not absorb it. A dummy load must be a pure resistance to give a good match.

T7C04.concept: SWR (standing wave ratio) compares how well the antenna's impedance matches the feed line. It is a ratio: when the two are equal, all power is accepted and nothing reflects back.
T7C04.hint: SWR is a ratio comparing two things. What does a ratio look like when the two things are exactly equal?
why: 50:50 is not how SWR is written. The 50 probably comes from 50 ohms, a common impedance, but SWR is not expressed that way.
SWR never reads zero. The lowest possible value, a perfect match, is still a ratio of one to one.
1:1 means the antenna and feed line impedances are equal, so no power is reflected. That is a perfect match.
A full-scale reading means a very high SWR, which is a severe mismatch, the opposite of a perfect match.

T7C05.concept: High SWR means power is reflected back toward the transmitter. That can put excess voltage or current on the final transistors, so the radio automatically cuts power to keep them safe.
T7C05.hint: Reflected power comes back to the radio's final stage. Which parts there are most at risk?
why: Reflected power from a high SWR can overstress the RF output transistors, so the radio folds back its power to protect them.
The power reduction is a self-protection feature. It is not there to meet FCC spectral purity rules.
The limit is not the power supply's current. The reduction is deliberate protection of the output stage.
Reducing power does not change the SWR. SWR depends on the match between antenna and feed line, not on power level.

T7C06.concept: SWR (standing wave ratio) of 1:1 is a perfect match between feed line and antenna. The bigger the first number, the worse the match and the more power is reflected.
T7C06.hint: Compare the reading with the ideal value for SWR. Is it close to ideal or far from it?
why: SWR is a ratio describing match, not a loss in decibels. 4:1 does not mean a loss of 4 dB.
A good match is close to 1:1. A reading of 4:1 is far from that.
SWR is not a gain figure. 4:1 does not mean a gain of 4 dB.
4:1 is well above the ideal 1:1, showing the antenna's impedance does not match the feed line. A good share of the power is reflected.

T7C07.concept: No feed line is perfect. The conductors have resistance and the insulation absorbs a little energy, so some of the signal is lost along the way, the same way any resistance warms up.
T7C07.hint: Energy cannot vanish. When current flows through something with resistance, what form does the lost energy take?
why: Lost power does not raise SWR. Feed line loss actually makes the SWR measured at the transmitter look lower than it really is.
Harmonics are created in the transmitter, not by loss in the feed line.
Power lost in a feed line is converted into heat, in the resistance of the conductors and in the insulating material.
Feed line loss makes the signal weaker. It does not distort it.

T7C08.concept: SWR can be worked out by comparing power going toward the antenna (forward) with power coming back (reflected). An instrument that senses power in each direction can provide both numbers.
T7C08.hint: To find SWR you need to know about power travelling in two opposite ways along the line. Which instrument can tell them apart?
why: A voltmeter measures voltage between two points. An ordinary voltmeter cannot tell forward power from reflected power.
An ohmmeter measures DC resistance. It cannot measure how RF power behaves on a feed line.
Iambic pentameter is a rhythm used in poetry, not an instrument. It is a joke choice.
A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately, and SWR can be calculated from those two readings.

T7C09.concept: Coax depends on its insulation staying clean and dry. Water that gets in through a cracked jacket or a poorly sealed connector corrodes the conductors and sharply raises loss.
T7C09.hint: Most coax lives outdoors for years. What does the weather bring that a cable must be sealed against?
why: Moisture contamination is the most common cause of coax failure. Water inside the cable corrodes the shield and increases loss.
Solder flux contamination is not the cause of coaxial cable failure the question is looking for.
Changes in transmitter power do not damage coax as long as the cable is used within its ratings.
Continuous transmitting within the cable's power rating does not cause failure. It is not what the question describes.

T7C10.concept: The outer jacket is the cable's raincoat. Sunlight's ultraviolet light breaks down plastics that are not made to resist it, and a cracked jacket lets water in.
T7C10.hint: Think about what happens to ordinary plastic left in the sun for years, and what the jacket is there to keep out.
why: Ultraviolet light does not change the resistance of the metal conductors. The jacket is what it harms.
The jacket does not carry the signal, so losses in the jacket are not the concern.
Ultraviolet light and RF signals do not mix to cause interference. This is not a real effect.
Ultraviolet light makes an unprotected jacket brittle and cracked, and the cracks let water into the cable.

T7C11.concept: The dielectric is the insulation between a coax cable's center conductor and its shield. Foam is partly air, and air absorbs less signal energy than solid plastic.
T7C11.hint: Foam is plastic full of tiny air pockets. How does air compare with solid plastic at soaking up a passing signal?
why: Foam dielectric is not more resistant to moisture than solid dielectric, so this is not its advantage.
Foam dielectric does not have higher voltage breakdown than solid dielectric, so this is not its advantage.
Foam dielectric has less loss per foot than solid dielectric, so more of the signal reaches the other end.
Both kinds of cable are made at 50 ohms. Foam does not give a better impedance match.

T7D01.concept: Electric potential is another name for voltage, the electrical push between two points. It is measured in volts, and each basic meter is named after the unit it measures.
T7D01.hint: Electric potential has a more common everyday name and a unit. Meters are usually named after their unit.
why: An ammeter measures current, the flow of electricity, in amperes.
A voltmeter measures electric potential, which is voltage, in volts.
A potentiometer is a variable resistor, such as a volume control. Despite its name it is a component, not the meter used here.
An ohmmeter measures resistance, the opposition to current, in ohms.

T7D02.concept: Voltage is a difference between two points, so the meter's two probes touch the two ends of the component. The meter sits alongside the part without breaking the circuit.
T7D02.hint: Voltage is a difference between two points. Do you need to break the circuit open to compare two points?
why: In series means the circuit is broken and the meter inserted in the current path. That is how current is measured, not voltage.
In parallel means the probes go across the component, one on each end, so the meter reads the voltage difference between them.
Quadrature means a 90-degree phase difference between two signals. It is not a way to connect a meter.
In phase describes two signals whose cycles line up in time. It is not a way to connect a meter.

T7D03.concept: Current is the flow through a circuit. To measure it, the flow has to pass through the meter, like a water meter fitted into a pipe.
T7D03.hint: Picture a water meter. Where does it have to sit for all of the water to be counted?
why: In series means the circuit is opened and the meter inserted in the path, so all the current flows through the meter.
In parallel is how voltage is measured. A meter set for current placed across a component can cause a short circuit.
Quadrature means a 90-degree phase difference between two signals. It is not a way to connect a meter.
In phase describes two signals whose cycles line up in time. It is not a way to connect a meter.

T7D04.concept: Electric current is the flow of charge and is measured in amperes. Each basic meter is named after the unit it measures.
T7D04.hint: What unit is current measured in? Meters are usually named after their unit.
why: An ohmmeter measures resistance in ohms, not current.
An electrometer is not the instrument normally used to measure current in a circuit. It is not what the question describes.
A voltmeter measures voltage, the electrical push, not the flow of current.
An ammeter measures electric current in amperes. The name comes from the ampere.

T7D05.concept: An ohmmeter uses Ohm's law. It has its own battery, pushes a small known current through the part, reads the voltage that appears, and works out the resistance from the two.
T7D05.hint: Ohm's law links three quantities. If the meter supplies one and measures a second, it can work out the third.
why: The meter passes a small known current through the component and measures the voltage across it. Resistance is voltage divided by current.
Putting a variable resistor in parallel with the circuit is not how an ohmmeter works.
Putting a variable resistor in series with the circuit is not how an ohmmeter works.
An ohmmeter does not vary the voltage and watch the current change. It applies a small current and measures the resulting voltage.

T7D06.concept: On the resistance setting a multimeter supplies its own small test current and expects a dead circuit. Connecting it to a live voltage forces outside current through that delicate circuit.
T7D06.hint: One meter setting sends out its own small test signal and expects nothing to push back. What happens if something does?
why: Trying to read resistance on the voltage setting just gives a meaningless reading. It does not harm the meter.
A multimeter measures between its two probes. Neither probe has to be connected to ground, and leaving ground off does no harm.
On the resistance setting the meter is not built to have voltage applied. Connecting it to a live voltage can damage it.
A multimeter does not need to warm up, and skipping a warm-up cannot damage it.

T7D07.concept: A multimeter is several basic meters in one case. It measures the fundamental electrical quantities: voltage, current and resistance.
T7D07.hint: A multimeter is a few basic single-purpose meters in one case. Which simple quantities can be read with just two probes and no radio signal?
why: Signal strength and noise are measured by a receiver's S meter or special test equipment, not by a multimeter.
Impedance and reactance at radio frequencies need an instrument such as an antenna analyzer, not a basic multimeter.
Voltage and resistance are standard multimeter measurements, along with current.
Not all are right. A multimeter does not measure signal strength and noise, or impedance and reactance.

T7D08.concept: Solder has a core of flux, a cleaner that helps the metal flow and bond. Electronics need a mild flux. A corrosive flux made for plumbing keeps eating at wires and parts afterwards.
T7D08.hint: One kind of solder is made for plumbing and sheet metal. Its cleaning agent keeps attacking metal long after the joint cools.
why: Acid-core solder leaves a corrosive residue that eats away wires, component leads and circuit board traces. It is meant for plumbing.
Lead-tin solder is the traditional solder alloy for electronics work.
Rosin-core solder is the standard choice for electronics. Its rosin flux is mild and does not corrode the joint.
Tin-copper solder is a lead-free alloy that is used in electronics.

T7D09.concept: A cold solder joint forms when the joint was not hot enough or moved while cooling. The solder does not flow and bond properly, and the surface shows it.
T7D09.hint: Picture solder that never melted fully and flowed smoothly. What would its surface look like next to a good joint?
why: Dark black spots are not the sign of a cold joint. They are not what the question describes.
A bright or shiny surface is what a good tin-lead solder joint looks like.
A cold joint looks rough or lumpy and dull, because the solder did not melt and flow fully onto the metal.
A greenish tinge suggests corrosion, not a cold solder joint.

T7D10.concept: An ohmmeter sends a small current into whatever it touches. A discharged capacitor soaks up that current as it charges, then takes less and less as it fills.
T7D10.hint: The meter's battery starts filling the capacitor. How does the current flowing change as it fills, and how would the meter show that?
why: At first the capacitor draws current and looks like a low resistance. As it charges the current falls, so the reading climbs.
Decreasing resistance would mean current growing over time. A charging capacitor draws less and less current.
A steady reading does not show the charging action. With a capacitor the reading changes over time.
Alternating between open and short circuit is not how a capacitor behaves on an ohmmeter.

T7D11.concept: An ohmmeter supplies its own small test current. Any other voltage in the circuit upsets the reading and can damage the meter, so the circuit must be dead.
T7D11.hint: The ohmmeter brings its own source of electricity. What should be true of every other source in the circuit?
why: There should be no applied voltages at all during a resistance measurement, so checking that they are correct is the wrong precaution.
With the circuit not powered, the only current is the meter's own, so the reading is right and the meter is safe.
Grounding the circuit is not what an ohmmeter needs. It measures between its two probes.
An ohmmeter measures with its own small direct current. The circuit's operating frequency does not matter because the circuit should be off.

T8A01.concept: Amplitude modulation (AM) carries voice by varying the strength of the signal. A full AM signal has a carrier and two mirror-image sidebands; single sideband keeps just one of those sidebands.
T8A01.hint: A full AM signal has a carrier and two sidebands. Ask which of these modes is built from just part of that same signal.
why: Spread spectrum spreads a signal across a wide range of frequencies. It is a different technique, not a kind of AM.
Packet radio is a way of sending data in small error-checked bundles. It names a data method, not a kind of AM.
Single sideband is AM with the carrier and one sideband removed, leaving one sideband that still carries the whole voice.
Phase shift keying sends data by changing the timing (phase) of the signal, not its strength.

T8A02.concept: VHF packet radio usually sends data as audio tones through an ordinary VHF voice radio, so it uses the same modulation those radios use: frequency modulation or the closely related phase modulation.
T8A02.hint: Think about the kind of ordinary handheld or mobile radio most hams already own for 2 meters, and what modulation it uses.
why: VHF packet tones are fed into a normal VHF radio, which uses frequency modulation (FM) or phase modulation (PM).
SSB (single sideband) is used for weak-signal VHF voice and for HF, but it is not the common choice for VHF packet.
AM (amplitude modulation) is rarely used on VHF by amateurs and is not the common packet method.
PSK (phase shift keying) is a keyboard data mode seen mostly on HF, not the usual VHF packet modulation.

T8A03.concept: A narrower signal packs its power into less spectrum, and the receiver lets in less noise. That is why the narrow voice mode, not the wide repeater mode, is chosen for weak, long-distance VHF and UHF contacts.
T8A03.hint: For a faint signal you want all the power squeezed into as little bandwidth as possible. Which voice mode is narrowest?
why: FM (frequency modulation) is wide and needs a fairly strong signal to sound clear, so it suits local and repeater work.
DRM is not the voice mode amateurs commonly use for weak-signal VHF and UHF contacts.
SSB (single sideband) is narrow, about 3 kHz, so it stays readable when signals are weak over long paths.
PM (phase modulation) behaves much like FM: wide, and best for strong local signals.

T8A04.concept: Voice repeaters on VHF and UHF use frequency modulation or its close cousin phase modulation. These give clear, quiet audio on strong local signals and are what handheld and mobile radios are built for.
T8A04.hint: Think of the everyday handheld radio. Its audio is clear and free of static once the signal is strong enough. Which modulation gives that?
why: AM (amplitude modulation) varies signal strength and picks up more static. It is not the usual repeater mode.
SSB (single sideband) is used for weak-signal and HF voice, not for typical voice repeaters.
PSK (phase shift keying) is a data mode, not a common repeater voice mode.
Repeaters and the radios that use them carry voice with frequency modulation (FM) or phase modulation (PM).

T8A05.concept: Bandwidth is how much spectrum a signal occupies. The less information sent per second, the less space needed. A carrier simply switched on and off for Morse code needs very little.
T8A05.hint: Rank the choices by how much information each sends per second. The simplest signal takes the least room.
why: FM voice is the widest of these, roughly 10 to 15 kHz.
SSB voice is about 3 kHz wide: narrow for voice, but far wider than Morse code.
CW (Morse code by on-off keying) needs only about 150 Hz, the narrowest of these signals.
Slow-scan TV sends pictures as audio tones and takes about as much room as a voice signal.

T8A06.concept: By convention, hams use upper sideband on the higher bands (20 meters and up, including all VHF and UHF) and lower sideband on the low HF bands such as 40 and 80 meters. Both stations must use the same sideband.
T8A06.hint: The convention depends on frequency. Where do these bands sit compared with the low HF bands such as 40 and 80 meters?
why: Upper sideband is the convention on the higher bands, including 10 meters, VHF and UHF.
Lower sideband is the convention on the lower HF bands such as 40, 80 and 160 meters.
Every SSB signal has one sideband suppressed, so this does not name which one is used.
Inverted sideband is not the name of the sideband normally used here.

T8A07.concept: An SSB voice signal is about 3 kHz wide, while an FM voice signal is about 10 to 15 kHz wide. SSB uses much less spectrum, which also helps with weak signals.
T8A07.hint: Compare how much room each mode takes up on the band.
why: SSB is harder to tune: a small frequency error makes the voice sound unnatural. FM is the more forgiving mode.
FM is better at rejecting static and weaker signals, so this is not an SSB advantage.
SSB occupies about 3 kHz, against roughly 10 to 15 kHz for FM voice.
SWR (standing wave ratio) describes the antenna and feed line match. The voice mode does not change it.

T8A08.concept: The useful part of speech covers roughly 300 Hz to 3000 Hz. SSB sends just one copy of that audio range, so the signal is about as wide as the voice itself.
T8A08.hint: SSB sends one copy of the speech frequencies and nothing else. How wide is the range of tones needed for clear speech?
why: 1 kHz is too narrow to carry understandable speech.
One sideband carries the speech range, so a typical SSB voice signal is about 3 kHz wide.
6 kHz is about the width of a full AM voice signal, which has two sidebands.
15 kHz is in the range of an FM voice signal, not SSB.

T8A09.concept: FM spreads the voice over more spectrum than the audio itself needs, which is part of why it sounds clean. A repeater FM voice signal is several times wider than an SSB voice signal.
T8A09.hint: It is several times wider than a 3 kHz SSB signal, but far narrower than an FM broadcast station.
why: Less than 500 Hz is the range of narrow modes such as Morse code, far too little for FM voice.
About 150 kHz is in the range of FM broadcast radio, not amateur repeater voice.
An FM voice signal on a VHF repeater takes roughly 10 to 15 kHz.
50 to 125 kHz is many times wider than amateur FM voice.

T8A10.concept: Fast-scan TV sends full-motion video like analog broadcast television. Moving pictures hold a huge amount of information, so the signal needs megahertz of spectrum, the same as an old analog TV channel.
T8A10.hint: This is the same kind of signal as an old analog broadcast TV channel. How wide was one of those channels?
why: More than 10 MHz is wider than this type of TV signal needs.
AM fast-scan TV matches an analog broadcast TV channel, which is about 6 MHz wide.
About 3 MHz is too narrow for a standard AM fast-scan TV signal.
About 1 MHz is much too narrow for full-motion analog video.

T8A11.concept: CW is a carrier turned on and off to form Morse code. That carries very little information per second, so it needs only a sliver of spectrum, far less than any voice mode.
T8A11.hint: Think about how little information on-off Morse keying sends each second compared with a voice, and what that means for the room it needs.
why: 2.4 kHz is about the width of an SSB voice signal.
On-off keying at normal Morse speeds needs only about 150 Hz.
1000 Hz is several times more than a CW signal needs.
15 kHz is about the width of an FM voice signal.

T8A12.concept: An FM receiver locks onto the strongest signal on the channel and hides weaker ones. This is called the capture effect. On SSB, two signals are both heard at once, mixed together.
T8A12.hint: Think about what you hear when two stations transmit on the same FM channel at the same moment.
why: FM voice quality is usually very good on strong signals, so this is not its drawback.
The FM receiver captures the strongest signal and the others are hidden, so only one can be heard at a time.
FM is easier to tune than SSB: you just select the channel.
SWR (standing wave ratio) depends on the antenna system, not on the modulation used.

T8B01.concept: Telemetry means measurements sent from a distance. A satellite beacon reports on the spacecraft itself, such as battery voltage, temperatures and solar panel output, so its operators know how it is doing.
T8B01.hint: Telemetry is the spacecraft reporting on itself. What would its operators most want to know?
why: Reporting the strength of received signals is not what beacon telemetry typically carries.
A precise time-of-day service is not what satellite beacons typically send.
Beacon telemetry reports the health and status of the satellite, such as voltages and temperatures.
Signal strength reports and precise time are not typical beacon content, so not all of the items are true.

T8B02.concept: A satellite has limited power to share among everyone using it. An uplink that is too strong takes more than its share, so the satellite has less left for other stations and their signals fade or vanish.
T8B02.hint: The satellite is a shared resource with a small power budget. What happens to everyone else when one station hogs it?
why: Mode changes need deliberate command signals from the control station, not just a strong user signal.
A too-strong uplink grabs most of the satellite's output, so other users are weakened or shut out.
Overloading the batteries is not the effect the question describes. The harm falls on other users.
A strong user signal does not reboot the control computer. That is not the effect described.

T8B03.concept: A satellite tracking program calculates where a satellite is and will be. From that it can show its path on a map, list when and where it rises and sets for you, and predict how its frequency will appear to shift.
T8B03.hint: Once software knows the orbit and your location, think about everything it can calculate from the satellite's position and speed.
why: Tracking programs do draw maps with the satellite's real-time position and ground track.
They do list the time and the compass direction (azimuth) and height angle (elevation) for the start, peak and end of a pass.
They do calculate the frequency you will actually hear, corrected for Doppler shift from the satellite's motion.
Maps, pass times with pointing angles, and Doppler-corrected frequencies are all provided, so all three items are true.

T8B04.concept: Amateur satellites are not limited to one mode. Some are FM repeaters in space, some have linear transponders that relay SSB and CW, and many carry data.
T8B04.hint: Different amateur satellites are built in different ways. Ask whether any of the listed modes is actually ruled out.
why: SSB (single sideband) voice is used through satellites with linear transponders.
FM voice is used through satellites that act as single-channel FM repeaters.
CW (Morse code) and data are used on many satellites, including for beacons and telemetry.
SSB, FM, and CW or data are all in common use on amateur satellites, so all three items are true.

T8B05.concept: A beacon is a signal a satellite sends by itself, without anyone calling it. It lets you confirm the satellite is in range and usually carries telemetry about the spacecraft's condition.
T8B05.hint: In radio, a beacon is something you listen for, not something you look at.
why: A beacon is a signal, not a piece of hardware such as an antenna.
A satellite beacon is a radio signal, not a visible light.
A beacon is not a reflective surface. It is something the satellite transmits.
A beacon is a transmission from the satellite carrying information about its status.

T8B06.concept: Keplerian elements are a set of numbers that describe a satellite's orbit: its shape, tilt and where the satellite is along it. A tracking program uses them, plus your location, to predict passes.
T8B06.hint: To predict where a satellite will be, the software needs a mathematical description of its path around Earth.
why: Transmit power has nothing to do with where the satellite is, so the program does not need it.
Keplerian elements describe the orbit, which is what the program needs to calculate positions.
The program calculates Doppler shift as an output. A Doppler observation is not an input.
Transmit power and a Doppler observation are not inputs, so not all of the items are true.

T8B07.concept: Doppler shift is the change in frequency you observe when a transmitter moves toward or away from you, like a siren dropping in pitch as it passes. Satellites move fast, so the effect is noticeable.
T8B07.hint: Think of how a passing siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it leaves.
why: The orbit itself does not change. Only the frequency you observe does.
Receiving on one band and transmitting on another describes how a satellite relays signals, not Doppler shift.
The satellite's motion relative to your station makes its signal appear higher in frequency as it approaches and lower as it leaves.
Doppler shift is a physical effect on any signal, not a digital mode.

T8B08.concept: Satellite modes are named with two letters: the uplink band first, then the downlink band. U stands for UHF (the 70-centimeter band) and V stands for VHF (the 2-meter band).
T8B08.hint: The letters stand for two frequency ranges, and the order tells you which one goes up and which comes down.
why: The 15-meter and 10-meter bands are HF bands. U and V do not stand for HF.
U is UHF and V is VHF, uplink first: you transmit up on 70 centimeters and listen on 2 meters.
U and V stand for UHF and VHF radio bands, not ultraviolet light.
U/V names the two bands used. It does not mean the frequencies are variable.

T8B09.concept: Many satellites slowly tumble or spin. As they turn, their antennas point and tilt differently toward you, so the signal strength rises and falls in a regular rhythm.
T8B09.hint: The name of the effect describes something the spacecraft itself is doing.
why: Noise from the sun is not what causes this regular fading.
As the satellite and its antennas rotate, the signal reaching you gets stronger and weaker in turn.
Doppler shift changes the frequency you observe, not the signal strength.
Interfering uplink signals are a different problem and do not cause this rhythmic fading.

T8B10.concept: Most amateur satellites fly only a few hundred kilometers up. That close to Earth they must move very fast, circling the planet in about an hour and a half, so each pass over you lasts only minutes.
T8B10.hint: These satellites cross your sky in minutes. Think about how high they fly and how long one full trip around takes.
why: Low Energy Orbit is not a real term for this. The name is about height, not battery power.
Low Elevation Orbit is not what LEO means. Elevation near the horizon depends on the pass, not the orbit type.
Low Equilibrium Orbit is not a real term.
LEO is Low Earth Orbit: close to Earth, with one trip around taking roughly 100 minutes.

T8B11.concept: Amateur radio signals are open by design. Satellite telemetry is sent in publicly documented formats, and no license is needed just to receive, so anyone with a suitable receiver can listen.
T8B11.hint: A license covers transmitting. Think about whether just listening is restricted in amateur radio.
why: Receiving needs no license or permission, so anyone may receive satellite telemetry.
The control operator is not the only one who may listen. Telemetry is open to all.
No encryption key is needed. Amateur telemetry is not hidden from the public.
No key from AMSAT and no license are required to receive telemetry.

T8B12.concept: A linear transponder relays a whole slice of band and shares its power among all users. The satellite's beacon is a handy yardstick for how strong one fair signal should be on the downlink.
T8B12.hint: You can hear your own signal coming back down. Think about what known, steady signal you could measure it against.
why: Telemetry reports the spacecraft's condition. It does not give you a report on your own signal.
Listening for distortion is not the method described and does not tell you when power is too low.
If your downlink signal is about as strong as the beacon, your uplink power is about right.
Other users may themselves be too strong or too weak. The method described uses the beacon as the reference.

T8C01.concept: Radio direction finding means using an antenna that favors one direction to work out where a signal comes from. Bearings taken from several places cross at the source.
T8C01.hint: A radio signal arrives from somewhere. Think about how you could trace it back to its source with a receiver and an antenna.
why: Echolocation uses reflected sound, as bats do. It does not find radio transmitters.
Doppler radar measures the speed of objects such as rain or vehicles. It is not the method for finding interference.
Radio direction finding uses directional antennas to take bearings on a signal and trace it to its source.
Phase locking is a circuit technique for holding a frequency steady, not a way to locate a signal.

T8C02.concept: In a hidden transmitter hunt (a fox hunt), you track a signal to its source. An antenna that hears best in one direction lets you turn it and see where the signal is strongest or weakest.
T8C02.hint: You need equipment that can tell you where a signal is coming from, not how well your own station is working.
why: An SWR meter checks how well your own antenna is matched. It tells you nothing about where another signal is.
A directional antenna hears best one way, so turning it shows the bearing to the hidden transmitter.
A directional wattmeter measures power flowing in your own feed line, not the direction of a distant signal.
The SWR meter and wattmeter do not help find a transmitter, so not all of the items are useful.

T8C03.concept: Some on-air events are competitions: for a set number of hours, operators try to log as many contacts as they can, usually exchanging a short piece of information each time.
T8C03.hint: Think about which activity keeps score by counting the contacts made before time runs out.
why: Simulated emergency exercises practice passing messages in a disaster drill, not racking up contacts.
A net is an organized on-air meeting run by a net control station, not a race for contacts.
A hidden transmitter hunt is about locating one signal, not contacting many stations.
Contesting is the activity of making as many contacts as possible within the contest period.

T8C04.concept: In a contest many stations are waiting for the same contact, so speed and clarity matter. Give your full call sign and the required exchange, then move on.
T8C04.hint: Many others are waiting their turn. Think about what keeps each contact quick while still legal and complete.
why: A partial call sign is not proper identification and forces the other station to ask again, which wastes time.
A second contact with the same station is a duplicate. It adds nothing and takes time from others.
Sending just your identification and the required exchange keeps contacts fast and accurate for everyone.
Extra words such as a request to copy only slow the contact down.

T8C05.concept: The Maidenhead grid system divides the world into rectangles, each named with letters and numbers such as FN31. Hams use these short codes to say where they are, especially on VHF and in contests.
T8C05.hint: Think of the squares on a map, each with its own short label.
why: A grid locator is a short code of letters and numbers that stands for an area on the Earth's surface.
Azimuth and elevation are pointing angles for an antenna, not what a grid locator labels.
A grid locator is a code, not a test instrument for amplifiers.
A grid locator is a code, not a direction finding instrument.

T8C06.concept: IRLP links repeaters over the internet. A user controls a node from the radio keypad: the tones made by pressing the number keys tell the node which distant node to connect to.
T8C06.hint: You control the node from your radio. What on a handheld radio lets you send numbers?
why: Nodes are not controlled by speaking a password.
Keypad tones, called DTMF, sent over the air tell the node what to connect to or disconnect from.
Access over the air is by radio, so there is no internet password to type.
CTCSS is a low continuous tone that opens a repeater's squelch. It cannot send node numbers or commands.

T8C07.concept: VoIP turns speech into digital data, sends it across the internet, and turns it back into sound at the other end. Hams use it to link repeaters and stations far apart.
T8C07.hint: Read the name word by word. It describes what is carried and what carries it.
why: VoIP is a way of carrying voice, not a set of station identification rules.
Spotting DX (distant) stations online is done by spotting networks, not by VoIP.
VoIP does not measure modulation quality.
VoIP delivers voice over the internet as digital data.

T8C08.concept: IRLP uses the internet as a long link between radio systems. You talk into your local repeater by radio, and your voice comes out of a repeater that may be in another country.
T8C08.hint: Read the full name. It tells you what is being joined together and by what means.
why: IRLP joins amateur radio systems such as repeaters to each other through the internet, using VoIP.
IRLP carries voice between radio systems. It does not provide web browsing over radio.
Real-time lists of active DX (distant) stations come from spotting networks, not IRLP.
IRLP does not measure signal strength.

T8C09.concept: Some internet linking systems can only be entered with a radio. One of them also lets a licensed ham connect straight from a computer or smartphone app, with no radio at their end.
T8C09.hint: One of these systems has an app you can run on a computer or phone to reach distant repeaters.
why: IRLP is entered over the air with a radio, using keypad tones.
D-STAR is a digital voice system used with D-STAR radios. It is not the answer described here.
DMR is a digital voice system used with DMR radios. It is not the answer described here.
EchoLink lets a licensed ham connect to repeaters from a computer or smartphone, without a radio.

T8C10.concept: EchoLink lets people key up real amateur transmitters over the internet, so it must make sure every user is licensed. Each user's license is checked before access is granted.
T8C10.hint: The system puts your voice on the air through someone else's transmitter. What must it be sure of first?
why: There is no required training course for EchoLink.
You do not have to buy a license for the software to use EchoLink.
You must register your call sign and show proof of your license, so only licensed hams can transmit through it.
Any licensed amateur can use it. A General Class license is not required.

T8C11.concept: A gateway is a door between two networks. In amateur radio it is a station that passes traffic between the radio side and the internet side.
T8C11.hint: Think of the general networking word for a point where one network joins another.
why: A gateway is a station that links other amateur stations to the internet.
A repeater receives a signal and retransmits it by radio to extend range. It does not by itself connect to the internet.
A digipeater receives data packets and retransmits them by radio.
A beacon transmits one-way signals for checking propagation or for experiments.

T8D01.concept: A digital mode sends information as coded data, not as a direct copy of the voice waveform. Many very different systems fall under that heading.
T8D01.hint: Check each item on its own: does it send information as coded data?
why: Packet radio sends data in error-checked bundles, so it is digital.
IEEE 802.11 is the Wi-Fi standard, which carries digital data by radio.
FT8 is a weak-signal digital mode that sends short coded messages.
Packet radio, IEEE 802.11 and FT8 all send coded data, so all three items are true.

T8D02.concept: FT8 sends very short, fixed-format messages in timed 15-second slots using a narrow signal. Computer decoding lets it work with signals too weak for the ear to hear.
T8D02.hint: FT8 is popular because contacts succeed even when the band sounds dead.
why: FT8 is narrow and carries text data, not wideband FM voice.
FT8 is a digital mode that decodes signals well below the noise level, where voice would be lost.
FT8 has nothing to do with multiplexing channels on FM repeaters.
FT8 sends short text messages, not television pictures.

T8D03.concept: APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) sends short data packets that other stations relay and plot on maps. The packets can hold many kinds of small, useful data.
T8D03.hint: APRS packets are small and general purpose. Consider whether any listed kind of short data would not fit.
why: APRS stations commonly send their GPS position so they show up on a map.
APRS can carry short text messages between stations.
APRS weather stations send readings such as temperature and wind.
Position, text messages and weather data can all be sent by APRS, so all three items are true.

T8D04.concept: NTSC is the name of the analog color television standard once used for broadcast TV in North America. Amateur fast-scan TV uses the same kind of signal.
T8D04.hint: The letters come from a committee that set a North American broadcast standard in the mid-1900s. Think about the technology of that time.
why: NTSC is not a digital standard and has nothing to do with encryption.
NTSC is not a satellite uplink mode.
NTSC is an analog fast-scan color TV signal, the old broadcast standard.
NTSC is an analog signal format, not a compression scheme.

T8D05.concept: APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) shares positions and short messages by packet radio, shown live on a map. It is useful at events and emergencies where organizers need to see where everyone is.
T8D05.hint: The R in APRS stands for Reporting. Think about what stations report and how others view it.
why: APRS shows station locations on a map in real time along with short digital messages for local coordination.
Counting PACTOR packets is not an APRS function. PACTOR is a separate data mode.
Linking repeaters by voice over the internet is done by systems such as IRLP and EchoLink, not APRS.
APRS does not count the stations signed into a repeater.

T8D06.concept: PSK sends data by shifting the phase of a signal, meaning the point in its wave cycle, between set values. PSK31 is a well-known keyboard-to-keyboard mode that uses it.
T8D06.hint: A wave has three things you can change: its strength, its frequency, and its timing within the cycle. PSK changes the third.
why: Pulse Shift Keying is not what PSK stands for.
PSK is Phase Shift Keying: data is sent by changing the phase of the signal.
Packet Sampled Keying is not a real term.
Power Sampled Keying is not a real term.

T8D07.concept: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) is a digital voice system that splits one channel into two alternating time slots. Two separate conversations take turns many times a second on the same channel.
T8D07.hint: DMR repeaters can carry more than one conversation on a single channel. Think about how they could share it.
why: DMR time-multiplexes: two digital voice signals take rapid turns on one 12.5 kHz repeater channel.
Automatic position tracking describes APRS, not DMR.
DMR is a voice system, not a logging technique.
DMR does not transmit on two repeater inputs at once. It shares one channel in time.

T8D08.concept: Packet radio breaks data into small packets. Each one is labeled with where it is going and carries a check value so errors can be found, and a bad packet is sent again.
T8D08.hint: Think of what a parcel needs to arrive reliably: an address, a way to tell it was damaged, and a way to ask for another.
