why: Each packet carries a checksum, a number calculated from the data that lets the receiver detect errors.
Each packet has a header with the call sign of the station it is addressed to.
Packet uses automatic repeat request: a packet received with errors is sent again.
The checksum, the addressed header and automatic repeat request are all part of packet radio, so all three items are true.

T8D09.concept: CW stands for continuous wave: a steady carrier switched on and off. The pattern of short and long bursts spells out Morse code.
T8D09.hint: It is the oldest way of sending messages by radio, using a key.
why: CW is a way of transmitting, not a kind of propagation.
CW is not a 2-meter FM digital mode. It is used on nearly all amateur bands.
CW is not an error correction method.
CW (continuous wave) is the common name for a Morse code transmission.

T8D10.concept: WSJT-X is a suite of weak-signal digital modes. Different modes in it suit different difficult paths, from bouncing signals off the Moon or meteor trails to low-power beacons that test propagation.
T8D10.hint: The suite was built for signals that are extremely weak or very brief. Check whether each activity fits that.
why: Earth-Moon-Earth (bouncing signals off the Moon) is supported by WSJT-X modes.
Weak signal propagation beacons are supported: the WSPR mode is part of the suite.
Meteor scatter, using brief reflections from meteor trails, is supported by WSJT-X modes.
Moonbounce, propagation beacons and meteor scatter are all supported, so all three items are true.

T8D11.concept: ARQ stands for automatic repeat request. The receiver checks each block of data, and if it finds an error it asks the sender to send that block again.
T8D11.hint: The R and Q hint at what the receiving station does when a block of data arrives damaged.
why: ARQ is not a video format. It is used with data transmissions.
ARQ has nothing to do with encrypting satellite commands.
With ARQ the receiving station detects errors and asks for the data to be sent again.
This is a made-up description. ARQ is not a compression method.

T8D12.concept: An amateur mesh network is a high-speed data network, mostly on amateur microwave bands. Each node links by radio to its neighbors, and data hops from node to node. It is usually built from reprogrammed Wi-Fi gear.
T8D12.hint: Think about where hams could find inexpensive, mass-produced hardware that already sends fast data by radio.
why: Amateur mesh networks are data networks built from commercial Wi-Fi equipment running modified firmware.
A mesh network is a data network, not a digital voice mode based on DMR.
Mesh networks are ground-based and do not use satellite TV hardware.
Linking repeaters worldwide over the internet describes systems such as IRLP or EchoLink, not a mesh network.

T9A01.concept: A beam is a directional antenna. Like a flashlight reflector, it does not make more power; it squeezes the signal toward one direction, so it is stronger there and weaker elsewhere.
T9A01.hint: Think of a beam of light from a flashlight compared with a bare bulb.
why: The name does not come from the building material. Beams are usually made of round tubing or rods, and the word describes the radiation pattern.
A beam is the opposite of omnidirectional (equal in all compass directions), and it is not named after a person.
A beam, such as a Yagi, focuses transmitted and received signals mainly in one direction, which gives gain that way.
A beam has one main direction, not two. Two opposite lobes is closer to the pattern of a simple dipole.

T9A02.concept: Loading makes a physically short antenna act electrically longer so it resonates on a lower frequency. The usual way is a coil (inductor) placed in the radiating element.
T9A02.hint: Loading is an electrical trick for an antenna that is physically too short for its band. Which part stores energy without wasting it?
why: A coil (inductor) placed in the element makes a short antenna behave as if it were longer. This is inductive loading.
A resistor does not make an antenna resonant. It only turns transmitter power into heat.
A base spring is a mechanical part that lets a mobile whip bend. It is not electrical loading.
Making elements stronger against wind is mechanical design. Antenna loading in this sense is an electrical change.

T9A03.concept: A radio wave has an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles. Polarization is named after the electric field, which lines up with the antenna element: a vertical element gives vertical polarization.
T9A03.hint: A radio wave has two fields at right angles to each other. Only one of them is used to name the polarization.
why: The shape of the driven element (the element connected to the feed line) does not define polarization. Its orientation matters, not its shape.
Polarization is the direction of the wave's electric field. A vertical element makes a vertical electric field.
The magnetic field is at right angles to the electric field, and it is not the one used to name polarization.
The directions in which a signal is radiated are described by the radiation pattern. Polarization is how the field is oriented as it travels.

T9A04.concept: A handheld's short flexible antenna is a much-shortened antenna with a coil inside. It is convenient, but it radiates and receives less well than a full-sized quarter-wave antenna.
T9A04.hint: The short antenna is a compromise made for convenience. Think about what is given up when an antenna is made much smaller than full size.
why: A short flexible antenna is far shorter than a quarter wavelength, so less of the power is radiated. That is low efficiency.
It is not circularly polarized. Held upright, it radiates a mostly vertically polarized signal like other verticals.
Desensitization is a receiver being overloaded by a strong nearby signal. A less efficient antenna does not make that worse.
An antenna does not care whether the signal is analog or digital. It works the same for both.

T9A05.concept: Antenna length and resonant frequency move in opposite directions. A shorter wire fits a shorter wavelength, which is a higher frequency, like a shorter guitar string giving a higher note.
T9A05.hint: Picture a guitar string: what happens to the note when the vibrating part of the string changes length?
why: A longer dipole fits a longer wavelength, so its resonant frequency goes down, not up.
Coils in series make the antenna electrically longer, which lowers the resonant frequency.
A shorter dipole fits a shorter wavelength, and a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency.
Capacitive loading at the ends also makes the antenna electrically longer, lowering the resonant frequency.

T9A06.concept: Gain comes from focusing the signal. An antenna that radiates all around has little gain; a directional antenna with several elements concentrates its signal and has much more.
T9A06.hint: Sort the antennas into those that radiate all around and those that focus the signal one way.
why: A 5/8 wave vertical has a little more gain than a quarter-wave vertical, but it still radiates in all compass directions.
An isotropic antenna is a theoretical point that radiates equally in every direction. It is the reference with no gain at all.
A J pole is an omnidirectional vertical with about the gain of a half-wave antenna, well below a directional beam.
A Yagi is a beam antenna with several elements that focus the signal in one direction, giving the most gain of these four.

T9A07.concept: A vehicle's metal body acts as a shield around an antenna inside it. Much of the signal is blocked or absorbed, which is why mobile stations use an antenna mounted outside.
T9A07.hint: Think about what surrounds the radio and its antenna when you sit inside a car.
why: The metal body blocks much of the signal going out and coming in, so a handheld inside the vehicle is weaker both ways.
The problem is not antenna bandwidth. The signal is simply being blocked by the metal around the antenna.
A lower SWR (standing wave ratio, a measure of matching) would mean a better match, not a weaker signal.
The handheld does not overheat from this. The drawback is a weaker signal outside the vehicle.

T9A08.concept: An antenna works best when its length matches a fraction of the wavelength. On the 2 meter band, a quarter of the wavelength is about 19 inches, a handy size for a vertical.
T9A08.hint: Start from the band name, which gives the wavelength, and work out how 19 inches (about half a meter) compares with it.
why: A quarter-wave vertical is a basic antenna with no special gain. Its size, not gain, is the reason for 19 inches.
A half wavelength on 2 meters is about 1 meter, roughly 38 to 39 inches, twice as long as this antenna.
One quarter of 2 meters is 0.5 meter, about 19.7 inches. A practical antenna is slightly shorter, so 19 inches is a resonant quarter-wave.
RF exposure depends on power, distance and time, not on choosing a 19 inch length.

T9A09.concept: A 5/8-wavelength vertical is taller than a quarter-wave and pushes more of its signal out low toward the horizon, where distant stations are. That extra signal toward the horizon is gain.
T9A09.hint: A mobile station wants its signal to go out toward the horizon. Think about what a longer vertical does to the pattern.
why: The 5/8-wave whip concentrates more signal at low angles toward the horizon, so it has more gain than a quarter-wave.
It radiates at a lower angle, not a higher one. The lower angle is what makes it useful for mobile work.
Lower SWR (a measure of matching) is not its advantage. A 5/8-wave whip needs a matching coil to match the feed line.
Lower impedance is not the benefit described. The advantage is how the signal is concentrated toward the horizon.

T9A10.concept: A half-wave dipole radiates best at right angles to its wire and almost nothing off its ends. The pattern looks like a doughnut with the wire running through the hole.
T9A10.hint: Picture a doughnut with the antenna wire running through the hole. Where is the dough thickest?
why: A dipole is not equal in all directions. It has weak spots, called nulls, off the ends of the wire.
The ends of the wire are where the dipole radiates least. These are its nulls.
The feed line carries power to the antenna and does not set the direction of the strongest signal.
Broadside means at right angles to the wire. That is where a half-wave dipole's signal is strongest.

T9A11.concept: Antenna gain is not extra power. The antenna reshapes its pattern to send more signal one way and less another. Gain says how much stronger that favored direction is than a reference antenna.
T9A11.hint: An antenna cannot create power. Think of squeezing a balloon: it bulges out one side when pushed in on another.
why: An antenna adds no power to the transmitter. It can only redirect the power it is given.
Gain is not extra power needed at higher frequencies. That is not what the term means.
Gain is how much stronger the signal is in a chosen direction than it would be from a reference antenna, such as a dipole or isotropic.
Gain compares signal strength, not impedance (the opposition a circuit presents to alternating current).

T9B01.concept: Water inside a coax connector or cable raises loss and causes corrosion. Any connector used outdoors should be sealed with tape or other weatherproofing, whatever its type.
T9B01.hint: Think about what rain does once it gets inside a connector, and whether any connector type is safe to leave bare outdoors.
why: The PL259 is not watertight, so it needs careful taping outdoors.
The BNC, a small bayonet (push and twist) connector, should not be relied on to keep rain out, so tape it outdoors.
The Type N is made to resist moisture better than the others, but sealing it outdoors is still good practice.
All three connector types listed should be weatherproofed outdoors to keep water out of the connector and the coax.

T9B02.concept: Coaxial cable has a characteristic impedance set by its construction. Amateur transceivers and most amateur antennas are designed for 50 ohms, so 50-ohm coax is the standard.
T9B02.hint: The feed line should match what the transceiver's antenna jack is designed for. Think of the usual figure for amateur gear.
why: 8 ohms is a common loudspeaker impedance, not a coaxial cable impedance.
50 ohms matches the output of amateur transceivers, so it is the most common coax impedance in amateur stations.
600 ohms is a value associated with open-wire parallel line, not coaxial cable.
12 ohms is not a coax impedance. The number may bring to mind 12 volt power supplies, which is unrelated.

T9B03.concept: Coax keeps the signal inside its shield, so it can run along metal, through walls or be coiled without much effect. That convenience, not top performance, makes it the usual choice.
T9B03.hint: Coax is not the best at any single measure. Think about what makes something popular for everyday use.
why: The shield keeps the signal inside, so coax can be routed near metal and through walls with few special precautions.
Coax does not have the lowest loss. Open-wire parallel line, for example, has less loss than ordinary coax.
Coax is not the highest-power feed line. Power handling is not the reason it is so common.
Coax is not the cheapest feed line, and low price is not the reason it is so widely used.

T9B04.concept: A transceiver wants to see its design impedance, normally 50 ohms. An antenna tuner sits between radio and antenna system and transforms whatever impedance is there into what the radio expects.
T9B04.hint: The transmitter is happiest with one particular load. The tuner is the adapter in the middle.
why: The tuner transforms the impedance of the antenna and feed line so the transceiver sees the impedance it is designed for.
It does not tune a receiver to stations. Choosing the frequency is done by the radio's own tuning.
An antenna already works for both transmit and receive without a tuner. The radio switches between them.
Selecting an antenna for each band is the job of an antenna switch, not an antenna tuner.

T9B05.concept: Coax loss rises with frequency. The same cable that loses little on HF can lose a large share of the signal at UHF, so higher bands need better cable or shorter runs.
T9B05.hint: Think about why operators on UHF pay more attention to cable quality and length than operators on HF.
why: Characteristic impedance is set by the cable's dimensions and insulation. It does not drop as frequency rises.
Loss goes the other way. Higher frequencies lose more signal in the same length of cable.
Characteristic impedance stays essentially the same across frequency. A 50-ohm cable stays 50 ohms.
More of the signal turns to heat in the conductors and insulation as frequency goes up, so loss increases.

T9B06.concept: Connectors that work well on HF can cause loss and mismatch at UHF. The Type N connector is built to keep a constant impedance, so it performs well above 400 MHz.
T9B06.hint: At UHF a connector must hold a steady impedance or it causes loss. Ask which of these was designed with that in mind.
why: The PL-259 is fine at HF and VHF, but its impedance is not constant, so it is a poorer choice above 400 MHz.
The Type N keeps a constant impedance and low loss at UHF and higher, and it resists moisture.
RS-213 is not an RF connector type. The similar name RG-213 is a kind of coaxial cable.
The DB-25 is a 25-pin data connector for computer and control cables, not an RF connector.

T9B07.concept: The PL-259 is the threaded plug found on most HF and many VHF radios, often called a UHF connector despite working poorly at UHF. It screws on and is not sealed against water.
T9B07.hint: Think of the screw-on plug on the back of most base and mobile radios, and which bands those radios cover.
why: The PL-259 is a poor choice for microwaves. Type N and other constant-impedance connectors are used there.
The PL-259 is not watertight, which is why it must be sealed when used outdoors.
The PL-259 is the usual connector on HF and many VHF radios and antennas.
The PL-259 screws on with a threaded shell. The bayonet (push and twist) connector is the BNC.

T9B08.concept: Feed line loss is transmitter power turned to heat before reaching the antenna. Wet connectors, a poor match and every extra connector in the line each add some loss.
T9B08.hint: Consider each item separately and ask whether it would waste some of the signal on the way to the antenna.
why: Water in a connector causes corrosion and can soak into the cable, which raises loss.
With high SWR (a poor match), power reflects back and forth along the line and more of it is lost as heat.
Each connector adds a small loss and a possible bad contact, so several in one line add up.
Water intrusion, high SWR and multiple connectors are all real sources of feed line loss.

T9B09.concept: SWR depends on the match between feed line and antenna. If the reading jumps around, something in the antenna system is changing, and the usual cause is an intermittent connection.
T9B09.hint: SWR reflects the physical state of the antenna and feed line. What could make that state change from moment to moment?
why: A thunderstorm causes static noise in the receiver, but it does not change the match of your antenna system.
A loose connection makes and breaks contact, so the load on the line keeps changing and the SWR reading jumps.
Over-modulation distorts the transmitted signal and makes it too wide. It does not change the antenna match.
Overload from a strong local station is a receiver problem, not a change in SWR.

T9B10.concept: RG-58 is thin, flexible coax; RG-213 is much thicker. Both are 50 ohms, but the larger conductors of the thick cable waste less signal and carry more power.
T9B10.hint: One of these cables is about twice as thick as the other. Think about what larger conductors do to wasted signal.
why: The difference is significant. Over a long run or at VHF and UHF, the thin cable loses much more signal.
Two shields is not what separates these cables. The difference that matters is size and loss.
RG-213 is the thicker cable with larger conductors, so it loses less signal at any given frequency.
This is reversed. The thicker RG-213 handles more power than the thin RG-58.

T9B11.concept: Much of a cable's loss comes from the insulation between its conductors and from small conductors. Hardline has a large solid shield and mostly air inside, so very little signal is lost.
T9B11.hint: Think about which material between the conductors would waste the least signal, and which cable has the largest conductors.
why: 50-ohm flexible coax uses solid or foam plastic insulation and a braided shield, which lose more than hardline.
Multi-conductor unbalanced cable is not a low-loss RF feed line and is not what the question describes.
Air is a nearly lossless insulator, and hardline has large solid conductors, so it has the lowest loss of these.
75-ohm flexible coax is still flexible coax with plastic insulation, so it loses more than air-insulated hardline.

T9B12.concept: SWR compares the load, usually the antenna, with the feed line. A perfect match is 1:1 and all power is accepted. The worse the match, the more power reflects back and the higher the SWR.
T9B12.hint: SWR arises when some power bounces back from the far end of the feed line. What decides how much bounces?
why: SWR shows how closely the load impedance matches the feed line. A reading of 1:1 is a perfect match.
The ratio of amplifier output power to input power is the amplifier's gain, not SWR.
Transmitter efficiency compares RF power out with DC power in. It has nothing to do with standing waves.
SWR does not measure the quality of the station ground. It describes the match on the feed line.

T0A01.concept: A storage battery holds a lot of energy at low voltage. The voltage is too low to push much current through dry skin, but a metal path across the terminals lets a huge current flow at once.
T0A01.hint: Think about what happens when a wrench falls across both posts of a car battery. Is the danger the voltage or the current?
why: Twelve volts is normally too low to drive a harmful current through dry, unbroken skin, so shock is not the hazard this question is after.
A direct metal path lets hundreds of amperes flow. That heats metal red hot, can start a fire, and can make the battery burst.
Radio signals do not make battery electrolyte give off poison gas. This is not a real hazard.
Only the short-circuit hazard is real here. The shock and poison gas items are false, so not every choice is correct.

T0A02.concept: The body runs on tiny electrical signals. Outside current passing through it can cook tissue, upset the signals cells use, and make muscles clamp, including the heart and the hand gripping a wire.
T0A02.hint: Consider more than one kind of harm: heat, the body's own electrical signalling, and what muscles do when current hits them.
why: Current flowing through the resistance of the body makes heat, which can burn tissue inside and out.
Nerves and the heart work by small electrical signals, and outside current can upset them.
Current makes muscles tighten on their own, which can stop you letting go of a live wire.
Heating, disrupted cell function and involuntary muscle contraction are all real effects of current in the body.

T0A03.concept: US house wiring uses colour to mark each wire's job: black for hot (the wire that carries voltage from the panel), white for neutral (the return), and green or bare for safety ground.
T0A03.hint: Three wires, three colours, three jobs. Recall which colours mark the return wire and the safety wire, then see which job is left.
why: Neutral, the return wire, has white insulation in US wiring.
Black marks the hot wire, the one that carries the 120 volts from the panel and can shock you.
The equipment ground, the safety wire tied to the metal case, is green or bare copper.
Negative is a DC term, as on a battery. AC house wiring has hot and neutral, not positive and negative.

T0A04.concept: A fuse is a deliberate weak link: a thin strip of metal that melts and opens the circuit when too much current flows, before wires or parts overheat.
T0A04.hint: A fuse is a thin piece of metal placed in the path of the current. Ask what happens to it when far too much current flows.
why: Ripple is leftover AC on a DC supply. Filter capacitors smooth it; a fuse does nothing about it.
When current goes above the fuse rating, the fuse element melts and breaks the circuit, cutting off power.
A fuse does not limit normal current, and a current far below its rating can still give a dangerous shock.
Only removing power on overload is true. The ripple and shock-prevention items are false.

T0A05.concept: A fuse is sized to open before the wiring and parts it protects get too hot. A bigger fuse lets far more current flow through a circuit that was only built for the smaller amount.
T0A05.hint: The fuse rating is matched to what the wiring and device can stand. What does the circuit go through while a bigger fuse stays intact?
why: The opposite is true. A fuse rated for more current is less likely to blow, which is exactly the problem.
Ripple is leftover AC on a DC supply and has nothing to do with the fuse rating.
Up to four times the intended current could flow without the fuse opening, overheating wires and parts until something burns.
A fuse drops almost no voltage, and a higher-rated one drops even less. Low voltage is not the risk.

T0A06.concept: Shock protection comes in layers: a ground wire on every piece of AC gear, all the cases tied to one ground so no voltage appears between them, and no stored charge left inside before you reach in.
T0A06.hint: Think of every way voltage could reach your hands: through a metal case, between two pieces of gear, or from parts that hold a charge.
why: The third wire grounds the metal case, so a fault inside trips the breaker instead of making the case live.
With every case tied to one ground, the cases stay at the same voltage, so touching two at once does not put a voltage across you.
Capacitors store charge, so high-voltage ones can shock you long after the power is off.
Three-wire cords, a common safety ground and discharged high-voltage capacitors are all good shock protection.

T0A07.concept: A lightning arrester sends a surge on the coax to ground. It works best where the cables come into the house, on a grounded plate, so the surge is diverted before it gets inside.
T0A07.hint: You want the surge sent to earth before it reaches your equipment or your living space. Where on the cable run is the last chance for that?
why: At the radio the surge has already travelled through the house, and there is no good earth connection there.
The antenna feed point is high in the air, far from a short path to earth, and the surge would still follow the coax down.
The AC service panel is for house power wiring. The coax feed line does not pass through it.
A grounded panel at the entry point gives the surge a short path to earth before the coax comes indoors.

T0A08.concept: A fuse or breaker must sit in the path of the current (in series) on the hot wire, so that when it opens, the equipment is cut off from the voltage source.
T0A08.hint: When the protective device opens, you want nothing downstream left connected to the voltage. Which wire brings the voltage in?
why: In series, all the current passes through the fuse, and opening the hot wire removes the voltage from everything after it.
If the neutral opened while the hot stayed connected, the equipment would look dead but still be live.
In parallel, the fuse would sit beside the load instead of in its path, so blowing it would not stop the current.
A parallel connection does not sit in the path of the current, so it cannot interrupt the circuit on either wire.

T0A09.concept: Bonding means joining grounds with a heavy conductor. If every ground rod is tied together, they all rise and fall in voltage together, so no dangerous difference appears between them.
T0A09.hint: During a lightning strike, two separate earth connections can sit at very different voltages. How would you stop a difference from forming?
why: Sealing with caulk or tape is not the rule here, and it does nothing to keep the grounds at the same voltage.
Distance between rods does not make them safe. Unconnected rods can still be at different voltages during a strike.
Tying all the grounds together with heavy wire or strap keeps them at the same voltage, so current does not flow through your gear.
Resonance is an antenna idea. Safety ground rods are not tuned to any frequency.

T0A10.concept: Moving energy in or out of a battery too fast turns part of it into heat inside the cells. The chemistry can also release gas, which may be flammable or build up pressure.
T0A10.hint: Pushing a lot of current through a battery quickly wastes some energy inside it. What form does that wasted energy take?
why: High current heats the cells and can drive gas out of them, which can lead to fire or a burst battery.
Ripple is leftover AC on the output of a power supply. It is not a battery hazard.
Electric shock is not what fast charging or discharging causes. The danger from high battery current is heat, gas and fire.
Overvoltage is not what the question describes. The danger from high current is heat and gas.

T0A11.concept: A capacitor stores electric charge like a small tank. The filter capacitors in a power supply can stay charged, sometimes at high voltage, after the supply is switched off or unplugged.
T0A11.hint: Which part inside a power supply has the job of storing energy, and does it empty itself the instant the switch goes off?
why: Circulating currents in the DC filter is not a real hazard once the power is off.
Leakage flux is stray magnetism from a transformer while it runs. It is not a shock hazard after switch-off.
Kickback diodes absorb the spike from a relay coil. They are not a hazard left behind in a power supply.
Filter capacitors can hold their charge after power is removed, so touching them can still give a shock.

T0A12.concept: A meter and its probes have a maximum voltage they can safely stand. Above that, the insulation can break down and the voltage can reach your hands.
T0A12.hint: The only things between your hands and the circuit are the meter and its probes. What would you check about them first?
why: A voltmeter should have very high impedance (opposition to current) so it barely loads the circuit. Low impedance is wrong.
The meter and leads must be built for that voltage, or their insulation can fail and expose you to it.
A circuit should never be grounded through the meter. That would send current through the meter and could be dangerous.
A voltmeter has no frequency setting to match. This is not a high-voltage precaution.

T0B01.concept: Lightning is a very fast, very large pulse of current. It follows the easiest path, so a ground wire should run to earth by the shortest, straightest route.
T0B01.hint: Picture a huge, sudden rush of current looking for earth. What shape of path would it follow most easily?
why: A drip loop sheds water from a feed line entering a building. In a ground wire it only adds length and bends.
Bends at right angles are bad for lightning grounds. The fast pulse resists turning corners and may jump off the wire.
A short, direct run gives lightning the easiest path to earth, so it is less likely to go somewhere else.
Only short, direct connections is good practice. The drip loop and right-angle bend items are not.

T0B02.concept: A fall from a tower can easily be fatal, so climbing depends on three things together: knowing how, wearing proper fall-protection gear, and staying attached to the tower the whole time.
T0B02.hint: Think about what a climber needs in skill, in equipment and in habit. Is any one of them enough alone?
why: Climbing safely is a learned skill, and training comes before the first climb.
Staying tied off means a slip at any moment is caught, including while moving up or down.
An approved harness is made and tested to hold a falling person without injuring them.
Training, constant tie-off and an approved harness are all required when climbing a tower.

T0B03.concept: A climber who is hurt, stuck or hanging in a harness cannot help themselves. Someone on the ground must always be there to watch, assist and call for help.
T0B03.hint: Imagine something goes wrong while you are up there and cannot get down. Who knows about it?
why: A fall or injury can happen with no electrical work at all, so this does not make climbing alone safe.
Climbing itself is the risk, whatever the job at the top, so this does not make climbing alone safe.
A fall from well under 20 feet can kill or cripple. No height limit makes climbing alone safe.
It is never safe to climb without a helper or observer who can assist and summon help.

T0B04.concept: Power lines are among the deadliest hazards in antenna work. A tower, mast or antenna that touches one becomes live, along with anyone holding it.
T0B04.hint: Before raising a tall metal object, look around and above the site. What nearby thing could kill you on contact?
why: A wrist strap protects sensitive electronic parts from static at a workbench. It is not a tower safety item.
A tower base should be well grounded, not insulated. Insulating it does not prevent lightning strikes.
Contact between a tower or antenna and an overhead power wire can electrocute everyone touching it, so find the wires and stay clear.
Only staying clear of overhead wires is a real precaution. The wrist strap and insulated base items are false.

T0B05.concept: A turnbuckle is a threaded fitting that tightens a guy line by turning. Wind makes the line shake, and shaking can slowly turn it. A wire threaded through it stops it from rotating.
T0B05.hint: A turnbuckle tightens by being turned. What could make it turn by itself over months of wind?
why: A thin safety wire is not strong enough to hold a guy line if the turnbuckle broke. That is not its job.
The wire passes through the turnbuckle so it cannot rotate, which stops vibration from slowly unscrewing it.
Lightning grounding is done with heavy conductors and ground rods at the base, not with a turnbuckle safety wire.
Guy tension is checked with a separate gauge or method. The safety wire measures nothing.

T0B06.concept: Plan for the worst case: the antenna or mast falling over in any direction. Even then, nothing should be able to reach the power wires, with a margin of 10 feet to spare.
T0B06.hint: Do not think only about where the antenna stands. Think about everywhere it could land if it came down.
why: This multiply-by-1.5 formula is not a real rule and is not what the question describes.
The height of the power line alone ignores how tall the antenna and its support are, so it does not guarantee clearance.
Wavelength affects how an antenna works, not how far its parts can reach when it falls.
If no part of a falling antenna can come within 10 feet of the power wires, it stays clear of them even in the worst case.

T0B07.concept: A crank-up tower is made of sections that slide inside each other and are held up by a cable. If the cable lets go, the sections drop and act like a guillotine on hands and feet.
T0B07.hint: The sections of this tower slide past each other and are held up by a cable. Picture standing on it when that cable fails.
why: There is no safety rule against painting a crank-up tower.
Every tower should be grounded. A rule against grounding would be dangerous and is false.
Fully lowered, or with locks holding the sections, they cannot slide down and crush a climber if the cable fails.
Only the climbing rule is real. The never-paint and never-ground items are false.

T0B08.concept: A tower is a prime lightning target, so it needs several low-resistance paths to earth: a long rod at each leg, with the rods and the tower all joined together.
T0B08.hint: A tower has more than one leg, and lightning carries enormous current. Would you give it one small path to earth or several large ones?
why: One short four-foot rod is far too little earth contact to carry lightning current safely.
An RF choke opposes fast-changing current, so it would block lightning from reaching ground. That is the opposite of what is needed.
A water pipe is not a proper tower ground. It may not reach earth well, and it would lead lightning into the house.
An eight-foot rod at each leg, all bonded to the tower and to each other, spreads the current into the earth by several paths.

T0B09.concept: Utility poles carry high-voltage wires at the top. Any antenna or wire fixed to the pole can touch them or be touched by a broken line, and it is not your pole to use.
T0B09.hint: Look at what else is mounted on that pole, and at what would happen if your wire came loose near it.
why: Poor antenna performance is not the reason. The question is about a danger to life.
An antenna cannot unbalance a power transformer. This is not a real effect.
An antenna or its wires touching a high-voltage line can become live and kill you or someone else.
Only contact with high-voltage lines is a real reason. The induced-voltage and transformer items are false.

T0B10.concept: Lightning current rises so fast that even a small kink in a wire opposes it. At a sharp corner the current may leap off the wire and arc to something nearby.
T0B10.hint: Think of a fast car on a road. What kind of road shape makes it leave the road?
why: Lightning ground wire may be bare or insulated. Requiring only non-insulated wire is not a real rule.
Bends at right angles are exactly what to avoid, since the lightning pulse may jump off the wire at the corner.
Gentle, sweeping curves keep the path easy for the fast pulse, so the current stays in the wire all the way to earth.
Grounds should be bonded together into a common ground, not kept apart.

T0B11.concept: Grounding is an electrical safety matter, and electrical safety for buildings and structures is set by the electrical code your local government has adopted, not by the radio regulator.
T0B11.hint: Ask who inspects the wiring when a house is built. The same kind of authority covers grounding of structures.
why: FCC Part 97 governs how amateur stations operate. It does not set tower grounding requirements.
The electrical code in force where you live sets the grounding requirements for towers and antennas.
FAA rules cover marking and lighting of tall structures for aircraft safety, not grounding.
UL is a product safety testing body. Its practices are not what sets tower grounding requirements.

T0C01.concept: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. Radio waves have far too little energy per wave packet to do that, whatever the transmitter power, so they are in the other family.
T0C01.hint: Radiation comes in two families, split by whether it can strip electrons from atoms. Where do radio waves sit compared with X-rays?
why: Gamma rays are very high-energy rays from radioactive material, far above radio waves in frequency.
Ionizing radiation can strip electrons from atoms. Radio waves do not have enough energy to do that.
Alpha radiation is particles thrown out by radioactive atoms, not an electromagnetic wave at all.
Radio waves cannot strip electrons from atoms, so they are non-ionizing. Their main effect on the body is heating.

T0C02.concept: Maximum permissible exposure (MPE) is the limit on RF field strength for people. The body absorbs RF best in the VHF range, where it acts like a resonant antenna, so the limit is strictest there.
T0C02.hint: The limit is tightest where the human body soaks up RF most easily. Think about which wavelengths are closest to the size of a person.
why: At 3.5 MHz the wavelength is much longer than a body, absorption is weaker, and the allowed exposure is higher.
50 MHz lies in the VHF range where the body absorbs RF most efficiently, so the allowed exposure is lowest.
At 440 MHz the body absorbs less efficiently than at VHF, so the allowed exposure is higher than at 50 MHz.
At 1296 MHz the allowed exposure is higher than at 50 MHz, because it is well above the body's resonant range.

T0C03.concept: Duty cycle is the fraction of time the transmitter is on. RF limits are based on exposure averaged over time, so transmitting half the time gives half the average, leaving room for twice the level.
T0C03.hint: The limit is on the average over time. If the signal is only there half the time, how does the allowed level while it is on compare?
why: A factor of 3 does not match the numbers. Halving the on-time changes the average by a factor of 2, not 3.
This is backwards. Less transmitting time lowers the average exposure, so the allowed level goes up, not down.
100 percent divided by 50 percent is 2. Half the on-time means half the average, so twice the power density is allowed.
An adjustment is allowed, because the limits are based on exposure averaged over time.

T0C04.concept: The RF a person receives depends on how strong the field is where they stand and how well the body absorbs it. Power, frequency, distance and the direction the antenna beams all change that.
T0C04.hint: Picture a person standing near an antenna. List everything about the signal, the antenna and where they stand that changes what reaches them.
why: More power means a stronger field, and the body absorbs some frequencies more than others.
The field weakens quickly as you move away from the antenna.
An antenna sends more energy in some directions than others, so it matters where the person is.
Frequency, power, distance and the antenna's radiation pattern all affect a person's RF exposure.

T0C05.concept: The body takes in RF energy best when the wavelength is close to body size, much like a tuned antenna. Limits are set tighter at those frequencies and looser where absorption is weaker.
T0C05.hint: An antenna picks up best at the frequency that matches its size. Could a human body behave in a similar way?
why: This is not the reason the limits vary. The limits follow how well the body absorbs each frequency.
This is false. Lower frequency fields do enter the body, they are just absorbed less efficiently.
Higher frequency fields are not transient, meaning short-lived, by nature. This is not a real effect.
Absorption depends on frequency, so the limit is strictest where the body takes in the most energy.

T0C06.concept: You must be able to show your station meets the RF exposure limits. The FCC accepts several ways of doing that: working it out from published guidance, modelling it, or measuring it.
T0C06.hint: There are two broad approaches to finding a field strength: working it out on paper or by computer, and going out with instruments.
why: FCC OET Bulletin 65 gives formulas and tables for estimating RF exposure from a station.
Antenna modelling software can calculate the field strength around your antenna.
A calibrated field strength meter measures the actual field directly.
Calculation from OET Bulletin 65, computer modelling and calibrated measurement are all accepted methods.

T0C07.concept: RF current heats whatever it flows through. Skin touching an antenna that is transmitting takes that current at one small spot, which heats fast and burns, even at modest power.
T0C07.hint: RF energy's main effect on the body is heating. What would concentrated heating at one small point of contact do?
why: Electrocution is not the hazard this question describes. RF on an antenna injures by heating at the point of contact.
RF current entering the skin at the contact point heats it quickly and causes a painful burn that can be deep.
Radio signals are non-ionizing. An antenna does not give off ionizing radiation.
Only the RF burn is correct. The electrocution and ionizing radiation items are not, so not every choice is correct.

T0C08.concept: The antenna is the part that radiates. Exposure falls quickly with distance, so putting the antenna higher or farther from people is the most direct way to cut what reaches them.
T0C08.hint: Find the part of the station the radio energy actually leaves from, then think about where people are in relation to it.
why: Moving the antenna higher or farther away puts more distance between people and the source of the field.
The transmitter box is not what radiates. Moving it while the antenna stays put does not change the field near people.
Raising the duty cycle means transmitting a larger share of the time, which increases average exposure.
Only relocating antennas reduces exposure. Moving the transmitter does not, and a higher duty cycle makes it worse.

T0C09.concept: An RF exposure evaluation is only valid for the station as it was evaluated. Change the power, band, feed line, antenna or its position and the fields around it change too.
T0C09.hint: Your safety check was done for one particular setup. What happens to its conclusions when the setup is no longer the same?
why: You are not required to report station changes to the FCC. You keep the station compliant yourself.
Any change to the transmitter or antenna system can change the exposure, so the evaluation must be done again.
SWR shows how well the antenna matches the feed line. A low reading says nothing about exposure levels.
Equipment approval is about product safety. It does not show that the fields around your antenna are within limits.

T0C10.concept: RF exposure limits are based on heating, which builds up over time. So what counts is the average over several minutes, and a transmitter that is on only part of the time delivers a lower average.
T0C10.hint: The body responds to RF by slowly warming. Does a slow effect like that depend on brief instants or on the total over a period?
why: The less of the time you transmit, the lower the exposure averaged over the period, and the limits are based on that average.
The peak level is the same whenever the transmitter is on, however often that is. Duty cycle changes the average, not the peak.
Feed line loss does reduce power at the antenna, but it is a separate factor and is not what duty cycle means.
Heating inside the amplifier is an equipment matter. It has nothing to do with exposure of people.

T0C11.concept: Exposure is averaged over a set period of minutes. Duty cycle describes how much of that period the transmitter is actually putting out a signal.
T0C11.hint: The word cycle here is about time on versus time off. Decide which of those two the figure counts.
why: The gap between lowest and highest power output is not duty cycle. Duty cycle is about time, not power levels.
PEP is peak envelope power. Comparing it with average power is not the definition of duty cycle.
Duty cycle is the share of the averaging time during which the transmitter is on the air.
This is the reverse. Duty cycle counts the time spent transmitting, not the time spent silent.

T0C12.concept: Ionizing radiation, such as X-rays and radioactivity, carries enough energy to break chemical bonds and damage DNA. RF does not, but it can still harm by heating tissue.
T0C12.hint: The difference lies in what each kind can do to the molecules inside a cell, not in how far it travels or how it is measured.
why: RF cannot break chemical bonds or damage DNA. That is what separates it from ionizing radiation.
RF is measured with ordinary instruments such as field strength meters. This is not a real distinction.
RF travels great distances, which is how radio works. It is not limited to a few feet.
RF is not perfectly safe. Strong fields heat body tissue, which is why exposure limits exist.

T0C13.concept: The person whose name is on the licence answers for everything the station does, including the RF fields it creates around family, neighbours and passers-by.
T0C13.hint: Think about who controls the power, the antenna and where it is placed. Responsibility follows control.
why: The FCC sets the exposure limits, but it does not check each station. Meeting them is up to the station.
The licensee controls the station, so the licensee must make sure nobody is exposed above the limits.
People nearby usually have no idea when or how the station transmits, so they cannot be the responsible party.
A zoning board deals with land use and structures. It is not responsible for RF exposure limits.
